Researchers ask whether changing the pH of water alters where a small carboxylic acid ends up when the water is shaken with a water-immiscible organic solvent. Each vessel contains equal volumes of the two solvents at the same temperature. The aqueous layers are buffered at pH 3.8, 4.8 or 5.8. The graph shows the percentage recovered in the organic layer at each pH. Each vessel gives nearly complete recovery. column2: MCAT and USMLE::MCAT::Critical Analysis and Reasoning Skills
column4:
A city considered removing a row of benches outside its railway station. In six weeks of observation, its consultant recorded a seated occupant in only one of every ten scans. The consultant's arithmetic was impeccable. A shopkeeper, asked whether the benches were useful, answered by pointing to a woman standing at the timetable. Before the benches appeared, she said, the woman would have waited inside the shop, where a place to rest was assured. The woman had never actually sat on a bench. A councillor treated the story as an attempt to substitute sentiment for counting. That criticism goes too far. The story suggests a second count one might make: how often people who need occasional rest now choose the route past the station. It provides no count of its own, and the shopkeeper might have misread a customer's motives. Still, a measure cannot earn authority over an entire question merely by being more exact than the alternatives. Its authority extends to the thing it measures. Empty benches are excellent evidence about occupancy and rather less decisive evidence about what a street allows.

What role does the shopkeeper’s story play in the argument?
column6: It suggests a testable benefit that occupancy observations miss.
column7: The passage explicitly acknowledges uncertainty about the customer's motives.

column2: MCAT and USMLE::MCAT::Critical Analysis and Reasoning Skills
column4:
An exhibition of pottery placed two nearly identical bowls on a table near the entrance. Visitors were invited to pick them up. Most did so by slipping a thumb inside the rim and spreading the fingers underneath. Only then did a difference become apparent. One bowl tipped forward unless the hand moved toward its base. The other came to rest almost without adjustment. In the adjoining gallery a sign explained that both vessels had been made from the same drawing. One maker had thinned the clay near the foot; the other had left it there.

A critic admired the demonstration but questioned its place in an art exhibition. Balance belonged to the history of use, he wrote, and the bowls had long since ceased to carry anyone's supper. To exhibit them as works of art was precisely to release them from the demand that they perform well at a table. He would have placed them behind glass, where a viewer could attend to the very slight change of outline that the two feet produced.

His objection has some force. A comfortable grip would be an odd requirement for a vessel made to stand on an altar. Nor is there much reason to suppose that the bowl which settled most readily into the average visitor's hand was therefore the better work. But the test at the entrance did something other than rank the bowls by convenience. Having lifted one and set it down, a visitor could look again at the foot and see where the outline had led her to expect weight that was scarcely there. What her hand discovered gave her eye a question.

In the middle room the curator had tried another experiment. Here a large storage jar stood behind a barrier, beside a small dry piece of unfired clay that visitors could lift. Several visitors complained that the sample told them nothing about lifting the jar. They were right. Even an exact fragment from the jar wall would give unreliable guidance about the effort of raising the whole vessel. A sign asking visitors to imagine that effort on the strength of the sample would invite a mistake. A sign asking them to notice the texture that firing had changed would make a narrower promise, though it would also need to establish that the two clays had begun alike.

The difference between the rooms turns on the inference a visitor is asked to make. The lifted bowl can be set down and inspected again; the surprise belongs to the object now in view. The lump of clay can also surprise, but the surprise belongs initially to the lump. To carry it across the barrier to the jar takes an argument. It is no answer to announce that museums should engage all the senses. The critic, on the other hand, would remove an occasion for looking closely merely because it began with the hand. Both positions would be easier to defend if they paid less attention to counting the senses at work and more to tracing a particular observation to the thing it is supposed to illuminate.

Why does the author introduce a vessel made for an altar?
column5:
1. To show that sacred vessels typically have heavier feet.
  2. To concede a limit to convenience as a standard of artistic judgment.
  3. To suggest that the two entrance bowls were sacred objects.
  4. To concede that handling cannot aid a visual judgment.
column6: To concede a limit to convenience as a standard of artistic judgment.
column7: Ease of grip would be a poor general test of quality. The author can accept that while defending the entrance display.
column8: Original passage and item · AAMC CARS framework · https://students-residents.aamc.org/whats-mcat-exam/critical-analysis-and-reasoning-skills-section-overview

column2: MCAT and USMLE::MCAT::Critical Analysis and Reasoning Skills
column4:
The minutes of the coastal council described every decision as unanimous. This puzzled a visitor who had heard two members disagree sharply in the bakery that morning. At the evening meeting she watched the chair ask whether anyone wished to object. Nobody spoke. The minutes, she concluded, were impeccable records of a ceremony that concealed the council’s real opinions. Her conclusion attracted a local historian, who invited her to sit through a second meeting and this time to bring a watch.

At the second meeting the chair read out a proposal to replace the steps to the harbor. Several members looked down. Seven seconds passed before a boat repairer began, very softly, to describe the old steps under a high tide. Nobody interrupted. When she had finished, the chair read the proposal again, with the lowest step left in place. He asked for objections, waited and closed the item. The visitor checked the minutes afterward. They gave the repaired steps a single sentence. The interval and the repairer had disappeared together.

The historian asked the visitor when a vote had taken place. She pointed to the final silence. He pointed to the earlier one. Neither, on reflection, was prepared to call the earlier silence a vote. It had allowed someone to frame a difficulty without first declaring herself an opponent. Once she had spoken, the council faced a different question. Unanimity at the end was compatible with genuine disagreement at the start, even if every member had been entirely candid at both times.

It would be easy to turn this observation into praise of a patient chair. The historian resisted. A member who regularly needed an interpreter said that, by the time a proposal had been translated, the familiar pause was usually over. To the visitor, this sounded like evidence that the council ought to fix a longer interval. The interpreter had a different objection. Some proposals took three words to explain, others a paragraph. Adding the same number of seconds to each would sometimes give a translated objection room to develop and sometimes leave its speaker just as late as before. She wanted the chair to wait for a signal that everyone had heard the proposal, and only then begin waiting for objections.

No one suggested that the minutes should include a count of every second. A reader primarily concerned with which steps could be removed would learn little from such a table. A reader asking whose knowledge altered the decision would need something else. Recording the first wording, the later wording and the reason for the alteration would make the repairer visible. It would still reveal little about objections that had never had a chance to form. For that inquiry the visitor would need to watch when each member first had a practical opportunity to speak. The minutes had answered their own question accurately. The visitor’s error had been to think there was only one question.

Why does the repairer’s account of the high tide matter to the author’s argument?
column5:
1. It forces the chair to enter a formal objection into the published minutes.
  2. It changes the proposal before anyone is asked to approve its final wording.
  3. It establishes that the old steps were originally built without permission.
  4. It proves that every member privately favored the repairer’s alternative.
column6: It changes the proposal before anyone is asked to approve its final wording.
column7: The chair retains the lowest step after hearing the account. The final proposal differs from the initial one.

column2: MCAT and USMLE::MCAT::Critical Analysis and Reasoning Skills
column4:
A critic reviewing a comic strip about a man catching a train praised the artist for drawing an entire afternoon in three seconds. In the first panel the man was buying a ticket. In the second he stood on the platform looking at the clock. In the third he was seated by a window, holding a half-finished crossword. The critic meant that it took three seconds to look across the page. But it is doubtful whether anybody who had actually read those panels could say how much of the man's afternoon they contained.

The crossword is what makes the question interesting. We may imagine that the man began it after boarding and has been riding for some time. He may equally well have taken the paper from his coat with half the squares filled in from yesterday. A film director could withhold the same information. What is peculiar to the strip is that the reader who has reached the crossword can look back at the platform without leaving the last panel behind. The man's coat is there to be inspected. Its pockets bulge, though not in a way that settles the matter.

Some enthusiasts have suggested that the empty band between panels is where readers do the real work of imagining events. I doubt the band deserves quite so much credit. Cut the strip into separate cards and hand them over one by one. Readers will still infer that the man passed through a door to board the train, though no white band now separates two pictures. What the altered arrangement makes difficult is a different activity. To check the coat pockets a reader must ask for an earlier card, putting aside the view that gave the pockets their sudden interest.

This distinction would matter little if the artist's job were simply to reward alert readers with clues. The pockets, however, have no solution. Their usefulness lies in the brief possibility of revising what the crossword first seemed to mean. A page that permits such revision can feel unhurried even when its subject is a dash for a train. Another page can feel breathless while showing a man sitting perfectly still. The number of actions depicted will predict neither effect without some account of what it costs the eye to compare them.

For an exhibition the artist mounted the three drawings in separate rooms, with a bench in the room containing the crossword. Visitors spent longer there than they had spent reading the whole strip on paper. It is tempting to say that the exhibition had slowed the story down. It had unquestionably slowed the visitors down. But their added minutes might have been spent resting their feet, remembering the coat, or regretting that they had not looked at it more closely. The change in arrangement altered what kinds of attention were convenient. A stopwatch could report a consequence of that change without identifying the kind of attention responsible for it.

Why does the author mention that there was a bench in the final room?
column5:
1. To show that the artist expected the crossword to be solved there
  2. To establish that the room was larger than the other rooms
  3. To suggest that the exhibition improved the drawings' legibility
  4. To illustrate another possible reason for a longer visit
column6: To illustrate another possible reason for a longer visit
column7: Visitors may simply have rested. The timing measurement cannot identify what occupied their attention.
column8: Original passage and item · AAMC CARS framework · https://students-residents.aamc.org/whats-mcat-exam/critical-analysis-and-reasoning-skills-section-overview

column2: MCAT and USMLE::MCAT::Critical Analysis and Reasoning Skills
column4:
A survey of a hillside town asked residents to name the person they would consult about a difficult journey. The bus dispatcher received an astonishing number of nominations. A transport planner took the result as evidence that local knowledge was concentrated in one place. A new information service, she proposed, should begin by recording the routes the dispatcher knew. The dispatcher delighted her by agreeing to be interviewed. He perplexed her by spending most of the interview telling her whom he would telephone.

For a flooded lane he called a baker who drove through it before dawn. For an uncertain connection he asked the kiosk attendant at the lower station to look out of her window. Both people knew facts he could not supply. Neither received many nominations in the survey. The planner revised her diagnosis. The townspeople had named a well-known man out of habit and failed to recognize the real experts. If she could distribute the two workers’ numbers, residents could dispense with the dispatcher and go directly to the source.

Her assistant tried the proposal on a journey of his own. He telephoned the baker about a lane, received a precise answer, and set out. At a fork beyond the bakery he learned that the uphill bus had changed its winter timetable. The baker had given good information about the question he was asked. The assistant had chosen the wrong question to ask first. The dispatcher, hearing the destination rather than the name of the lane, would have checked the connection before troubling anyone about the road.

The survey had allowed its respondents to name only one person. From the answer the planner had first inferred possession of many facts and then mere popularity. The same answer was consistent with a third possibility. The dispatcher knew which uncertainty could make all the others irrelevant, and who could settle it cheaply. Such knowledge is hard to capture by transcribing answers to individual travel questions. It consists partly in the order in which questions deserve to be put. Nor would handing out a directory necessarily distribute it. A directory can name every witness without indicating whose testimony one needs today.

This conclusion does not establish that directing travelers to the dispatcher is always wise. During one storm his line was engaged for an hour. Several residents who knew only a single stretch of road exchanged messages and worked out a route while callers to the office were still waiting. Under ordinary conditions a single familiar contact spared travelers the effort of assembling a chain of inquiries. Under crowded conditions the same arrangement delayed them. The survey had asked whom people would consult without saying how many other people would be consulting that person at the same moment.

A more informative inquiry would preserve the planner's original question and add two observations. Follow an actual request through the people whose reports shape the eventual answer. Then see how that chain changes when many requests arrive together. Counting nominations still tells us where requests are likely to enter. That is worth knowing, provided we resist the attractive assumption that where a request enters is also where its answer resides.

What did the original survey directly record?
column5:
1. Who supplied the greatest number of independently verified route facts.
  2. How callers distributed requests during an actual storm.
  3. Whom respondents said they would approach about a difficult journey.
  4. What proportion of residents completed each proposed route.
column6: Whom respondents said they would approach about a difficult journey.
column7: A nomination identifies a proposed first contact. The survey did not follow the request further.

column2: MCAT and USMLE::MCAT::Critical Analysis and Reasoning Skills
column4:
The island ferry used to carry as many market carts as would fit, taking them in the order in which they reached the slip. Shopkeepers called this a fair arrangement. The ferryman, who saw the slip before dawn, was less sure. One cart often waited there empty. Its owner had a second cart in which his goods could be brought down once a place was secure. The shopkeeper who owned one cart had to load it before setting out. The ferryman had never seen anyone cut the line. What troubled him was how much a place at its head could already have cost.

The council introduced a book in which places for Tuesday could be claimed on Monday afternoon. The rule was one place per shop, and a place that had not been taken up by eight on Tuesday morning reverted to the queue at the slip. For several months the new arrangement did exactly what its defenders had promised. The two-cart owner stopped stationing an empty cart at the shore. A baker with one cart could finish her Monday work knowing that her flour would cross the next morning.

Then the boat arrived on a windy Tuesday with room for only six of the eight carts in the book. The ferryman carried the first six names. One of the two disappointed merchants asked why Monday afternoon's order should decide a shortage that had not existed until Tuesday. The council chairman replied that somebody must go last. The merchant agreed. He had not asked for a ninth place or even for the sixth. He wanted to know what claim each name in the book represented.

It turned out that the bakery and the fish stall had understood their entries differently. To the baker, writing her name meant being able to make a promise to a customer. She would gladly accept a later crossing if she could learn of it before taking the order. To the fish seller, a name in the book meant a release from standing about; when the boat was small he preferred places to go first to goods that would spoil. Both had signed the petition for reservations. The petition had asked whether merchants wished to stop waiting at the slip on Mondays. Nobody had asked them to settle a Tuesday in bad weather.

The council finally kept six places in the book and left two to be assigned at the slip when the larger boat arrived. This reduced the number of promises it could honor on an ordinary day. The chairman called it an expensive way of admitting that the size of a boat can vary. He was right about the expense. Yet naming the two places separately gave the islanders an advantage that his first scheme had lacked. They could now argue over which late carts should go aboard without having to discover, in the middle of an argument about fish, that they had also been arguing about the meaning of a promise.

Why did the ferryman question the fairness of the original queue?
column5:
1. The earliest merchants regularly received more deck space than the size of their carts required.
  2. A merchant with spare equipment could hold a place while goods were still being prepared.
  3. The ferryman was expected to decide which merchants could afford the crossing.
  4. Customers could prevent rival carts from being loaded by changing orders at the slip.
column6: A merchant with spare equipment could hold a place while goods were still being prepared.
column7: The empty cart effectively purchased early arrival through ownership of a second cart.

column2: MCAT and USMLE::MCAT::Critical Analysis and Reasoning Skills
column4:
Halfway through an old detective story, a woman leaves a dining room by a door that the author has forgotten to provide. I owe this discovery to a carpenter who came to our reading group once and never returned. He had drawn the house on the back of a grocery receipt. The exterior walls closed neatly, the stairs took up a credible amount of space, and the woman was apparently standing in a cupboard. The rest of us had spent the evening discussing her reasons for leaving dinner. We felt vaguely injured by the receipt.

It was suggested that an author might fairly be charged rent only for the rooms the story actually uses. Nobody had inquired where the family kept its coal. Why should anyone ask what lay beyond that particular door? The carpenter had an unexpectedly literary answer. The woman later says that she heard the last part of the dinner conversation from the passage. Whether the dining room opened onto that passage bore on the truth of what she said. Our interpretations of her conduct had quietly assumed a house in which it was possible to listen.

Over the next month our group acquired a taste for drawing plans. It was a disagreeable month. In a short story about a visit to a dying brother, we spent a quarter of an hour fitting a bathroom between a bedroom and an attic staircase. One member proposed shifting the staircase. Another abolished the bathroom. Either alteration left the visit exactly as painful as it had been before. We had learned how to find an inconsistency without learning when it cost the story anything.

I would give the carpenter's receipt a place in an edition of the detective story, though I would put it at the end. A reader should first have a chance to trust the woman. Seeing the plan in advance turns an ordinary remark about overhearing into an examination question about architecture. Read afterward, the plan gives a reader an interesting choice. One can amend the house, as an editor might amend a misspelling, and continue to believe her. Or one can let the walls stand and wonder who supplied the woman with the words she claimed to have overheard. I doubt that the author intended this choice. I find it a real one all the same.

Our carpenter sent us a note in response to the minutes of that meeting. He regretted that we had all taken the trouble to draw houses. He himself had started with the woman's assertion about hearing. A dining room door had been the cheapest part of the assertion to check. If she had claimed to recognize a distant voice, he wrote, he would have wanted the opinion of a singer. I have kept his receipt in my copy of the book. When I lend the book, I leave the receipt in its envelope, and leave the envelope unsealed.

A new story's town clock skips an hour, but no event, alibi or character's impression depends on the time. How would the narrator most likely treat the discrepancy?
column5:
1. As a reason to doubt every character in the town
  2. As a possible factual correction of limited interpretive consequence
  3. As proof that the author intended to represent grief
  4. As evidence that the book should open with a timetable
column6: As a possible factual correction of limited interpretive consequence
column7: The clock resembles the bathroom puzzle unless its timing changes something the story asks a reader to believe.

The exterior walls closed neatly, the stairs took up a credible amount of space, and the woman was apparently standing in a cupboard. The rest of us had spent the evening discussing her reasons for leaving dinner. We felt vaguely injured by the receipt.

It was suggested that an author might fairly be charged rent only for the rooms the story actually uses. Nobody had inquired where the family kept its coal. Why should anyone ask what lay beyond that particular door? The carpenter had an unexpectedly literary answer. The woman later says that she heard the last part of the dinner conversation from the passage. Whether the dining room opened onto that passage bore on the truth of what she said. Our interpretations of her conduct had quietly assumed a house in which it was possible to listen.

Over the next month our group acquired a taste for drawing plans. It was a disagreeable month. In a short story about a visit to a dying brother, we spent a quarter of an hour fitting a bathroom between a bedroom and an attic staircase. One member proposed shifting the staircase. Another abolished the bathroom. Either alteration left the visit exactly as painful as it had been before. We had learned how to find an inconsistency without learning when it cost the story anything.

I would give the carpenter's receipt a place in an edition of the detective story, though I would put it at the end. A reader should first have a chance to trust the woman. Seeing the plan in advance turns an ordinary remark about overhearing into an examination question about architecture. Read afterward, the plan gives a reader an interesting choice. One can amend the house, as an editor might amend a misspelling, and continue to believe her. Or one can let the walls stand and wonder who supplied the woman with the words she claimed to have overheard. I doubt that the author intended this choice. I find it a real one all the same.

Our carpenter sent us a note in response to the minutes of that meeting. He regretted that we had all taken the trouble to draw houses. He himself had started with the woman's assertion about hearing. A dining room door had been the cheapest part of the assertion to check. If she had claimed to recognize a distant voice, he wrote, he would have wanted the opinion of a singer. I have kept his receipt in my copy of the book. When I lend the book, I leave the receipt in its envelope, and leave the envelope unsealed.

  3. It makes the drawing of the exterior easier to reconcile with the scale of the plan.
  4. It gives an independent way to estimate how long the visitor remained indoors.

column2: MCAT and USMLE::MCAT::Critical Analysis and Reasoning Skills
column4:
A fishing town tried selling the day's catch without attaching the boat's name to the boxes. The auctioneer called it an experiment in judging fish by fish. For years, a few boats had fetched high prices even on mornings when their catches looked much like their neighbors'. Buyers said that the difference was deserved. The crews of those boats packed their fish in ice sooner. By noon a difference invisible at the quay would become obvious in a shop. Crews without a famous name had a different complaint. Cooling their own fish just as quickly did them little good if no buyer would look in their direction.

During the trial the auctioneer gave each box a number. A buyer could open a box, examine its contents and pay whatever seemed fitting. The harbor office kept the list of numbers and boats so that a shop could still report a spoiled purchase. On the first morning, the range of prices narrowed. Some crews hailed the change as proof that their better-known neighbors had been selling an expensive name. Their neighbors pointed to the very same figures as proof that careful work went unrewarded once its author was hidden.

A reporter proposed to settle the matter by visiting the shops that afternoon. If fish from the famous boats kept better, surely that would vindicate the old prices. The visits would certainly be worth making. But suppose she did find such a difference. She would have learned something about the information a name had carried before the trial. She would still know little about what an unfamiliar crew could accomplish under arrangements that allowed it to profit from equally careful work. For that question, the morning of the change was a particularly bad day to choose. Every box then on sale had been packed under habits formed during the old auction.

The harbor office eventually offered an additional service. Buyers could request a record of afternoon inspections for the last ten boxes packed by any crew, identified by a persistent code. After several months, a crew with a poor early record began fetching higher prices following a run of favorable inspections. The auctioneer celebrated the return of judgment by particulars. Yet no buyer who consulted the record was judging one box by its contents alone. Ten previous boxes had entered the bargain too.

It would be a mistake to treat that dependence as an embarrassment. A shop buying at dawn needs evidence about a condition it will face at noon. The choice at the quay is partly a choice about which histories deserve to travel with a box. A familiar name carries a history whose beginning may be beyond anyone's memory and whose errors may be costly to challenge. A short inspection record can be revised by later catches, although it too may mislead when an inspector visits one shop much later in the day than another. Asking how a history can be corrected gives the town a more useful question than asking how to dispense with history altogether.

Which difficulty facing shopkeepers gives past observations their value in the passage?
column5:
1. The auctioneer fixes a price before anyone can open a box.
  2. The harbor office refuses to identify spoiled purchases.
  3. The condition important to a shop becomes fully apparent after the auction.
  4. The quantity in a box can be measured only at the shop.
column6: The condition important to a shop becomes fully apparent after the auction.
column7: The shop buys at dawn and cares about how the fish keep until noon.

column4:
A fishing town tried selling the day's catch without attaching the boat's name to the boxes. The auctioneer called it an experiment in judging fish by fish. For years, a few boats had fetched high prices even on mornings when their catches looked much like their neighbors'. Buyers said that the difference was deserved. The crews of those boats packed their fish in ice sooner. By noon a difference invisible at the quay would become obvious in a shop. Crews without a famous name had a different complaint. Cooling their own fish just as quickly did them little good if no buyer would look in their direction.

During the trial the auctioneer gave each box a number. A buyer could open a box, examine its contents and pay whatever seemed fitting. The harbor office kept the list of numbers and boats so that a shop could still report a spoiled purchase. On the first morning, the range of prices narrowed. Some crews hailed the change as proof that their better-known neighbors had been selling an expensive name. Their neighbors pointed to the very same figures as proof that careful work went unrewarded once its author was hidden.

A reporter proposed to settle the matter by visiting the shops that afternoon. If fish from the famous boats kept better, surely that would vindicate the old prices. The visits would certainly be worth making. But suppose she did find such a difference. She would have learned something about the information a name had carried before the trial. She would still know little about what an unfamiliar crew could accomplish under arrangements that allowed it to profit from equally careful work. For that question, the morning of the change was a particularly bad day to choose. Every box then on sale had been packed under habits formed during the old auction.

The harbor office eventually offered an additional service. Buyers could request a record of afternoon inspections for the last ten boxes packed by any crew, identified by a persistent code. After several months, a crew with a poor early record began fetching higher prices following a run of favorable inspections. The auctioneer celebrated the return of judgment by particulars. Yet no buyer who consulted the record was judging one box by its contents alone. Ten previous boxes had entered the bargain too.

It would be a mistake to treat that dependence as an embarrassment. A shop buying at dawn needs evidence about a condition it will face at noon. The choice at the quay is partly a choice about which histories deserve to travel with a box. A familiar name carries a history whose beginning may be beyond anyone's memory and whose errors may be costly to challenge. A short inspection record can be revised by later catches, although it too may mislead when an inspector visits one shop much later in the day than another. Asking how a history can be corrected gives the town a more useful question than asking how to dispense with history altogether.

Why can both groups of crews appeal to the narrowing of prices on the first morning?

1. Either fairer bidding or poorer information could narrow the spread.
  2. It shows buyers knew more about the day’s catch once boat names disappeared.
  3. It shows each numbered lot contained fish of much the same quality.
  4. The numbered auction and the ten-box inspection record started on the same morning.
column6: Either fairer bidding or poorer information could narrow the spread.
column7: Removing a name could suppress an unwarranted premium or erase informative differences. The price spread alone fits either account.

column2: MCAT and USMLE::MCAT::Critical Analysis and Reasoning Skills
column4:
At the first rehearsal of a dance that had gone unperformed for thirty years, two dancers reached the far corner of the stage on different feet. The video from the original production was quite clear. In it the leading dancer arrived on her left. The rehearsal director let the difference pass. Ten minutes later he stopped the music because the following dancer had looked up a fraction too soon. An observer might reasonably have wondered how the director could be so generous about a whole step and so exacting about a glance.

The director later offered an explanation. In that passage the follower was to change direction only after noticing that the leader had turned. If she lifted her eyes early, she appeared to know what was coming. Her subsequent turn would then look like obedience to a count. When she looked up later, the same turn could look like a discovery. As for the foot, the new leader had a longer stride than the original one. Insisting on the left would have made him shorten the last step so conspicuously that the audience might have taken the adjustment for a hesitation.

It would be easy to say that the director preserved the spirit of the dance by departing from its letter. But this formula is too hospitable. Almost any departure can find lodging in a word as spacious as spirit. The delayed glance was a small, observable requirement, as much a part of the letter as the foot in the recording. What the director supplied was a reason for insisting on one visible detail while allowing another to vary. That reason could be challenged. Someone might watch both versions and find that the earlier glance made no perceptible difference, or that an arrival on the right turned the leader's shoulders away from the follower and made the encounter unreadable.

A former member of the company objected that the glance had never been discussed when the dance was new. This is important testimony about what the original dancers were told. It is less decisive about what their performances accomplished. Two dancers who have worked together for years may arrive at a timing neither has ever needed to name. Conversely, a director who speaks at length about discovery may be unable to produce anything onstage beyond two people turning on cue. An explanation acquires no authority merely by being eloquent, any more than it loses all authority because it came late.

A rehearsal is unusually well equipped to settle the narrower dispute. The dancers can alter the glance while leaving the approach substantially intact. They can also let the leader arrive on either foot and ask watchers what, if anything, becomes harder to see. Such trials will not retrieve everything an audience saw thirty years ago. They can establish whether the director's distinctions do any work in the production being made today. That is a modest claim for a revival. It is also more demanding than tracing a sequence of footprints.

Which claim best captures the author’s position on reviving the dance?
column5:
1. Every observable difference from the recording requires the same justification.
  2. A choice about which details to preserve should be answerable to what spectators can perceive.
  3. Original performers alone can distinguish a choreographic requirement from an accident.
  4. The most faithful revival is the one that changes the fewest audience expectations.
column6: A choice about which details to preserve should be answerable to what spectators can perceive.
column7: The author wants reasons for differential treatment of details and proposes testing the perceptual consequences.

column2: MCAT and USMLE::MCAT::Critical Analysis and Reasoning Skills
column4:
A town hires temporary workers to paint its schools every summer. For years the foreman interviewed applicants in the order in which they arrived on the first Monday of April. It was a clean arrangement in one respect. Anyone could look out of the window and tell whose turn came next. It was a troublesome arrangement in another. The earliest bus reached town at six, by which time people who owned cars or lived nearby had sometimes filled the first day's sheet. No applicant was denied an interview, but the last interviews commonly took place after most of the jobs had been promised.

The town clerk proposed drawing lots for interview times. At a public meeting she described the draw as a way of giving the same chance to every name in the box. A retired painter objected that the jobs belonged to people, not to slips of paper. He knew a father who could come to an interview only before his morning shift. The draw might assign the father an afternoon or might give him six in the morning. Calling the two slips equally good, the painter said, was a privilege available only to the box.

During the first summer of the draw the clerk allowed people to exchange times in pairs. She kept a careful account. A surprising number of interviews took place on the day originally assigned, and she took this as evidence that the painter had exaggerated the trouble. He asked to see her ledger. Two applicants who had attended on their appointed days, he discovered, had hired a neighbor to watch their children. Another had forfeited half a shift. They had adapted themselves to their appointments, exactly as the clerk said. The ledger told her little about what the adapting had cost.

The painter's objection to the ledger does not settle the merits of the draw. Under the old rule the man who slept in his car outside the office also paid a price that no one entered in a book. Moreover, the first people in the line had not necessarily been the best painters. Something had to determine whom the foreman saw first. A queue and a drawing each made one consideration visible and left several others for applicants to manage as best they could.

For the next summer the clerk kept the draw but asked each applicant in advance for the hours during which an interview was possible. She promised to draw among applicants available for a particular time. She also began recording how many competitors each time had attracted. A neighbor of the retired painter called this an admirably simple solution. The painter disagreed. His point had been that an interview at six and one at two might have different values. The new ledger, at last, gave him a chance to see just how many people were bidding for each. He was willing to call that an improvement. Whether the resulting differences were fair was a question he wanted to put to the next public meeting.

Why is the arrival time of the first bus relevant to the old hiring system?
column5:
1. Interviewers were recruited from among the bus passengers.
  2. Bus fares had to be paid out of the foreman's hiring budget.
  3. Bus riders had no chance at the earliest interview slots.
  4. Every applicant arriving after six lost the right to an interview.
column6: Bus riders had no chance at the earliest interview slots.
column7: Transport affected position in line, and available jobs dwindled during the interviews.

column2: MCAT and USMLE::MCAT::Critical Analysis and Reasoning Skills
column4:
At the first performance of a new comedy, a guest asked the playwright why she had put the best joke on the poster. Anyone who had passed the theater knew what the porter would say when the principal guest finally arrived. The playwright offered a ticket for the following evening on the condition that her critic sit among people who had already seen the play. He accepted, partly because he imagined that an audience deprived of its surprise would save him the trouble of making his case.

On the second evening the laughter began before the porter spoke. As he took an extraordinary time to straighten a dish on the hall table, someone in the gallery started to chuckle. When the line came, the house laughed again. The critic now conceded that a joke could survive foreknowledge. What he had heard, he said, was the agreeable recognition one feels on meeting an old friend. The playwright did not dispute the pleasure of recognition. She asked what, on his account, the porter had been doing with the dish.

The dish mattered because his hands had work his position forbade his voice to do. He wanted the distinguished visitor to wait, but could scarcely order a man of that rank to stand in the doorway. Straightening something that was already straight gave him a fragment of authority. The spectator waiting for the familiar line could watch that authority change hands. A newcomer searching for the likely speaker might miss the change entirely. The joke on the poster disclosed the words. It did not disclose what the actor would manage to do before he said them.

There is a temptation here to promote all second performances above all first ones. On her way home the playwright supplied a reason to resist it. Earlier that evening another actor had dropped a glove, apparently by accident. The porter had caught it without interrupting his speech. On learning later that the catch was rehearsed, the critic admitted that part of his pleasure had vanished. What had delighted him had been the apparent rescue of a scene from a mishap. He could still admire the skill of the catch, but rehearsal had changed the deed he understood himself to have witnessed.

The two incidents put different demands on ignorance. In the business with the dish, knowing the destination freed the spectator to examine the journey. In the business with the glove, believing that the actor had no map was part of what made the journey exciting. We should therefore ask a narrower question than whether publicity spoils a comedy. Which pleasure depends on the audience holding a particular belief about what can happen next? A producer who answers that question may decide to print a line in large letters and keep silent about a falling glove. Both decisions could express equal confidence in the actors.

Why does the playwright ask what the porter was doing with the dish?
column5:
1. The critic has mistaken which performer delivered the familiar line.
  2. Recognition of familiar words alone cannot account for the interest of his delay.
  3. The porter has silently substituted a different ending for the printed one.
  4. The dish is evidence that the audience misheard the punch line.
column6: Recognition of familiar words alone cannot account for the interest of his delay.
column7: The question directs attention to an action that precedes the words everyone expects.

column4:
At the first performance of a new comedy, a guest asked the playwright why she had put the best joke on the poster. Anyone who had passed the theater knew what the porter would say when the principal guest finally arrived. The playwright offered a ticket for the following evening on the condition that her critic sit among people who had already seen the play. He accepted, partly because he imagined that an audience deprived of its surprise would save him the trouble of making his case.

On the second evening the laughter began before the porter spoke. As he took an extraordinary time to straighten a dish on the hall table, someone in the gallery started to chuckle. When the line came, the house laughed again. The critic now conceded that a joke could survive foreknowledge. What he had heard, he said, was the agreeable recognition one feels on meeting an old friend. The playwright did not dispute the pleasure of recognition. She asked what, on his account, the porter had been doing with the dish.

The dish mattered because his hands had work his position forbade his voice to do. He wanted the distinguished visitor to wait, but could scarcely order a man of that rank to stand in the doorway. Straightening something that was already straight gave him a fragment of authority. The spectator waiting for the familiar line could watch that authority change hands. A newcomer searching for the likely speaker might miss the change entirely. The joke on the poster disclosed the words. It did not disclose what the actor would manage to do before he said them.

There is a temptation here to promote all second performances above all first ones. On her way home the playwright supplied a reason to resist it. Earlier that evening another actor had dropped a glove, apparently by accident. The porter had caught it without interrupting his speech. On learning later that the catch was rehearsed, the critic admitted that part of his pleasure had vanished. What had delighted him had been the apparent rescue of a scene from a mishap. He could still admire the skill of the catch, but rehearsal had changed the deed he understood himself to have witnessed.

The two incidents put different demands on ignorance. In the business with the dish, knowing the destination freed the spectator to examine the journey. In the business with the glove, believing that the actor had no map was part of what made the journey exciting. We should therefore ask a narrower question than whether publicity spoils a comedy. Which pleasure depends on the audience holding a particular belief about what can happen next? A producer who answers that question may decide to print a line in large letters and keep silent about a falling glove. Both decisions could express equal confidence in the actors.

1. The sequence must become funnier once the ending is known.
  2. A second viewing should erase all pleasure in the rescue.
  3. Publicizing the dialogue should restore the audience’s belief in the event.
  4. Viewers may still admire skill after their admiration for spontaneous courage fades.
column6: Viewers may still admire skill after their admiration for spontaneous courage fades.
column7: This parallels the glove catch, where learning about rehearsal changes the perceived deed.

column4:
The cooperative that shared a kiln among the potters of a coastal town had no official night watch. Somebody nevertheless had to stay with a firing until the kiln could safely be left. A potter might volunteer because a neighbor had covered for her last winter, because his own pots occupied most of the shelves, or because the other potters had small children. Asked who owed whom a night, members would usually name several considerations and then admit that the considerations did not point in quite the same direction. An economist visiting the workshop described the result as a system of exchange without accounts. That was close enough to win nods from the members and imprecise enough to conceal their most interesting disagreement.

When the cooperative doubled in size, a treasurer proposed that one night on watch earn one credit. Anyone who had used up her credits would take the next available shift. The proposal appealed especially to newcomers. An established potter could decline a night with a two-word reference to a sick aunt. A newcomer with an equally sick relative might have to tell a long and embarrassing story before the request seemed reasonable. A credit in the book would entitle either to say no without giving an account of her household. It would be easy to mistake the old members' discretion for a courtesy that the new members enjoyed equally.

After a season of bookkeeping, however, two experienced members objected that the accounts omitted the work of instructing novices. Teaching someone to load the kiln might save the cooperative many spoiled firings, yet no credit was issued for it. The treasurer offered to add a column for instruction. This reply pleased the member who did most of the teaching. It failed to satisfy the other, who had never taught a novice. Her complaint was that the new arrangement settled in advance which acts the members could invoke when deciding a shift. Before the ledger, she said, a contribution that nobody had thought important on Monday could be recognized as decisive on Friday. With another column there would merely be two things the cooperative had already thought of on Monday.

The distinction is easy to miss if we ask members only whether they consider the distribution of nights fair. Both critics might give the same low rating, and the newcomer, glad of her credit, a high one. If the credit for teaching were introduced, a rise in the average rating could be perfectly genuine without answering the second critic. Her concern would be better tested by watching what happens the first time a member offers a reason for changing shifts that the ledger has no place to record.

Nothing in this account requires the cooperative to abandon credits. A member who can politely decline without describing an ill relative has gained something that a richer communal discussion would not supply. The choice worth investigating is whether a posted balance must settle every case, or whether a member may occasionally reopen a case without being forced to reopen the door to her private life.

What feature of the ledger concerns the critic who has never taught a novice?
column5:
1. It places too little monetary value on the skilled work of teaching.
  2. It makes the grounds for changing shifts depend on categories chosen in advance.
  3. It gives newcomers more opportunities to decline a shift than established members.
  4. It leaves the cooperative unable to determine how many shifts a member has worked.
column6: It makes the grounds for changing shifts depend on categories chosen in advance.
column7: Her objection concerns which reasons can be considered, including contributions that acquire significance only later.

column2: MCAT and USMLE::MCAT::Critical Analysis and Reasoning Skills
column4:
When a resident of the square needed a ladder, she used to knock on the door of a man who painted houses. He kept three ladders and usually had one to spare. A researcher visiting the square called this a system of exchange. She assumed that the painter remembered his loans and could one day call in an equivalent number of favors. When he died, however, nobody could recall his having asked for much of anything. The researcher might have concluded that this was a remarkably poor system for keeping accounts. The painter's daughter suggested that she had been looking at the wrong account altogether.

Her father liked being the person who could supply a ladder. Children knew his name before they were tall enough to carry one. New residents learned which bell to ring. A neighbor who had borrowed the longest ladder said he had returned it with a bag of plums. The painter took two plums and sent the rest upstairs to a family who had recently moved in. Perhaps he expected the family to repay him. But the daughter recalled that the painter did not even introduce himself when he brought up the bag. The neighbor who supplied it, on the other hand, still told the story twenty years later.

One could call that durable recollection a kind of payment. Yet the word would conceal a distinction that matters. In a debt, the person owed can ordinarily say what would count as settling it. A painter owed a day's labor may forgive the day, or ask for two afternoons instead. The painter of the square could do neither with a story. He could encourage his neighbor to tell it, but he could not decide when that neighbor had remembered him sufficiently. The good he obtained from lending depended on someone else's continuing freedom over what to make of it.

The square now owns a communal ladder kept in a shed. There is a sign-out sheet, and the resident who returns the ladder late loses borrowing privileges for a week. Some older residents regard the shed as a chilly successor to the painter's kitchen. They forget that some newcomers had been too shy to ring his bell. The sign-out sheet tells a newcomer exactly what she owes and when she will be free of the obligation. A precise rule can be a considerable kindness to someone who does not yet know how a neighborhood interprets a favor.

If we count ladders carried home, the shed might easily prove the better institution. If we count stories, the painter might win. Neither result could tell us what would happen if the shed employed an attendant whose job was to strike up conversations. Someone paid to welcome you can become a friend. But the terms of employment can purchase only the greeting. Whether the meeting gives either person a standing in the other's life is a question that remains open after both have done everything required of them.

Suppose every new borrower has a pleasant conversation with the paid attendant but nobody seeks out the attendant again. Which inference best fits the final paragraph?
column5:
1. The attendant failed to meet the formal job requirement.
  2. Friendly conversation can never coexist with paid employment.
  3. An institution can reliably arrange greetings without guaranteeing an enduring relationship.
  4. The borrowers have a debt they can settle only by visiting the attendant at home.
column6: An institution can reliably arrange greetings without guaranteeing an enduring relationship.
column7: The argument separates the encounter that can be arranged from the standing two people may later grant one another.

column2: MCAT and USMLE::MCAT::Critical Analysis and Reasoning Skills
column4:
The first thing an editor proposed to cut from my little volume of sea poems was the line that consisted entirely of the word “again.” She penciled the word onto the end of the previous line and read the passage aloud. I had to admit that her reading was indistinguishable from mine. We paused in the same place and stressed the same syllables. She considered the experiment conclusive. So did I, though I thought we had established something quite different.

On the page, the previous line ended with a father telling his daughter that the tide had taken her boat. The reader might have supposed that the loss was the occasion for the poem. On reaching the short line, one had to revise that supposition. Apparently there had been other boats, or other losses that the father put in the same class. Of course the editor's version disclosed that history too. What it took away was a small interval in which the reader could be honestly mistaken. A pause in a reading can sometimes do this work. But in our two readings neither of us made such a pause. Knowing what was coming, we carried the earlier words forward to meet it.

There is an old classroom exercise in which a poem is printed as prose and students must guess where the poet put the breaks. I used to give high marks for accurate guesses. Then a student divided a description of a kitchen just before the word “knife.” In the original the knife lay harmlessly among the forks. In her version the preceding line left an elderly woman alone at the kitchen table, and the knife arrived as a small threat. She had guessed incorrectly, but she could tell me precisely what her arrangement made a reader expect. The student who had reproduced the original arrangement could tell me only that it looked right.

It would be foolish to conclude that a poem improves with the number of reasonable mistakes it invites. There are poems in which every line arrives at its close as neatly as a boat comes into its berth. The pleasure of those endings lies partly in having foreseen them. Nor does a short line work its spell upon a reader who already sees the whole page at a glance. My volume will find such readers, and I shall have to let them pass through that interval at their own speed.

I kept the line, and accepted the editor's next suggestion, which was to remove a full stop after it. Without the stop, the solitary word could glance backward at the loss while already belonging to the description of the returning tide below. It would be odd to say that I thereby preserved the poem exactly as I first imagined it. My editor helped me find another use for the space whose first use she had almost erased.

A student breaks a different poem at unexpected places and gives a precise account of the expectations each break creates. How would the narrator most likely assess the exercise?
column5:
1. Take the student’s account of each changed expectation seriously.
  2. Award full marks only if the student's reading reproduces the original rhythm.
  3. Treat the student's breaks as superior whenever they introduce suspense.
  4. Require proof that the original poet considered the same divisions.
column6: Take the student’s account of each changed expectation seriously.
column7: The kitchen example values an explained effect while leaving open which arrangement best serves the poem.

column4:
An editor preparing a new edition of a novel found the word “harbour” written twice on the last page of the author's manuscript. In the first printed edition the second occurrence was gone. The editor put it back. To a reader who asked why, she replied that it was her business to let the author speak. Yet the deletion might have been the author's own correction in proof. No proof sheets survive. The editor had made a choice on good evidence, but her account of that choice sounded more certain than her evidence allowed.

The reader's proposed remedy was an edition that reproduced the manuscript photographically. Nobody could then accuse an editor of silently changing a word. At the library they laid a photograph beside the manuscript. A crease in the paper made one of the letters look considerably darker in the photograph. On the original, the reader could tilt the sheet and see that the dark stroke was a shadow. He conceded that a photograph answered some questions about the manuscript very well. It had also raised a new question that could be settled only by returning to the sheet. Even deciding which instrument would give unmediated access to the novel seemed to require the judgment of an editor.

Years earlier, a theater company had asked visitors to read the last page aloud. Almost everyone paused at the repeated word. In the recordings the pause sounded like a person returning to a place she had left. This pleased the editor, who considered return the novel's great subject. It did not please her enough to count as proof. The actors had worked from copies in which she herself had restored the repetition. Their response showed what the repetition could do to a listener. It could tell her very little about who had deleted it.

She finally printed the repeated word in the text and added a note giving the reading of the first edition. The note was a single line. A colleague objected that a single line could hardly convey the hours of comparison the decision had required. That objection mistook the work the note had to do. A purchaser need not learn every step by which an editor had reached a decision in order to try reading the page the other way. For this particular difference, a short note put the experiment within reach of anyone with the book.

There are disagreements for which that economy would fail. If two surviving chapters arranged a sequence of events differently, a list of altered page numbers might leave the alternative nearly impossible to experience. Printing both chapters could be justified. The appropriate space for an alternative depends less on the number of scholarly hours expended than on what the reader must do to recover it. A useful edition can express a preference while making the cost of disagreeing with it reasonably small.

Why does the author reject the colleague's objection to the one-line note?

column2: MCAT and USMLE::MCAT::Critical Analysis and Reasoning Skills
column4:
In the first impression of a woodcut I own, the moon above a stretch of flooded fields is nearly black. In a later impression it is the white of the paper. At a sale last winter a dealer described the white moon as a correction. He pointed out that a moon reflected in floodwater ought to shine and that the artist had lived long enough to authorize the later printing. This sounded sensible until I put the impressions side by side. Each contains two moons, if one counts the reflection. The dealer had given me a reason for altering one of them.

A woodcut prints the surfaces the cutter leaves standing. To make a dark moon white, someone had only to take a shallow shaving off the block. In the water, however, the thin lines of the original reflection remain exactly where they were. They leave gaps which the eye can join into a pale disk. Against the dark moon overhead those gaps look like a reflection broken by wind. Beneath the new white moon I see instead the labor of joining them. The second print makes me aware of something I had done quite comfortably in front of the first.

A letter written when the block was new mentions the moon. The printer complains that so much solid black beside fine lines makes an even impression difficult. He asks leave to lighten the sky. No reply survives. The letter makes a practical explanation for a change quite attractive. It does not show that a complaint about uneven ink led anyone to cut precisely the shape we see. A printer can ask to lighten a sky without asking for a white moon, just as a buyer can ask for a cheerful picture without requesting a particular smile.

I would nevertheless give the dealer one concession. If a catalogue promises the last state of the block issued in the artist's lifetime, the white moon belongs on its cover. Faced with a request for the print that best shows how little ink the eye needs to make water shine, I would reach for the earlier sheet. These choices do not depend on ranking printers above artists or early thoughts above late ones. They depend on noticing what an example has been asked to exemplify.

At home the prints hang on opposite walls. A visitor has to turn away from one to see the other. Friends have proposed hanging them together to permit a more accurate comparison. For comparing the cuts I agree and take them down. For looking at the field I prefer the turn. You carry across the room an expectation about where the water will catch the light; almost every time the other print disappoints it slightly. That small disappointment is what persuaded me to buy the second impression. One white moon by itself could not have produced it.

What did the dealer mean by calling the later moon a correction?
column5:
1. He thought the block had been damaged after the first printing.
  2. He thought the first sheet had been falsely attributed to the artist.
  3. He thought the later impression resolved a pictorial problem in the earlier one.
  4. He thought reflection lines had been accidentally omitted from the later sheet.
column6: He thought the later impression resolved a pictorial problem in the earlier one.
column7: His argument appeals to how the moon ought to look and to the possibility of authorization.

column2: MCAT and USMLE::MCAT::Critical Analysis and Reasoning Skills
column4:
In the first impression of a woodcut I own, the moon above a stretch of flooded fields is nearly black. In a later impression it is the white of the paper. At a sale last winter a dealer described the white moon as a correction. He pointed out that a moon reflected in floodwater ought to shine and that the artist had lived long enough to authorize the later printing. This sounded sensible until I put the impressions side by side. Each contains two moons, if one counts the reflection. The dealer had given me a reason for altering one of them.

A woodcut prints the surfaces the cutter leaves standing. To make a dark moon white, someone had only to take a shallow shaving off the block. In the water, however, the thin lines of the original reflection remain exactly where they were. They leave gaps which the eye can join into a pale disk. Against the dark moon overhead those gaps look like a reflection broken by wind. Beneath the new white moon I see instead the labor of joining them. The second print makes me aware of something I had done quite comfortably in front of the first.

A letter written when the block was new mentions the moon. The printer complains that so much solid black beside fine lines makes an even impression difficult. He asks leave to lighten the sky. No reply survives. The letter makes a practical explanation for a change quite attractive. It does not show that a complaint about uneven ink led anyone to cut precisely the shape we see. A printer can ask to lighten a sky without asking for a white moon, just as a buyer can ask for a cheerful picture without requesting a particular smile.

I would nevertheless give the dealer one concession. If a catalogue promises the last state of the block issued in the artist's lifetime, the white moon belongs on its cover. Faced with a request for the print that best shows how little ink the eye needs to make water shine, I would reach for the earlier sheet. These choices do not depend on ranking printers above artists or early thoughts above late ones. They depend on noticing what an example has been asked to exemplify.

At home the prints hang on opposite walls. A visitor has to turn away from one to see the other. Friends have proposed hanging them together to permit a more accurate comparison. For comparing the cuts I agree and take them down. For looking at the field I prefer the turn. You carry across the room an expectation about where the water will catch the light; almost every time the other print disappoints it slightly. That small disappointment is what persuaded me to buy the second impression. One white moon by itself could not have produced it.

How does the printer’s letter affect the argument about who chose the white moon?
column5:
1. It identifies the printer as the person who made the final cut without permission.
  2. It establishes the artist’s intention to make both moons match.
  3. It explains why the later impression appeared only after the artist’s death.
  4. It supplies a motive for alteration while leaving the specific choice unresolved.
column6: It supplies a motive for alteration while leaving the specific choice unresolved.
column7: A request to lighten the sky is more general than the actual intervention, and the reply is missing.

column2: MCAT and USMLE::MCAT::Critical Analysis and Reasoning Skills
column4:
The last time two brothers quarreled in my hearing, the affair concerned a letter. One brother had read it aloud to guests after finding it on the other’s desk. It was a letter the other brother had written to their father and decided against sending. A guest offered the following peace: “I forgive you for making me listen to it.” This produced a laugh, partly at the solemnity of a man who had stayed to hear every word. Yet the guest had put his finger on a real difficulty. If he had been made an uncomfortable accomplice, he had something of his own to forgive. A dozen such pardons would still have left the writer’s complaint unanswered.

We speak of forgiveness as a kind of payment made by the injured person. The image is convenient until we begin adding up the payments. Suppose the brother had read a hundred letters and a hundred hearers had generously released him. Has he acquired a balance against which the owner of the next letter must draw? The question is absurd, but only because a pardon travels so badly. It can follow the injury that gave someone a claim; it cannot be handed to the offender for use against the next claimant.

My friend objects that the owner of the letter might welcome a stranger’s intervention. Indeed he might. An apology delivered through a neighbor can reach a door that the offender has quite properly been forbidden to approach. But the neighbor who carries a reply saying “My brother forgives you” undertakes a different task from the neighbor who announces “I forgive you on his behalf.” Asked why the matter is settled, the first can produce the reply. The second must produce some reason why he was entitled to speak. Proximity to the scene supplies no such reason.

It would be a harsh conclusion to forbid the guest from doing anything until the owner spoke. He could put down his glass and decline to hear the rest. Later he could tell the company why repeating the letter would compound the injury. He might even resume his own friendship with the reader. In none of these acts would he be announcing that the brothers were reconciled. The mistake is to treat every withdrawal of hostility as a certificate which binds the people still in dispute.

There is, finally, a difficulty on the other side. Imagine that the brothers make peace and the guest continues to describe himself as a reluctant witness. Is he bound to swallow his complaint because the family has settled theirs? The owner can release a claim to privacy. He cannot retrospectively consent to the use of somebody else as an audience. The guest must establish that he really was imposed upon; the fact that he found the story entertaining might tell against him. What he need not establish is that the owner remains angry.

At the end of the evening the guest asked to carry a second letter across town. This was an improvement in manners and, more importantly, in grammar. He now had a verb for which he could supply the subject without borrowing a brother. Whether the brothers would read what he carried remained entirely up to them.

When the author says a pardon “travels so badly,” what limit is being described?
column5:
1. It loses force when delivered through a neighbor.
  2. Its sincerity fades as time passes.
  3. It applies to a particular person’s claim.
  4. It depends on witnesses agreeing about the harm.
column6: It applies to a particular person’s claim.
column7: The imagined balance of pardons fails because each injury gives a particular person standing.

column4:
When the town orchestra decided to restore its oldest set of performance parts, the librarian expected the players to welcome her proposal. She would give each musician a clean copy of the printed score and put the worn originals in the archive. The first violinist held up a page on which someone had drawn a pair of spectacles over a bar of rests. The notes themselves were easy, she said. The spectacles meant to look up and catch the conductor's cue. A clean part would tell her exactly how long to wait, provided everybody else waited exactly that long too.

In a sense the mark belonged to a performance that had already ended. The conductor who needed watching had retired, and a later player had crossed out several of his instructions. Yet the violinist used the spectacles under the new conductor. She watched for a cue and, on finding none, listened to the oboes. What she had inherited was a question about the entry, together with a convenient place to ask it. An instruction can outlive the circumstances that made it correct by teaching its next reader where to exercise judgment.

It would be easy to turn this observation into a defense of saving every pencil mark. Consider the cellist who had written the name of a street beside a change of tempo. Nobody could remember whose address it was. A volunteer proposed copying the name in red so that future players would appreciate its age. That would have given the inscription a prominence it had never enjoyed while it meant something. The street name might interest a historian, but age offered a poor reason for placing it on the stand of a working musician.

The librarian eventually offered the orchestra two services. The archive would photograph every page before it was repaired. For the playing copies she invited musicians to bring an old part to rehearsal and report which marks they had actually consulted. One violist objected that this favored the experienced. A beginner might pass over a mark precisely because nobody had explained it. The librarian agreed and asked the musicians to exchange desks for one rehearsal. Each player was to lend a stranger a part and listen to the questions it provoked.

The resulting copies were neither clean nor crowded. Some familiar instructions disappeared when their owners found that they could give no account of using them. An inconspicuous line connecting two notes survived when a novice asked whether the second should answer the first. The former owner had never named the relationship, but the two players could demonstrate it by playing the phrase in different ways. They could also disagree about which way sounded better. The archive preserved the line as a fact about an earlier page. The playing copy preserved it as an invitation to hear a difference. Those are two distinct reasons for keeping the same stroke of pencil, and a library serving both purposes can afford to be exacting about each.

column5:
1. Historical evidence and a working prompt serve different purposes.
  2. Accurate photographs preserve every feature that affects musical expression.
  3. The best playing copy reproduces the oldest surviving performance.
  4. A disagreement between players prevents the archive from authenticating a mark.
column6: Historical evidence and a working prompt serve different purposes.
column7: The archive records what was on the page. The playing copy retains markings that can inform a present decision.

column2: MCAT and USMLE::MCAT::Critical Analysis and Reasoning Skills
column4:
On the first evening of rehearsal, the translator of a comedy came equipped with three English versions of a single sentence. In the original, a lodger asks the landlady for a key. Her answer can refer equally well to a key for the front door and a key to a problem. Only when she hands him a pencil does the second sense become unmistakable. The translator's first version preserved both meanings of the word. On paper it was an elegant solution. On stage the audience saw the pencil in the landlady's hand before the lodger finished speaking. The line attracted an appreciative murmur, but nobody laughed at the handover.

The director proposed putting the pencil in a drawer. To the translator's surprise, this restored the laugh without changing a syllable. He had been treating the double meaning as a possession of the sentence, like the number of letters in its last word. Yet what the scene required was an interval during which one interpretation felt sufficiently secure to be worth overturning. In rehearsal the visible pencil had spent that interval quietly making the other interpretation available. The audience could admire the workmanship once it spotted the trick, much as one might admire a folding chair. Admiration did not give the chair a second opportunity to collapse.

It would be easy to turn this episode into a defense of literal translation. After all, the words had survived and a piece of staging had come to their rescue. A second scene makes the lesson less comfortable. An official, asked to grant a permit, uses a formal expression that in his language begins like an acceptance and ends like a refusal. The nearest English equivalent announces the refusal in its first three words. No arrangement of desks can deprive an audience of words it has heard. The translator substituted a promise to give the matter his personal attention, followed, after a ceremonious search of his calendar, by the announcement that he is retiring that afternoon. The audience was allowed to hope for roughly as long as before. The expression itself was gone.

A critic objected that nearly any joke could now stand in for any other, provided somebody timed it with a watch. That objection catches a danger but mistakes the measure. The lodger's embarrassment depends on his confidence that a familiar word means what he needs it to mean. The applicant's disappointment depends on his willingness to hear bureaucratic courtesy as a commitment. A sudden noise at exactly the right second could startle either man and elicit a laugh. It could not expose either habit of mind. The question for a rehearsal is what the audience has been invited to believe, and on whose behalf, just before it has reason to reconsider.

This account leaves translators with considerable freedom and a rather exacting obligation. They may move a pencil, change an idiom or invent an appointment. They owe the audience a chance to make the particular mistake from which the scene draws its force. Sometimes that chance is secured by keeping a word. Sometimes keeping the word is precisely what makes the chance disappear.

At a preview, spectators laugh when the official announces his retirement. Which further observation would most directly challenge the claim that this version preserves the original reversal?
column5:
1. Several spectators remember waiting for permits and recognize the official’s courteous tone.
  2. Spectators laugh sooner when the actor searches the calendar more slowly.
  3. Several spectators can describe the desk more precisely than the words of the promise.
  4. Most spectators already hear a refusal before the calendar search starts.
column6: Most spectators already hear a refusal before the calendar search starts.
column7: The laughter could have another cause if the audience never expected the official to help. Timing and set differences alone would not settle that question.
