column2: MCAT and USMLE::MCAT::Critical Analysis and Reasoning Skills
column4:
For the first hour of sitting for my portrait, I tried to hold a pleasant expression that I imagined I wore whenever I opened the door to a friend. The painter let me keep it until the effort began to show. Then she asked me to describe the walk to her studio. I have no great gift for describing streets, and presently I stopped trying to look pleasant and began trying to remember where the road bent. She put down the little brush with which she had been drawing my mouth and picked up a larger one.

When my sister saw the finished portrait, she objected that the eyebrows were wrong. Mine were quite level, she said, whereas the painter had made one higher. I fetched a photograph taken the week before. There they were, two short horizontal strokes looking as if they had been ruled. The painter fetched three pages of drawings. On the first my eyebrows were level, on the second the left one had gone up, and on the third it was coming down again. My sister laughed. She had often seen me make that movement when I was trying to fish a name out of my memory. She could recognize the gesture while disputing the accuracy of the particular face in which the painter had set it down.

It is tempting to give the painter an easy victory here. Say that the camera copies surfaces while the painter sees a person, and the case is closed. But the photograph had caught me leaning forward, shoulders lifted a little, listening to a question. That posture was familiar to my sister too. Nothing in the instrument had prevented it from recording a revealing moment. And there are perfectly competent painters whose subjects seem all to have spent the sitting waiting for the same train. A distinction between tools cannot explain why one image reminds us of its sitter and another merely of the instructions the sitter was trying to obey.

What the drawings supplied was evidence about a choice. An eyebrow that went up once when I sneezed might be accurately drawn as high. My sister would have needed a different story to find the sneeze convincing as a likeness. The return of a movement at the edge of an effort to remember gave the painter a reason for selecting it. A reason need not compel agreement. My colleague, who has mostly seen me listening in meetings, might reasonably have chosen the photograph.

I would be sorry if the gallery hung the three drawings alongside the portrait as a sort of proof. They changed my sister's mind by reminding her of times she had already seen me. A stranger could inspect every mark and still have no experience against which to recognize the gesture. The drawings can show that a painter noticed a recurring movement. Recognizing the person in that movement is a further event, and it takes place as much in front of the canvas as on it.

Which statement most closely captures the author's account of a convincing likeness?
column5:
1. A portrait is convincing when it records the greatest number of facial details.
  2. A chosen feature can call up an acquaintance’s experience of the sitter.
  3. Agreement among longtime acquaintances is a necessary test of a successful portrait.
  4. A viewer must see the preparatory material before recognizing the sitter.
column6: A chosen feature can call up an acquaintance’s experience of the sitter.
column7: The painter selects a recurring gesture and the sister connects it to her own memory.

column4:
The first thing a visitor noticed in the potters’ hall was the row of cracked vessels. They stood just inside the entrance, each on a little wooden block. Beyond them stretched the tables of finished ware. A guide explained that the cracked pieces had been placed at the entrance to teach apprentices how a kiln could go wrong. A visitor reasonably concluded that the village potters were unusually generous with their mistakes. Indeed, the guide had made precisely that point for years. Then an apprentice asked who had been allowed to choose the mistakes.

The question arose while the apprentice was repairing a block. Its underside bore the mark of the same potter whose name appeared on the vessel it carried. The other blocks proved similarly marked. The potters had apparently brought their own stands to the hall and taken them away when they wished. No committee had patrolled the kilns for failures. This small discovery did not make the guide’s account false. A potter who publicly shows a badly fired bowl shares knowledge that a neighbor might otherwise have to buy at the price of a ruined firing. It did, however, give the display a second possible use.

One cracked jar bore a band of blue so even that visitors often asked whether its maker had other jars for sale. Another potter had kept a collapsed vessel whose broad shoulder, preserved on one side, showed just how broad a shoulder she had dared to attempt. The cracks in these pieces certified that the makers had undertaken risks. A tidy potter who worked entirely within familiar limits might have found very little worth putting by the door. The custom offered a way of advertising ambition in a room where the overt praise of one’s own work was considered tiresome.

This interpretation annoyed the guide. If the potters hoped to gain customers, he asked, what became of their generosity? His question assumed that a useful lesson lost its value when its teacher also stood to gain. An apprentice still had to work out which fault had brought the shoulder down. Meanwhile the potter who had dared it had good reason to be present when the fault was discussed. Each party could obtain something unavailable from a shelf of flawless jars.

There is, however, a difficulty in treating the row as a record of village practice. An apprentice wishing to discover the most common cause of breakage would do poorly to count defects at the door. A dull and embarrassing mistake was easy to leave behind, and no one could count what never arrived. For that inquiry the apprentice would need access to the heaps behind the workshops. It would be equally foolish to take down the display and replace it with a random cartload from those heaps. The heap could tell us what came out of the kilns. The hall could tell us what the potters thought worth bringing to one another’s attention.

Why does the ownership of the wooden blocks matter to the author's argument?
column5:
1. The blocks indicate which pots the workshop considered too fragile to sell.
  2. The stands establish that adjoining pots came from the same workshop.
  3. The potters controlled which failures visitors saw.
  4. The blocks were part of the transaction by which a buyer acquired a pot.
column6: The potters controlled which failures visitors saw.
column7: A movable, individually marked stand gives the maker control over which vessel appears.

The first thing a visitor noticed in the potters’ hall was the row of cracked vessels. They stood just inside the entrance, each on a little wooden block. Beyond them stretched the tables of finished ware. A guide explained that the cracked pieces had been placed at the entrance to teach apprentices how a kiln could go wrong. A visitor reasonably concluded that the village potters were unusually generous with their mistakes. Indeed, the guide had made precisely that point for years. Then an apprentice asked who had been allowed to choose the mistakes.

The question arose while the apprentice was repairing a block. Its underside bore the mark of the same potter whose name appeared on the vessel it carried. The other blocks proved similarly marked. The potters had apparently brought their own stands to the hall and taken them away when they wished. No committee had patrolled the kilns for failures. This small discovery did not make the guide’s account false. A potter who publicly shows a badly fired bowl shares knowledge that a neighbor might otherwise have to buy at the price of a ruined firing. It did, however, give the display a second possible use.

One cracked jar bore a band of blue so even that visitors often asked whether its maker had other jars for sale. Another potter had kept a collapsed vessel whose broad shoulder, preserved on one side, showed just how broad a shoulder she had dared to attempt. The cracks in these pieces certified that the makers had undertaken risks. A tidy potter who worked entirely within familiar limits might have found very little worth putting by the door. The custom offered a way of advertising ambition in a room where the overt praise of one’s own work was considered tiresome.

This interpretation annoyed the guide. If the potters hoped to gain customers, he asked, what became of their generosity? His question assumed that a useful lesson lost its value when its teacher also stood to gain. An apprentice still had to work out which fault had brought the shoulder down. Meanwhile the potter who had dared it had good reason to be present when the fault was discussed. Each party could obtain something unavailable from a shelf of flawless jars.

There is, however, a difficulty in treating the row as a record of village practice. An apprentice wishing to discover the most common cause of breakage would do poorly to count defects at the door. A dull and embarrassing mistake was easy to leave behind, and no one could count what never arrived. For that inquiry the apprentice would need access to the heaps behind the workshops. It would be equally foolish to take down the display and replace it with a random cartload from those heaps. The heap could tell us what came out of the kilns. The hall could tell us what the potters thought worth bringing to one another’s attention.

The apprentice asks “who had been allowed to choose the mistakes.” Which earlier assumption does the wording quietly unsettle?
column5:
1. That the row of cracked pots can speak for all the failures.
  2. That a skilled maker can explain how a kiln went wrong.
  3. That visitors notice the cracked pieces before the finished ware.
  4. That apprentices learn to fire pots by looking at other makers’ work.
column6: That the row of cracked pots can speak for all the failures.
column7: The question introduces permission and selection into a scene that had seemed to offer ready access to the makers’ mistakes.

column2: MCAT and USMLE::MCAT::Critical Analysis and Reasoning Skills
column4:
If a town is where its residents sleep, the town I studied lost a third of its inhabitants every winter. If it is where they pay for their houses, it lost almost nobody. The first definition appealed to the physician who stocked the dispensary. The second appealed to a historian trying to explain why rents stayed high through the winter. Both could be answered from records. The more troublesome question came from a girl whose father was away for six months of every year. “When people say he has come back,” she asked, “where do they think he has been living?”

I began with two columns. I put a dot in the left column for every night a worker slept in town and a dot in the right for every night spent at the quarry. The pages made an impressive procession of seasons. They failed to distinguish between a mason who meant to move his family to the quarry and a mason who had spent the same number of nights there for twenty years while refusing every offer of a permanent cottage. The dots counted absences with admirable consistency. They did not count departures.

The obvious remedy was to ask each traveler what he intended. This produced an embarrassment of answers. One man assured me on Monday that he would come home for good when his apprentice qualified. On Wednesday he told the quarry manager he would remain as long as the older men needed him. A colleague suspected him of telling each listener what the listener wished to hear. Perhaps he was. But the apprentice might qualify without the older men ceasing to need him. Until those obligations actually collided, the man could sincerely entertain both intentions. To put his answers to a vote would be to give two interviews the work of one decision.

I therefore began recording occasions on which a choice cost someone something. One mason gave up a week’s quarry wages to attend a meeting about the town’s water supply. Another sent his sister the fare to join him after she lost her room in town. The first choice made a claim about the town credible. The second made a claim about the quarry credible. It does not follow that either choice extinguished the other attachment. Money is scarce enough to make some promises costly and sufficiently useful in both places to keep many promises alive.

This method has its own injustice. A mason who has savings can furnish the investigator with a handsome sacrifice. A mason who has none may spend the evening writing letters whose cost never appears in an account. The most convincing episode in a notebook can belong to the person most able to afford an episode. I keep the entries about fares and meetings, but I no longer arrange my subjects in order of what they surrendered.

When the physician next asked how many people would be in town in January, I gave her the count of beds likely to be occupied. I did not offer her a theory of residence in six pages. She needed to know whose cough she might hear. The girl’s question deserved the six pages, partly because the answer could change while the annual number of occupied beds stayed exactly the same.

Why does the physician favor a count based on sleeping arrangements?
column5:
1. It identifies which families can afford prescriptions.
  2. It helps estimate who will need local care in winter.
  3. It separates short winter visits from permanent moves.
  4. It reveals which patients identify the town as home.
column6: It helps estimate who will need local care in winter.
column7: The dispensary must serve the people physically present.
column8: Original passage and item · AAMC CARS framework · https://students-residents.aamc.org/whats-mcat-exam/critical-analysis-and-reasoning-skills-section-overview

column2: MCAT and USMLE::MCAT::Critical Analysis and Reasoning Skills
column4:
Every spring our library association prints a league table of the most requested books. The figures are exact enough. A borrower enters a title on a slip, hands it to the clerk, and the clerk records one request. Last year a trustee proposed that the association buy next year's books in proportion to the totals on those slips. A branch serving keen readers of gardening books would acquire more gardening books. A branch whose readers cared little for gardening would be spared them. The proposal sounded like a modest way of letting readers themselves write the purchase order.

I spent a morning beside the returns counter at two branches. At the first, the clerk knew that three copies of a popular garden manual had recently arrived. She pointed people toward a shelf so close to the counter that she could see the green covers from her chair. At the second branch a reader looking for that manual was told that the only copy had gone missing. He filled in a slip. By noon the first branch had put the manual into six hands and registered no requests for it. The second had registered four requests and put the book into no hands at all.

The trustee had made a reasonable inference from a different sort of record. If people unable to borrow a book invariably filled in a slip, four slips would indeed mark four occasions on which another copy might have helped. She had quietly extended that inference to a comparison of readers' interests across branches. Yet the success that a well-stocked branch enjoyed in meeting an interest also gave that interest a way to disappear from the list. One could buy exactly in proportion to the figures and, a year later, congratulate oneself on having reduced the recorded enthusiasm for precisely the books the new copies were serving.

There is a more uncomfortable complication. At a third branch the slips sit behind the counter. The clerk gladly provides one to anyone who asks. A reader first has to know that the little transaction is possible, then care enough to conduct it in front of three people waiting to borrow books. Moving the slips out onto a table might increase requests while leaving both the collection and the readers' wishes unchanged. That rise would be an achievement for the new arrangement. It would be a curious reason to charge the branch with a sudden failure to stock its shelves.

I would keep the figures. On a particular afternoon four unsuccessful searches for the same manual give a librarian a fine reason to telephone another branch. When deciding how to spend next year's money, I would ask the successful readers a question too. The slip was designed to help someone who had gone away empty-handed. Its designers deserve credit for recording a disappointment so that someone could act on it. They never arranged to count every occasion for delight.

In the last sentence, an “occasion for delight” refers most directly to which event?
column5:
1. A clerk receives public praise for filling a request.
  2. The association reports better figures in its annual table.
  3. A librarian secures a transfer from a competing branch.
  4. A reader successfully obtains a book they wanted.
column6: A reader successfully obtains a book they wanted.
column7: The phrase returns to the successful readers who have little reason to submit a slip.

column2: MCAT and USMLE::MCAT::Critical Analysis and Reasoning Skills
column4:
At the end of a laboratory demonstration, six people were asked which of two recorded voices had spoken first. Each wrote an answer on a folded card. They were then invited to talk. Within a minute they had reached agreement, and in the account which followed it was the agreement that drew all the attention. The investigator wanted to know whether people would surrender their judgment to their neighbors. Someone ought to have asked what judgment the neighbors were surrendering to.

Consider the participant who started the discussion. She described the first voice as tired. She had originally chosen the lower voice, and the others took her adjective to refer to it. Then a man at the far end of the table said that the higher voice reminded him of his mother when she had just come off a night shift. The first speaker immediately said that was the voice she meant. We could call this an instance of yielding to influence. A still more trusting account would call it the recovery of a memory. The folded card, when opened, supported the first account against the second only if the choice on the card had been a faithful account of what the woman remembered.

A card can faithfully record a vote while giving a poor account of a doubt. The instructions had offered two boxes and no place to write a qualification. Someone who regarded the voices as almost simultaneous had to make the same kind of mark as someone who had heard a long interval. Our investigator knew this and in a second demonstration asked for a confidence rating beside the box. Participants who changed their minds in discussion tended to have given low ratings. He took this to show that people had sensibly listened to others when their own memories were weak.

That interpretation deserves a little less confidence than the ratings have received. The quietest participant at the table may have had a perfectly clear recollection and considerable doubt about his ability to persuade five strangers. If he rated his prospect of defending a choice when the investigator thought he was rating the sound in his ear, the two men had placed different objects on the same scale. A number with a decimal point would do nothing to bring those objects closer.

A colleague proposes a different test. After the discussion, seat each participant alone and play the recordings in their original order. Ask whether the sequence sounds familiar. This could reveal a great deal about recognition, especially if the experiment sometimes replayed a reversed sequence. Yet the colleague wishes to learn whether the group made its members less willing to disagree in public. The advantage of her quiet room is also its handicap. Nobody in it has to disagree with anybody.

I would keep the quiet room and add a second question at the table. Before anyone speaks, ask each person privately how sure they are about what they heard and how sure they are that they could defend the answer aloud. The two estimates may march together. When they part company, we might at least learn which companion the public vote follows. Even then a vote would be a piece of conduct awaiting explanation. It would be a pity to spend another afternoon devising a finer instrument for recording the same mystery.

What does the author mean by two men putting “different objects on the same scale”?
column5:
1. They assign different numerical values to the same interval.
  2. They disagree over which voice deserves the adjective “tired.”
  3. They remember the instruction as giving different response options.
  4. They take the rating to concern different kinds of confidence.
column6: They take the rating to concern different kinds of confidence.
column7: Confidence in hearing and confidence in defending an answer can yield different ratings.

column2: MCAT and USMLE::MCAT::Critical Analysis and Reasoning Skills
column4:
When a harbor town lent its festival quilt to a museum, the museum proposed hanging it so that visitors could walk around it. The reverse was a confusion of stitches, knots, and faded names. On the front, each household that contributed a square had embroidered its name in blue. The museum called the reverse a record of the anonymous work that the attractive face concealed. The town’s sewing circle objected to that description. They had no objection to showing the back. They objected to the claim that turning a thing over necessarily told you who had made it.

The objection arose from a custom older than the present quilt. At the end of a festival, the quilt spent the winter with whichever household had most recently joined the circle. Its keeper was expected to mend loose squares before the spring procession. A keeper might sew several repairs in a single evening, or none for years. Sometimes a keeper asked a neighbor to make a difficult repair. The names on the front recorded the gift of cloth, not the hand that performed the embroidery. The stitches on the reverse recorded acts of maintenance, but no convention required a keeper to sign them. A viewer who credited every repair to the keeper of its year would be inventing a fairly plausible history.

The museum revised its label. It now said that the front documented membership while the reverse documented labor. This was closer, yet a woman from the circle pointed to an untouched square of thin green cotton. It was still sound because three successive keepers had protected it with a removable lining during the procession. The lining did not go into the display case. On the reverse, the best visible evidence of their particular care was precisely the absence of a repair. Even that absence would have meant little without someone’s account of the lining.

A historian suggested recording such accounts and playing them beside the quilt. Some members welcomed the proposal. Others recalled arguments over who had supplied a particular lining. To exhibit one recollection in a recorded voice, they said, might give it a finality that it had never possessed at the sewing table. Still, disagreement need not turn every account into mere decoration. Two neighbors could disagree about the maker of a lining while agreeing that it had been used, when it had been attached, and why the green cloth mattered. Their disagreement set limits on one claim without discrediting all the others.

The most informative exhibit would allow the visitor to handle different degrees of certainty. A seam can establish that a repair was made. A pair of recollections can explain the survival of an unbroken square. Neither must yield a name. The trouble with the original label was not its generosity toward forgotten hands. It was the assumption that fairness requires distributing credit with greater precision than the available traces allow.

Which claim best expresses the author’s position?
column5:
1. A museum can honor maintenance while distinguishing what the surviving evidence establishes about it.
  2. The identities of contributors can be recovered by combining every repair with its keeper’s dates.
  3. Unrecorded care should be excluded from museum interpretation because it cannot be demonstrated.
  4. The quilt should be displayed only by the community that owns it.
column6: A museum can honor maintenance while distinguishing what the surviving evidence establishes about it.
column7: The author supports interpreting care, including care without a visible repair, while limiting claims about individual credit.

column4:
Halfway through a short detective story, a landlady tells her visitor that the tenant upstairs has finally gone home. The sentence costs a translator an afternoon. In the language of the story the landlady uses a form of address that suggests a previous acquaintance with her visitor. It would be an odd form to use with a stranger, although a woman of her age might use it with someone considerably younger. The visitor's age has yet to be mentioned. Two pages later, when we learn that the visitor is her son, the landlady's speech sounds quite ordinary. A reader who happened to notice it on the first encounter may enjoy having noticed it. A reader who passed it by can later find it waiting on the page.

The translator's language supplies no corresponding distinction in its pronouns. One solution is to let the landlady call her visitor “dear.” But imagine the visitor addressed that way in a story full of brisk professional exchanges. What had been an unobtrusive irregularity might become the only conspicuously intimate word on the page. Another solution is to omit the distinction. The disclosure of the visitor's identity would still surprise, yet on returning to the scene a reader would find nothing there to reconsider. Both solutions preserve what the landlady tells the visitor about the tenant. They offer rather different terms on which a reader may come to know the landlady.

A third translator lets the landlady interrupt the visitor before he has quite finished explaining why he came. Several other conversations in the story have made a point of observing formal courtesies. Breaking that rhythm here gives a reader a small reason to suspect familiarity. An impatient landlady has ample reason to interrupt a stranger, too. The device borrows no particular word from the original. Its defense is that it permits two readings before the disclosure and makes one of them especially satisfying afterward.

It would be a mistake to turn this defense into a general license to put interruptions wherever a translator has lost a nuance. Suppose the landlady's unfailing courtesy, even under provocation, is what later persuades a witness to trust her. An interruption could then repair a local difficulty at the expense of a more distant part of the story. Before deciding how much ingenuity a sentence will bear, one has to ask what else the proposed solution obliges the book to say.

Nor would a survey showing equal numbers of surprised readers settle the matter. Two readers can be equally astonished by a revelation, yet only one may feel invited to turn back a page. If I could ask those readers a second question, I would ask what they hoped to find when they turned back. A translation owes something to that return journey. A clue that everyone sees at once, and a clue that nobody could possibly have seen, each affords the reader rather little occasion to make it.

A story later reveals that two correspondents share a household. In the original, an ambiguous phrase in an early letter later reads like a private joke. Which choice best follows the passage’s reasoning?
column5:
1. Explain the household custom in a footnote beside the early letter.
  2. Choose ordinary banter that becomes a private joke on rereading.
  3. Omit the phrase and give the correspondents more affectionate dialogue after the revelation.
  4. Make the early phrase puzzling enough that every reader will flag it as a clue.
column6: Choose ordinary banter that becomes a private joke on rereading.
column7: An unobtrusive phrase with a plausible second reading preserves the opportunity the author values.

column2: MCAT and USMLE::MCAT::Critical Analysis and Reasoning Skills
column4:
A lexicographer who made a dictionary of island speech once invited the ferry workers to her office to hear their voices. She played a recording of one worker telling another where to leave a coil of rope. On hearing it, the speaker insisted that the word for the covered landing had a vowel quite different from the one on the tape. To prove the point, he repeated the word slowly, several times. The dictionary now had two pronunciations from a single speaker and the problem of deciding which one to print.

An easy solution would be to treat the recording as the truth and the demonstration as a mistake. Nobody on the ferry had stopped work to consider a vowel. The recording had captured what people said when they were concerned with something else. But the demonstration, too, occurred during a recognizable activity. Asked to teach a stranger a word, the worker distinguished sounds he routinely allowed to run together when he spoke to his crew. If a visitor learned only the version on the tape, the worker might well correct her in precisely the way he had corrected himself.

One might instead print the deliberate version and call the other a matter of speed. Yet many exchanges on the ferry were slow, and the shortened vowel could be heard in those as well. What united them was a shared destination for the rope, the parcels, or the passengers. Nobody in such an exchange had to distinguish the landing from another place with a similar name. Attention to a contrast, the lexicographer suspected, mattered at least as much as the number of syllables per minute.

This suspicion was quite practical. A dictionary large enough to record every occasion on which a sound changed would be a collection of transcriptions, difficult to consult and likely to be obsolete by the time it was bound. A dictionary that printed just one sound without explanation would be convenient until the reader took it to the docks. The lexicographer printed both vowels with short descriptions of the circumstances in which she had heard each. She wanted the descriptions to be vulnerable to correction. A worker who used the longer vowel with his usual crew could now tell her exactly which part of her account needed attention.

At the launch, a teacher complained that the entry had left her pupils without an answer to a fairly simple question. Which vowel should they use at the examination? The complaint was reasonable, though the dictionary by itself could hardly settle it. A school could announce which form it expected in a formal reading, just as the ferry company could require its workers to give place names distinctly over the radio. Neither instruction would invalidate the conversation about the rope. Each would establish a reason to speak one way on a particular occasion. The dictionary's achievement was to make room for such a reason without quietly turning it into a rule for every occasion.

Which claim best expresses the author’s view of pronunciation in this dictionary?
column5:
1. A speaker’s most frequent pronunciation should govern formal instruction.
  2. A useful entry can document alternatives and specify conditions under which each was observed.
  3. A pronunciation produced for a stranger reveals how the speaker wishes to sound in all settings.
  4. Dictionary entries should confine themselves to recorded spontaneous speech.
column6: A useful entry can document alternatives and specify conditions under which each was observed.
column7: The lexicographer makes the observed variation usable by describing its contexts and leaving those descriptions open to correction.

column4:
A lexicographer who made a dictionary of island speech once invited the ferry workers to her office to hear their voices. She played a recording of one worker telling another where to leave a coil of rope. On hearing it, the speaker insisted that the word for the covered landing had a vowel quite different from the one on the tape. To prove the point, he repeated the word slowly, several times. The dictionary now had two pronunciations from a single speaker and the problem of deciding which one to print.

An easy solution would be to treat the recording as the truth and the demonstration as a mistake. Nobody on the ferry had stopped work to consider a vowel. The recording had captured what people said when they were concerned with something else. But the demonstration, too, occurred during a recognizable activity. Asked to teach a stranger a word, the worker distinguished sounds he routinely allowed to run together when he spoke to his crew. If a visitor learned only the version on the tape, the worker might well correct her in precisely the way he had corrected himself.

One might instead print the deliberate version and call the other a matter of speed. Yet many exchanges on the ferry were slow, and the shortened vowel could be heard in those as well. What united them was a shared destination for the rope, the parcels, or the passengers. Nobody in such an exchange had to distinguish the landing from another place with a similar name. Attention to a contrast, the lexicographer suspected, mattered at least as much as the number of syllables per minute.

This suspicion was quite practical. A dictionary large enough to record every occasion on which a sound changed would be a collection of transcriptions, difficult to consult and likely to be obsolete by the time it was bound. A dictionary that printed just one sound without explanation would be convenient until the reader took it to the docks. The lexicographer printed both vowels with short descriptions of the circumstances in which she had heard each. She wanted the descriptions to be vulnerable to correction. A worker who used the longer vowel with his usual crew could now tell her exactly which part of her account needed attention.

At the launch, a teacher complained that the entry had left her pupils without an answer to a fairly simple question. Which vowel should they use at the examination? The complaint was reasonable, though the dictionary by itself could hardly settle it. A school could announce which form it expected in a formal reading, just as the ferry company could require its workers to give place names distinctly over the radio. Neither instruction would invalidate the conversation about the rope. Each would establish a reason to speak one way on a particular occasion. The dictionary's achievement was to make room for such a reason without quietly turning it into a rule for every occasion.

What role do the slow exchanges on the ferry play in the argument?
column5:
1. They establish that all ferry workers pronounce the word identically.
  2. They show that the recorder changed the worker’s speaking speed.
  3. They identify the historically earlier of the two vowels.
  4. Speed alone cannot explain the worker’s shorter vowel.
column6: Speed alone cannot explain the worker’s shorter vowel.
column7: A short vowel during slow speech motivates looking at shared context and the need to distinguish destinations.

column4:
When the city opened its ceramics workshop, the first places went to people who could spend a Tuesday morning outside the door. Nobody proposed this as a principle of selection. The building opened on a Tuesday, the applications were on a table inside, and when the last place was taken the clerk put the table away. Within a year, however, people had begun to speak of a long wait in the rain as evidence that a potter deserved a wheel. A consequence of the opening hours had acquired the dignity of a qualification.

The city replaced the queue with a lottery. This seemed an admirably literal answer to the complaint that a night worker could not spend the morning on the steps. It also produced a surprise. Applicants who won a place sometimes failed to appear. The old queue had seldom produced an empty wheel. At the next meeting, advocates of the queue took these vacancies as proof that waiting had measured commitment after all.

There is something in their observation. An applicant who has already arranged leave and traveled to the workshop has overcome two obstacles that might otherwise prevent attendance. But to predict that someone will arrive is a narrower achievement than to discover who most wants to learn. The night worker who cannot ask for another morning off might rearrange an entire season of evenings for a weekly class. A visitor with a free morning might happily queue for a novelty and never touch clay again. The queue obtains evidence about one occasion at the cost of making other kinds of evidence invisible.

A member of the workshop committee suggested asking successful applicants to confirm by telephone two days before the first class, and offering released places to alternates. The proposal drew an objection from each side. A defender of the queue thought that a telephone call was too slight a sacrifice to establish seriousness. A defender of the lottery objected that some people could not answer a call at work. Both objections make sense if confirmation is another examination of merit. Its proponent had something less ambitious in mind. The workshop simply needed enough information to put a person in front of each wheel. A message left in the evening, or a reply by post, would serve that purpose if it reached the clerk in time.

The distinction matters because a modest administrative improvement can quietly change the question an institution thinks it has answered. If confirmations reduce the number of empty wheels, the clerk has learned something about arranging attendance. It would be a considerable leap to announce that the workshop now admits more deserving potters. Conversely, a comparison of the pots made by the two groups would tell us little about applicants whom both procedures excluded. Before the city sets another ingenious task for people who want to use a wheel, it might decide which uncertainty it really needs to remove. Some uncertainties, including what a person will come to love after trying it, are part of the point of opening a workshop.

Why does the author concede that advocates of the queue observed something real?
column5:
1. Queuing had already required some practical arrangements also needed for attending.
  2. The lottery had offered places to people who had never applied.
  3. Waiting revealed a willingness to practice throughout a season.
  4. Each empty wheel represented a loss of interest between the draw and the first class.
column6: Queuing had already required some practical arrangements also needed for attending.
column7: Arranging leave and transport supplies evidence relevant to arriving on that occasion. The author leaves the applicant’s degree of interest open.

column4:
The village clock was a poor instrument by the time the council voted to preserve it. Its minute hand sometimes gained in damp weather and sometimes lost in dry. The engineer who examined it warned that no ordinary repair would make it reliable enough to govern the departure of a train. This alarmed the councillors until somebody noticed that no train had departed from the village for thirty years. After that the engineer’s report was quoted as though it had proved that the clock had no use at all. Its defenders responded in the same spirit. They claimed that every family planned its day by the chimes. A week spent asking families would have relieved them of this attractive belief.

One baker offered a more modest account. She set her ovens by a cheap electric timer. What the old clock gave her, she said, was a moment in the afternoon when the people outside her door looked up together. A visitor might suppose that this demonstrated the charm of an antique sound. Yet the baker had nothing kind to say about the bell itself, which had a crack and struck her as rather shrill. She was describing an arrangement among listeners. Almost any sound would have served, provided everyone knew that everyone else could hear it. A hundred accurate watches, each vibrating discreetly against a wrist, could tell the time more faithfully while doing little for that arrangement.

At this point an advocate of economy might propose a loudspeaker. The proposal deserves a more civil hearing than antiquarians usually grant it. A message broadcast daily at the same hour could indeed coordinate attention. The trouble is that an announcement has a speaker. Somebody would have to decide what the daily message said. Even if the message were simply a recorded chime, somebody could decide tomorrow that the occasion was better used for a warning about litter. The old clock could be silenced or moved, so it enjoyed no absolute immunity from officials. But its mechanism was sufficiently stubborn to make a change of subject difficult. Its limited vocabulary was part of the arrangement.

This argument supplies no general warrant for saving clocks. In a neighboring town the striking of the hour might wake night workers without creating any publicly valued moment. Nor does it establish that this village should spend whatever repair might cost. It does suggest a question that neither the engineer nor the clock’s defenders had asked. If an object appears inefficient at its stated purpose, which of its constraints have people quietly made useful? An answer may justify repair, replacement, or removal. The point of asking is to keep the easiest thing to measure from silently selecting among those options. An inventory of accurate timepieces would settle whether the baker needed help timing her ovens. It would tell us very little about what happened outside her door.

Why does the author mention that the baker finds the bell shrill?
column5:
1. To show that a village tradition survives only if residents enjoy the sound
  2. To undermine the baker's account of when customers arrive
  3. To separate the value of shared attention from the aesthetic appeal of the sound
  4. To support replacing the existing clock with an accurate and quieter one
column6: To separate the value of shared attention from the aesthetic appeal of the sound
column7: She values how listeners attend together despite disliking the sound itself.

column4:
A translator of a coastal diary kept an unfamiliar word for the basket in which a fisher carried the day's catch. Her editor proposed simply “basket.” In defense of the original word the translator described its close weave, the curl of its handle, its tendency to list on an uneven deck. The editor replied that every basket in every language has a shape, and that a catalogue of shapes is not a diary. Both assumed that the word's work could be settled by inspecting the object. Yet later in the diary the same word is spoken to a son who has announced his departure. His father says only, “Take the basket.” By then the family has sold its boat. If the reader has had to pause at this word before, the father's remark may recall mornings of shared work. If the reader has paused at a dozen unexplained words on each page, it may recall only the difficulty of the translation. The translator's choice therefore depends partly on a resource that no dictionary lists: the attention she has already asked her reader to spend.

What resource limits the translator’s ability to make a particular unfamiliar word memorable?
column6: The reader's remaining attention for unfamiliar language.
column7: The author presents a pause as meaningful when it is distinctive and tiring when repeated indiscriminately.

column4:
When the city archive began digitizing petitions, volunteers received a practical instruction. Copy the words that appear on the page. A volunteer who found seven nearly identical petitions from a single street entered all seven. Another, facing two hundred printed petitions signed by different hands, entered the text just once and attached a list of names. Both believed they had obeyed. Yet a historian searching for a phrase about the price of coal would retrieve seven documents from the first street and one from the second. The difference was born at a desk decades after the coal had been burned.

One proposed remedy was to count signatures. A hundred names, on this view, ought to carry the same weight whether they arrived on one sheet or a hundred. That seems fair if the historian wants to know how many people were willing to put their names to a demand. But a signature gathered during a shift change could take seconds, while delivering a petition to the council might cost a day’s wages. A signature count retains an answer about participation while discarding evidence about the work of organizing it. The two streets might have differed most in precisely that respect.

A second remedy was to preserve photographs of every sheet. The photographs were welcome. One showed that what looked in transcription like a second signer was a witness attesting to the mark of someone who could not write. Yet photographs do little for the reader who is first deciding which street to investigate. That reader still encounters a list produced by choices about what counts as a document. A picture can correct a conclusion once the reader has found it. It cannot, by itself, tell the reader which pictures the search failed to bring together.

There was a further difficulty. A husband and wife sometimes signed one sheet under the name of their shop. Counting the sheet was easy. Counting the names meant deciding whether the couple, the shop, or the person who held the pen had made the demand. Even the apparently modest unit of a participant already contained an interpretation.

Some archivists took this argument as an objection to counting. Far from it. If no one counts anything, a street represented by one eloquent letter may fill half a chapter while a street represented by forty terse petitions gets a sentence. The discipline of counting can expose that imbalance. The difficulty begins when the count is allowed to travel without its question. “Forty petitions” sounds like a finding one can carry from an inquiry into participation to an inquiry into organization. In fact it fits neither inquiry particularly well until someone explains what those forty units were.

The archive eventually added two switches to its search. A reader could group results by physical sheet or by named participant, and could see the grouping used in a downloaded table. The archivists resisted adding a button labeled “best estimate.” Had a visitor asked for the best estimate of anything in particular, they could have helped. Their refusal was directed at the curious idea that the purpose of an estimate could be supplied after the estimate itself.

Suppose the archive retained both search switches but stopped labeling which grouping was used in downloaded tables. Which concern would remain most directly unresolved?
column5:
1. The original sheets would gradually become inaccessible to volunteers.
  2. Readers could no longer correct the spelling of names using photographs.
  3. The names of people who signed printed petitions would disappear.
  4. Another analyst might reuse a count without knowing what its units represented.
column6: Another analyst might reuse a count without knowing what its units represented.
column7: The recorded grouping preserves the meaning of a count when it leaves the search interface.

column2: MCAT and USMLE::MCAT::Critical Analysis and Reasoning Skills
column4:
At the first reading of a comedy, the director found a pause marked in the promptbook after a character announced that the house had been sold. A penciled note in the margin said “six seconds.” The production that supplied this book had been admired for the peculiar chill that passed through the room at precisely this moment. Our director set a watch on the rehearsal table. The actors waited six seconds. Nothing in particular happened.

The note had been written by a stage manager, who occupied a seat from which the room could be heard unusually well. She kept a record because the actor who spoke next had a habit of swallowing the first word of his line. At one performance the audience laughed at the announcement. The laugh grew, faltered as people understood who would lose their home, and went out in scattered coughs. Six seconds passed before the room was quiet enough for a softly spoken reply. The record was an accurate measurement of that evening. The difficulty arose when an accurate measurement was promoted to an instruction.

A sympathetic reader might replace “six seconds” with “wait for quiet.” That would work on an evening when the audience laughed. Yet on another evening silence fell at once. An actor who answered immediately made the reply sound like a practical objection to the sale. An actor who allowed the silence to sit for a moment made the same words sound like an acknowledgment of grief. Quiet supplied an opportunity to speak, but it did not choose between those meanings.

It is tempting to conclude that nothing worth preserving can be written down. The company's understudy offers a reason for resisting that conclusion. She had never seen the celebrated performance. The stage manager's note made her ask why anyone would count the interval at all. In answering, her colleagues recalled that the announcement had once been played as a joke and the reply had interrupted the laughter. That earlier failure was useful to her. Having heard what the actors had once overlooked, she could listen for it herself. A record may do its best work by provoking a question that its maker had no occasion to put on paper.

I would keep the number in a new promptbook, accompanied by the reason it had been measured. I would also keep the director's unsuccessful rehearsal with the watch. It shows a future company how easily a description can acquire authority when it sits beside an actor's line. Such a book will sometimes disappoint a reader looking for a way to recover the experience of one remarkable night. But a company does not need to reproduce the six seconds in order to inherit something from that night. It can inherit the responsibility for deciding what the coming reply will sound like to the people actually in the room.

Which statement best captures the author’s reason for retaining the timing note?
column5:
1. A precise record disciplines actors who tend to overstate an emotion.
  2. Accurate measurements become broadly reliable once several productions repeat them.
  3. Its purpose gives later actors a reason to try that timing.
  4. A production owes its audience the interpretation established by the original company.
column6: Its purpose gives later actors a reason to try that timing.
column7: The author retains both the number and its history so another company can make its own informed decision.

column2: MCAT and USMLE::MCAT::Psychological and Social Foundations
column4:
A counseling program studies whether supervisors' expectations influence trainee participation. Before a practice interview, each supervisor is randomly given either a note suggesting the trainee is hesitant or a neutral note. The labels are assigned at random and convey no information about the trainee. Trainees never see the notes. Each supervisor and trainee takes part in only one interview. In a second independently randomized condition, supervisors either choose when to invite a response or follow a script offering precisely four invitations. Researchers count invitations and trainee contributions in anonymized recordings. A coder who never sees the notes scores the recordings. In the free-format interviews, trainees average three contributions under the hesitant label and six under the neutral label. In scripted interviews, the corresponding means are four and five. No results for trainee ability outside this interview are collected.

Whose expectation is the label intended to manipulate?
column7: The trainee never sees the label. Any effect on trainee behavior must arise through another pathway.
column8: Snyder, Tanke and Berscheid · Social perception and interpersonal behavior · https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-3514.35.9.656 · Original simulated experiment

Those aged 30–39 contributed 6,000 woman-years and had 300 live births. In year 2, the respective exposures were 2,000 and 8,000 woman-years, and the birth counts were 200 and 400. column4: A relief association has a charter, a defined mission and designated positions for coordinating work. Which kind of social organization is described?

column2: MCAT and USMLE::MCAT::Psychological and Social Foundations
column4: A choir member describes their ensemble as “us” and a rival ensemble as “them.” Which ensemble is the in-group for this speaker?
column7: Membership and identification define the reference point.

column2: MCAT and USMLE::MCAT::Psychological and Social Foundations
column4: A speaker identifies only with a rival choir and now judges the first choir's performance. What is the first choir from this speaker's perspective?
column7: The group itself is unchanged, but the observer’s identification differs.
column8: AAMC category 8C · Subject reference: https://openstax.org/books/introduction-sociology-3e/pages/6-1-types-of-groups

column2: MCAT and USMLE::MCAT::Psychological and Social Foundations
column4: In a simple Hamilton's-rule model, helping costs one expected offspring and gives a recipient three additional expected offspring. Relatedness is 0.5. Does the indirect gain outweigh the direct cost?

column4: In another population helping costs one expected offspring and gives a recipient three. Relatedness is 0.25. Does the indirect gain now outweigh the direct cost?
column6: No. The weighted benefit is 0.75, below 1.

column8: AAMC category 8C · Subject reference: https://doi.org/10.1016/0022-5193(64)90038-4

column2: MCAT and USMLE::MCAT::Psychological and Social Foundations
column4: In a fish study, receptive individuals consistently approach one of two courtship displays when rivals cannot interfere. What component of sexual selection is being tested?
column7: The response measured is the chooser's preference.

column4: A second study holds chooser preference constant. Some fish consistently displace rivals from access to spawning sites. What mechanism now explains their mating advantage?

column2: MCAT and USMLE::MCAT::Psychological and Social Foundations
column4: A clinic evaluates every visit primarily by patients processed per hour. Which dimension of McDonaldization does the emphasis on counting illustrate?

column2: MCAT and USMLE::MCAT::Psychological and Social Foundations
column4: Another chain requires the same scripted encounter and layout at every location so visitors know what to expect. Which dimension of McDonaldization is emphasized?
column7: The experience is intentionally standardized across sites.
column8: AAMC category 8C · Subject reference: https://openstax.org/books/introduction-sociology-3e/pages/6-3-formal-organizations

column2: MCAT and USMLE::MCAT::Psychological and Social Foundations

column6: The effect of the assigned expectation on expression in this experiment.

column8: AAMC category 8C · Subject reference: https://openstax.org/books/psychology-2e/pages/10-4-emotion

column2: MCAT and USMLE::MCAT::Psychological and Social Foundations
column4: In an observational survey two gender groups differ in how often they report crying. Can the group averages alone establish that a particular display rule caused the difference?
column6: No. Exposure to the proposed norm was neither measured nor assigned.
column7: Investigate context and variation within groups.
column8: AAMC category 8C · Subject reference: https://openstax.org/books/psychology-2e/pages/10-4-emotion

column2: MCAT and USMLE::MCAT::Psychological and Social Foundations
column4: A large voluntary association elects officers, but the same few officials alone control nominations, finances and the agenda. Which sociological tendency does this illustrate?
column7: Formal participation can coexist with concentration of effective power.
column8: AAMC category 8C · Subject reference: https://openstax.org/books/introduction-sociology-3e/pages/6-3-formal-organizations

column2: MCAT and USMLE::MCAT::Psychological and Social Foundations
column4: A new association has a board, but members independently nominate candidates, control spending votes and regularly replace leaders. What evidence here shows that effective power has concentrated in a small elite?
column6: None in the described distribution of decisions.
column7: The mere existence of officers is insufficient.
column8: AAMC category 8C · Subject reference: https://openstax.org/books/introduction-sociology-3e/pages/6-3-formal-organizations

column2: MCAT and USMLE::MCAT::Psychological and Social Foundations

column7: It describes conduct attached to the position.
column8: AAMC category 8C · Subject reference: https://openstax.org/books/introduction-sociology-3e/pages/4-3-social-constructions-of-reality

column2: MCAT and USMLE::MCAT::Psychological and Social Foundations

column7: The observation concerns unequal treatment.
column8: AAMC category 8C · Subject reference: https://openstax.org/books/introduction-sociology-3e/pages/11-3-prejudice-discrimination-and-racism

column2: MCAT and USMLE::MCAT::Psychological and Social Foundations

column8: AAMC category 8C · Subject reference: https://openstax.org/books/introduction-sociology-3e/pages/4-3-social-constructions-of-reality

column4: A rider learns to press a button after a warning light but before any unpleasant sound starts. Why is the successful press classified as avoidance rather than escape?

column2: MCAT and USMLE::MCAT::Psychological and Social Foundations

column4: A child learned to respond to a 1000 Hz signal. Responses decline gradually as test tones differ more from 1000 Hz, despite no differential training. What does the gradient show?

column8: OpenStax · https://openstax.org/books/psychology-2e/pages/6-2-classical-conditioning

column2: MCAT and USMLE::MCAT::Psychological and Social Foundations
column4: A neuron's firing increases while a monkey watches a grasp but stays at baseline when the monkey performs that grasp. Which part of the evidence for a mirror-like response is missing?

column7: Observation-related activity alone is insufficient.
column8: di Pellegrino et al. · https://doi.org/10.1007/BF00230027

column2: MCAT and USMLE::MCAT::Psychological and Social Foundations
column4: When a child shouts, a valued activity stops. Shouting declines. Why is this consequence negative punishment instead of negative reinforcement?

column2: MCAT and USMLE::MCAT::Psychological and Social Foundations
column4: A pupil already blinks at a trained tone. A newly introduced light elicits no blink before any light–puff pairings. Which cue is neutral with respect to blinking at this point?

column8: OpenStax · https://openstax.org/books/psychology-2e/pages/6-2-classical-conditioning

column2: MCAT and USMLE::MCAT::Psychological and Social Foundations
column4: A driver fastens a seat belt, the annoying warning tone stops, and fastening becomes more frequent. Why is this removal not negative punishment?
