column7: The consequence functions as negative reinforcement.
column8: OpenStax · https://openstax.org/books/psychology-2e/pages/6-3-operant-conditioning

column2: MCAT and USMLE::MCAT::Psychological and Social Foundations
column4: Pressing a button still earns attention every time, but it now also costs a point. Responding falls. Why is the drop insufficient to identify operant extinction?
column6: The maintaining attention was never withdrawn.
column7: The added point-loss contingency can suppress responding without extinction.
column8: OpenStax · https://openstax.org/books/psychology-2e/pages/6-3-operant-conditioning

column2: MCAT and USMLE::MCAT::Psychological and Social Foundations
column4: Announcing a student's name after a question is intended as praise, but the student subsequently asks fewer questions. Does the announcement function as positive reinforcement here?
column6: No. Adding it reduced the future response rate.
column7: The effect on behavior determines whether a consequence reinforces it.
column8: OpenStax · https://openstax.org/books/psychology-2e/pages/6-3-operant-conditioning

column2: MCAT and USMLE::MCAT::Psychological and Social Foundations
column4: A child receives a loud reprimand after each interruption but interrupts more often over subsequent sessions. Does the reprimand meet the functional definition of positive punishment?
column6: No. The added consequence failed to reduce interruptions.
column7: If it increases the behavior, attention may be functioning as reinforcement.
column8: OpenStax · https://openstax.org/books/psychology-2e/pages/6-3-operant-conditioning

column2: MCAT and USMLE::MCAT::Psychological and Social Foundations
column4: Animals detect taste and light cues equally well before training, but link delayed nausea to taste more readily. What does matching detectability help rule out?
column6: Failure to sense the light as the sole explanation.
column7: With exposure and detection controlled, selective associability remains a plausible contributor.
column8: OpenStax · https://openstax.org/books/psychology-2e/pages/6-2-classical-conditioning

column2: MCAT and USMLE::MCAT::Psychological and Social Foundations
column4: A thirsty participant works for a plastic chip only after learning that chips buy water. Which item is the primary reinforcer, the chip or the water?
column7: The chip's reinforcing value depends on its learned exchange relation.
column8: OpenStax · https://openstax.org/books/psychology-2e/pages/6-3-operant-conditioning

column2: MCAT and USMLE::MCAT::Psychological and Social Foundations
column4: A clinic opens a walking route and walking increases. What additional observation would support reciprocal influence of behavior on the environment?
column6: Increased use leads the clinic to extend or improve the route.
column7: The new observation supplies a feedback direction beyond the initial effect of the environment.
column8: OpenStax · https://openstax.org/books/psychology-2e/pages/11-4-learning-approaches

column2: MCAT and USMLE::MCAT::Psychological and Social Foundations
column4: After a learned light response extinguishes, the experimenter pairs the light with food again before testing. Why is renewed responding insufficient evidence of spontaneous recovery?
column6: It could reflect reacquisition during the new pairings.
column7: Spontaneous recovery is tested after a rest without renewed training.
column8: OpenStax · https://openstax.org/books/psychology-2e/pages/6-2-classical-conditioning

column2: MCAT and USMLE::MCAT::Psychological and Social Foundations
column4: A therapist rewards only a fully tied shoelace from the first session, never reinforcing partial steps. Which feature would need to change to make this a shaping procedure?
column6: Reinforce progressively closer approximations to the completed knot.
column7: Repeating a fixed criterion alone does not shape an initially absent action.
column8: OpenStax · https://openstax.org/books/psychology-2e/pages/6-3-operant-conditioning

column2: MCAT and USMLE::MCAT::Psychological and Social Foundations
column4: After an initially unanimous discussion, a participant still supports the group's proposal in an anonymous follow-up weeks later. What does this add beyond public agreement?
column6: Evidence consistent with private acceptance or internalization.
column7: Persistence without an audience weakens an explanation based solely on immediate conformity.
column8: OpenStax · https://openstax.org/books/psychology-2e/pages/12-3-attitudes-and-persuasion

column2: MCAT and USMLE::MCAT::Psychological and Social Foundations
column4: A personally important message is delivered while listeners perform a demanding second task. Which prerequisite for central processing is reduced despite motivation?
column6: Ability to attend to and evaluate the arguments.
column7: High relevance alone may not overcome a competing cognitive load.
column8: OpenStax · https://openstax.org/books/psychology-2e/pages/12-3-attitudes-and-persuasion

column2: MCAT and USMLE::MCAT::Psychological and Social Foundations
column4: Arcade tickets stop buying prizes. Over repeated visits the tickets cease to motivate play. What previously gave the tickets reinforcing value?
column6: Their learned association with the exchangeable prizes.
column7: A conditioned reinforcer can lose value when that relation no longer holds.
column8: OpenStax · https://openstax.org/books/psychology-2e/pages/6-3-operant-conditioning

column2: MCAT and USMLE::MCAT::Psychological and Social Foundations
column4: After tone–puff training, one blink follows a tone alone and another follows an unexpected puff alone. Which blink is the unconditioned response?
column6: The blink elicited by the puff.
column7: The classification depends on the eliciting event, even when the movements look identical.
column8: OpenStax · https://openstax.org/books/psychology-2e/pages/6-2-classical-conditioning

column2: MCAT and USMLE::MCAT::Psychological and Social Foundations
column4: A machine makes a reward available at random times and holds it until the next press. Why can't a fixed count of presses guarantee a reward?
column6: Availability depends on a varying elapsed interval.
column7: This is a variable-interval schedule. Additional presses before availability do not satisfy a count requirement.
column8: OpenStax · https://openstax.org/books/psychology-2e/pages/6-3-operant-conditioning

column2: MCAT and USMLE::MCAT::Psychological and Social Foundations
column4: Rewards follow the third, then the ninth, then the second response after each reset; there is no clock rule and counts are unpredictable. Which schedule fits?
column7: The varying requirement is the number of responses, regardless of elapsed time.
column8: OpenStax · https://openstax.org/books/psychology-2e/pages/6-3-operant-conditioning

column2: MCAT and USMLE::MCAT::Psychological and Social Foundations
column4: A tone precedes an air puff. Across training blocks, the fraction of tone-only probes with a blink rises from 5% to 30% to 70%. Which learning phase is shown?
column7: The conditioned response develops as the tone predicts the puff.
column8: OpenStax · https://openstax.org/books/psychology-2e/pages/6-2-classical-conditioning

column2: MCAT and USMLE::MCAT::Psychological and Social Foundations
column4: Two people voluntarily advocate a view they oppose. One receives a large payment that fully explains the action. Which person has less need to change private attitudes to explain the advocacy?
column6: The person with ample external justification.
column7: An external reason reduces pressure to resolve inconsistency by changing belief.
column8: OpenStax · https://openstax.org/books/psychology-2e/pages/12-3-attitudes-and-persuasion

column2: MCAT and USMLE::MCAT::Psychological and Social Foundations
column4: An unchanged stimulus produces larger orienting responses on successive presentations. Which direction of change distinguishes sensitization from habituation?
column7: Habituation involves a response decrement.
column8: OpenStax · https://openstax.org/books/psychology-2e/pages/6-1-what-is-learning

column2: MCAT and USMLE::MCAT::Psychological and Social Foundations
column4: Food elicits salivation before a light has ever been paired with food. Which stimulus is unconditioned at this point?
column7: Its effect on salivation precedes training. The light begins as a neutral cue.
column8: OpenStax · https://openstax.org/books/psychology-2e/pages/6-2-classical-conditioning

column2: MCAT and USMLE::MCAT::Psychological and Social Foundations
column4: After a tone-evoked blink extinguishes, the tone is paired again with the puff. Blinking to the tone strengthens. What process is occurring?
column7: Restoring the predictive pairing differs from recovery after rest alone.
column8: OpenStax · https://openstax.org/books/psychology-2e/pages/6-2-classical-conditioning

column2: MCAT and USMLE::MCAT::Psychological and Social Foundations
column4: A fatigued listener stops responding to both a repeated tone and a clearly audible novel chime. What alternative to stimulus-specific habituation remains plausible?
column6: A generalized loss of alertness or response capacity.
column7: Failure to orient to either stimulus leaves nonspecific explanations open.
column8: OpenStax · https://openstax.org/books/psychology-2e/pages/6-1-what-is-learning

column2: MCAT and USMLE::MCAT::Psychological and Social Foundations
column4: Participants can earn rewards by reproducing an observed sequence. Why score the first attempt before any test feedback?
column6: To measure what was learned from the model before direct test reinforcement can teach the sequence.
column7: Later performance can reflect learning during the assessment.
column8: OpenStax · https://openstax.org/books/psychology-2e/pages/6-4-observational-learning-modeling

column2: MCAT and USMLE::MCAT::Psychological and Social Foundations
column4: Model-exposed and unexposed groups both improve from 2 to 6 correct sequences when offered an incentive. What group contrast supports an advantage from observing the model?
column7: The improvement is shared. The data do not isolate an exposure-specific benefit.
column8: OpenStax · https://openstax.org/books/psychology-2e/pages/6-4-observational-learning-modeling

column2: MCAT and USMLE::MCAT::Psychological and Social Foundations
column4: A novice discovers a new response by trial and error while alone, repeating it after personal rewards. What source of learning explains the change?
column7: This example requires no observed model or vicarious consequence.
column8: OpenStax · https://openstax.org/books/psychology-2e/pages/6-4-observational-learning-modeling

column2: MCAT and USMLE::MCAT::Psychological and Social Foundations
column4: A student avoids copying a colleague's shortcut after watching the colleague lose privileges for using it. What learning mechanism fits?
column7: The observer's behavior changes after witnessing a consequence delivered to the model.
column8: OpenStax · https://openstax.org/books/psychology-2e/pages/6-4-observational-learning-modeling

column2: MCAT and USMLE::MCAT::Psychological and Social Foundations
column4: The plot compares two arguments at two levels of speaker prestige. What is the strong-minus-weak argument effect within each prestige level?
column6: Zero percentage points at both levels.
column7: Read the two points within each prestige group. Endorsement differs between groups but does not change with argument strength.
column8: OpenStax · https://openstax.org/books/psychology-2e/pages/12-3-attitudes-and-persuasion

column2: MCAT and USMLE::MCAT::Psychological and Social Foundations
column4: A trial uses a famous speaker only for strong arguments and an unknown speaker only for weak arguments. Why is the effect of prestige unidentified?
column6: Prestige is confounded with argument quality.
column7: Independent variation is needed to separate the two effects.
column8: OpenStax · https://openstax.org/books/psychology-2e/pages/12-3-attitudes-and-persuasion

column2: MCAT and USMLE::MCAT::Psychological and Social Foundations
column4: An inattentive audience becomes more favorable when a celebrity endorses a proposal. Which route is implicated by reliance on source attractiveness?
column7: The deciding cue lies outside the merits of the argument.
column8: OpenStax · https://openstax.org/books/psychology-2e/pages/12-3-attitudes-and-persuasion

column2: MCAT and USMLE::MCAT::Psychological and Social Foundations
column4: Rewards occur on 10% of cue trials and 70% of otherwise matched no-cue trials. Does the cue predict more or fewer rewards?
column7: Reward probability is lower in the presence of the cue. The cue carries negative contingency.
column8: OpenStax · https://openstax.org/books/psychology-2e/pages/6-2-classical-conditioning

column2: MCAT and USMLE::MCAT::Psychological and Social Foundations
column4: A novel chime interrupts repetitions of a familiar tone. What control estimates whether the pause alone restores responding to the tone?
column6: A matched pause without the novel chime, followed by the familiar tone.
column7: Match the interval and familiar-tone sequence to isolate the new stimulus.
column8: OpenStax · https://openstax.org/books/psychology-2e/pages/6-1-what-is-learning

column2: MCAT and USMLE::MCAT::Psychological and Social Foundations
column4: Orienting probability is 0.1 on the last familiar tone, 0.8 on a new tone and 0.1 when the familiar tone returns. What evidence is there for dishabituation to the familiar tone?
column7: The response to novelty was strong but did not restore the response to the familiar tone.
column8: OpenStax · https://openstax.org/books/psychology-2e/pages/6-1-what-is-learning

column2: MCAT and USMLE::MCAT::Psychological and Social Foundations
column4: Two groups have the same number of cues and rewards. What probability outside cue periods must be reported to judge how informative a cue is?
column6: The probability of the reward when the cue is absent.
column7: Compare it with reward probability during the cue. Mere pairing counts are insufficient.
column8: OpenStax · https://openstax.org/books/psychology-2e/pages/6-2-classical-conditioning

column2: MCAT and USMLE::MCAT::Psychological and Social Foundations
column4: A warning light precedes an unpleasant sound. A button press during the light prevents the sound. What has been learned?
column7: The action prevents the aversive event before it begins.
column8: OpenStax · https://openstax.org/books/psychology-2e/pages/6-3-operant-conditioning

column2: MCAT and USMLE::MCAT::Psychological and Social Foundations
column4: After repeated pairings with an air puff, a blue square alone elicits a blink. What role does the square now have?
column7: Its predictive relation to the puff was learned.
column8: OpenStax · https://openstax.org/books/psychology-2e/pages/6-2-classical-conditioning

column2: MCAT and USMLE::MCAT::Psychological and Social Foundations
column4: A high tone predicts a puff but a low tone never does. After training only the high tone evokes a blink. What has the participant learned?
column7: Different response patterns track which cue predicts the outcome.
column8: OpenStax · https://openstax.org/books/psychology-2e/pages/6-2-classical-conditioning

column2: MCAT and USMLE::MCAT::Psychological and Social Foundations
column4: A raccoon initially deposits a trained token but later rubs it repeatedly in a species-typical manner before deposit. What interferes with task performance?
column7: A species-typical behavioral tendency intrudes on the trained response.
column8: OpenStax · https://openstax.org/books/psychology-2e/pages/6-3-operant-conditioning

column2: MCAT and USMLE::MCAT::Psychological and Social Foundations
column4: A patient believes exercise is beneficial but doubts being able to complete even a short walk. Which social cognitive construct is low?
column7: The doubt concerns the ability to perform the action, distinct from expecting a benefit.
column8: OpenStax · https://openstax.org/books/psychology-2e/pages/11-4-learning-approaches

column2: MCAT and USMLE::MCAT::Psychological and Social Foundations
column4: A human imaging study finds anterior insula activity during exposure to a disgusting odor and while viewing another person's disgusted face. What inference does the overlap support?
column6: Some regional processing is shared during experienced and observed disgust.
column7: Regional overlap alone cannot establish that the same individual neurons fire or that subjective experiences are identical.

column2: MCAT and USMLE::MCAT::Psychological and Social Foundations
column4: A participant presses a button that stops an unpleasant sound already playing. Repeated successful presses increase responding. What kind of avoidance-or-escape learning is this?
column7: The behavior terminates an aversive stimulus already underway.
column8: OpenStax · https://openstax.org/books/psychology-2e/pages/6-3-operant-conditioning

column2: MCAT and USMLE::MCAT::Psychological and Social Foundations
column4: After each reward, the first response at least 30 seconds later earns the next one. Which schedule operates?
column7: The fixed time must elapse and a response is required.
column8: OpenStax · https://openstax.org/books/psychology-2e/pages/6-3-operant-conditioning

column2: MCAT and USMLE::MCAT::Psychological and Social Foundations
column4: A machine delivers a token after every fifth correct response regardless of elapsed time. Which schedule operates?
column7: A fixed number of responses is required.
column8: OpenStax · https://openstax.org/books/psychology-2e/pages/6-3-operant-conditioning

column2: MCAT and USMLE::MCAT::Psychological and Social Foundations
column4: After learning a blink to a 1000 Hz tone, a participant also blinks to a previously unheard 950 Hz tone. Which process fits?
column7: The new cue resembles the trained stimulus.
column8: OpenStax · https://openstax.org/books/psychology-2e/pages/6-2-classical-conditioning

column2: MCAT and USMLE::MCAT::Psychological and Social Foundations
column4: A premotor neuron fires when a macaque grasps an object and when it observes a similar grasp. What response property defines its mirror-like activity?
column6: The same neuron responds during performance and observation of a corresponding action.
column7: A visual response alone does not establish this property.
column8: di Pellegrino et al. · https://doi.org/10.1007/BF00230027

column2: MCAT and USMLE::MCAT::Psychological and Social Foundations
column4: A trainee watches a colleague use a checklist and reproduces the sequence on the first attempt before receiving feedback. What learning route fits?
column7: The behavior was acquired from a model before direct reinforcement.
column8: OpenStax · https://openstax.org/books/psychology-2e/pages/6-4-observational-learning-modeling

column2: MCAT and USMLE::MCAT::Psychological and Social Foundations
column4: Completing a check turns off an irritating alarm. The worker performs checks more often. How is the consequence classified?
column7: Removal of an aversive stimulus increases the action.
column8: OpenStax · https://openstax.org/books/psychology-2e/pages/6-3-operant-conditioning

column2: MCAT and USMLE::MCAT::Psychological and Social Foundations
column4: Before any pairings, a blue square elicits no anticipatory blink. Relative to later training with an air puff, what role does the square initially have?
column7: Its ability to predict the puff has not yet been acquired.
column8: OpenStax · https://openstax.org/books/psychology-2e/pages/6-2-classical-conditioning

column2: MCAT and USMLE::MCAT::Psychological and Social Foundations
column4: A player loses a point after breaking a rule and subsequently breaks it less often. Which consequence is operating?
column7: Something valued is removed and the action declines.
column8: OpenStax · https://openstax.org/books/psychology-2e/pages/6-3-operant-conditioning

column2: MCAT and USMLE::MCAT::Psychological and Social Foundations
column4: Calling out in class once produced attention. When attention consistently stops following the behavior, calling out gradually falls. Which process fits?
column7: The consequence that maintained the action is withheld.
column8: OpenStax · https://openstax.org/books/psychology-2e/pages/6-3-operant-conditioning

column2: MCAT and USMLE::MCAT::Psychological and Social Foundations
column4: Adding a point after each completed exercise increases the number completed. How is the consequence classified?
column7: A stimulus is added and the future rate of the action rises.
column8: OpenStax · https://openstax.org/books/psychology-2e/pages/6-3-operant-conditioning

column2: MCAT and USMLE::MCAT::Psychological and Social Foundations
column4: An unpleasant buzzer is added after a forbidden action. The action becomes less frequent. How is the consequence classified?
column7: A consequence is added and the subsequent action rate falls.
column8: OpenStax · https://openstax.org/books/psychology-2e/pages/6-3-operant-conditioning

column2: MCAT and USMLE::MCAT::Psychological and Social Foundations
column4: A food taste becomes aversive after one episode of delayed illness while a simultaneous neutral sound does not. What principle does this selective association illustrate?
column7: Some cue–outcome associations are more readily learned than others.
column8: OpenStax · https://openstax.org/books/psychology-2e/pages/6-2-classical-conditioning

column2: MCAT and USMLE::MCAT::Psychological and Social Foundations
column4: Water increases responding in a thirsty participant without needing to be paired with another reward. What kind of reinforcer is it?
column7: Its value follows from a biological need.
column8: OpenStax · https://openstax.org/books/psychology-2e/pages/6-3-operant-conditioning

column2: MCAT and USMLE::MCAT::Psychological and Social Foundations
column4: Joining a walking group builds confidence. Greater confidence increases attendance, which strengthens the group's support. Which social cognitive principle fits?
column7: Personal beliefs, behavior and environment influence each other.
column8: OpenStax · https://openstax.org/books/psychology-2e/pages/11-4-learning-approaches

column2: MCAT and USMLE::MCAT::Psychological and Social Foundations
column4: A learned tone-evoked blink fades during tone-only trials. The next morning it briefly reappears before any new puff is delivered. Which process fits?
column7: A rest interval can reveal a previously extinguished response.
column8: OpenStax · https://openstax.org/books/psychology-2e/pages/6-2-classical-conditioning

column2: MCAT and USMLE::MCAT::Psychological and Social Foundations
column4: A therapist first reinforces reaching for a toothbrush, then touching it, then lifting it. What makes this shaping?
column6: The criterion moves toward the target behavior in successive steps.
column7: Reinforcement selects progressively closer approximations.
column8: OpenStax · https://openstax.org/books/psychology-2e/pages/6-3-operant-conditioning

column2: MCAT and USMLE::MCAT::Psychological and Social Foundations
column4: A student endorses a proposal in front of unanimous peers but privately rejects it. What does the public–private difference suggest?
column7: A public response change alone does not establish a durable private attitude change.
column8: OpenStax · https://openstax.org/books/psychology-2e/pages/12-3-attitudes-and-persuasion

column2: MCAT and USMLE::MCAT::Psychological and Social Foundations
column4: Two audiences receive the same evidence. One has time, relevant knowledge and a personal stake in the issue. Which audience is more likely to scrutinize argument quality?
column7: Elaboration depends in part on opportunity, ability and motivation.
column8: OpenStax · https://openstax.org/books/psychology-2e/pages/12-3-attitudes-and-persuasion

column2: MCAT and USMLE::MCAT::Psychological and Social Foundations
column4: Tokens begin to increase responding only after they can be exchanged for food or activities. What kind of reinforcer is a token?
column7: It gains value through its relation to other reinforcers.
column8: OpenStax · https://openstax.org/books/psychology-2e/pages/6-3-operant-conditioning

column2: MCAT and USMLE::MCAT::Psychological and Social Foundations
column4: Before any conditioning, an air puff directed toward the eye causes a blink. What is the blink in this trial called?
column7: It is elicited by the puff without training.
column8: OpenStax · https://openstax.org/books/psychology-2e/pages/6-2-classical-conditioning

column2: MCAT and USMLE::MCAT::Psychological and Social Foundations
column4: Rewards become available after unpredictable time intervals. The first response after availability earns the reward. Which schedule operates?
column7: The waiting time varies and responding is still required.
column8: OpenStax · https://openstax.org/books/psychology-2e/pages/6-3-operant-conditioning

column2: MCAT and USMLE::MCAT::Psychological and Social Foundations
column4: A reward comes after unpredictable numbers of responses averaging five. Which schedule operates?
column7: The response requirement varies around a mean.
column8: OpenStax · https://openstax.org/books/psychology-2e/pages/6-3-operant-conditioning

column2: MCAT and USMLE::MCAT::Psychological and Social Foundations
column4: A student freely writes an essay against their own view for a trivial reward. Later their private opinion moves toward the essay. What process could explain the change?
column7: With little external justification, changing one's attitude can reduce the inconsistency.
column8: OpenStax, Psychology 2e · https://openstax.org/details/books/psychology-2e · Learning and social psychology

column2: MCAT and USMLE::MCAT::Psychological and Social Foundations
column4: Another student writes the same essay under a strong external requirement. Under dissonance theory, why might private attitude change be smaller?
column6: The behavior already has a sufficient external explanation.
column7: The same overt action can produce different pressure to change one's beliefs.
column8: OpenStax, Psychology 2e · https://openstax.org/details/books/psychology-2e · Learning and social psychology

column2: MCAT and USMLE::MCAT::Psychological and Social Foundations
column4: Two groups experience the same number of food and light events. Only the group in which light predicts food develops increasing salivation on light-only probes. Which learning phase does this pattern support?
column7: The exposure-matched comparison makes a nonspecific change less compelling.
column8: OpenStax · https://openstax.org/books/psychology-2e/pages/6-2-classical-conditioning

column2: MCAT and USMLE::MCAT::Psychological and Social Foundations
column4: In a tone study, both paired and explicitly unpaired groups show the same rise in probe responses. Do those data isolate associative acquisition?
column7: An increase shared with the unpaired group can arise from nonspecific exposure or arousal.
column8: OpenStax · https://openstax.org/books/psychology-2e/pages/6-2-classical-conditioning

column2: MCAT and USMLE::MCAT::Psychological and Social Foundations
column4: A student sees a warning that a distracting alert is about to start, mutes it and never hears it. Muting in response to the warning increases. Which learning process fits?
column7: The response prevents the impending aversive event.
column8: OpenStax · https://openstax.org/books/psychology-2e/pages/6-3-operant-conditioning

column2: MCAT and USMLE::MCAT::Psychological and Social Foundations
column4: The alert is already playing before the student mutes it. Which change in the event sequence makes this escape rather than avoidance?
column6: The aversive stimulus began before the response.
column7: The action now terminates an ongoing event.
column8: OpenStax · https://openstax.org/books/psychology-2e/pages/6-3-operant-conditioning

column2: MCAT and USMLE::MCAT::Psychological and Social Foundations
column4: A commuter initially felt fine at a station. After several nauseating rides, the station's odor alone evokes nausea. Which stimulus has acquired a predictive role?
column7: The odor now elicits a learned anticipatory response.
column8: OpenStax · https://openstax.org/books/psychology-2e/pages/6-2-classical-conditioning

column2: MCAT and USMLE::MCAT::Psychological and Social Foundations
column4: A light sequence repeatedly precedes a drop of lemon juice. Later the lights alone evoke salivation. In this test is the light sequence the conditioned stimulus or the conditioned response?
column7: Salivation is the response elicited by the learned cue.
column8: OpenStax · https://openstax.org/books/psychology-2e/pages/6-2-classical-conditioning

column2: MCAT and USMLE::MCAT::Psychological and Social Foundations
column4: A student learns to submit an answer only when the border is green because submissions during a gray border never count. What has the learner acquired?
column7: The cues signal different consequences for the same response.
column8: OpenStax · https://openstax.org/books/psychology-2e/pages/6-2-classical-conditioning

column2: MCAT and USMLE::MCAT::Psychological and Social Foundations
column4: Before training a learner responds more often to a bright border than a dark one. Does that baseline difference establish learned discrimination from the experiment?
column7: Compare later responses against baseline and counterbalance which cue predicts the outcome.
column8: OpenStax · https://openstax.org/books/psychology-2e/pages/6-2-classical-conditioning

column2: MCAT and USMLE::MCAT::Psychological and Social Foundations
column4: An animal was trained to drop a token for food but increasingly handles the token with its species-typical food-manipulation movements instead. Food is still available for dropping. Which phenomenon fits?
column7: A species-typical action intrudes on the trained response.
column8: OpenStax · https://openstax.org/books/psychology-2e/pages/6-3-operant-conditioning

column2: MCAT and USMLE::MCAT::Psychological and Social Foundations
column4: Another animal stops dropping tokens only after tokens cease to earn food. No species-typical replacement action appears. What simpler explanation fits?
column7: Here the maintaining reinforcer was removed.
column8: OpenStax · https://openstax.org/books/psychology-2e/pages/6-3-operant-conditioning

column2: MCAT and USMLE::MCAT::Psychological and Social Foundations
column4: A learner says, “If I could practice regularly it would help, but I doubt I can manage the schedule.” Which belief is low?
column6: Self-efficacy for carrying out the practice plan.
column7: The learner already expects the action to be beneficial.

Researchers study why junior team members sometimes withhold a correct observation. Participants work alone on a series of classification problems. Each person privately selects an answer before seeing what they are told are the answers of three peers. On a set of critical trials, all three peers appear to have selected the same incorrect answer. The peers' responses are prerecorded, and participants in all conditions see the same responses to the same problems.

Participants are randomly assigned to give their second answer either out loud to the peers or privately on a keypad. Everyone is told that the second answer will be scored for accuracy. There is no reward for agreement. A separate set of otherwise comparable trials shows no peer answers. The outcome is the percentage of trials in which an initially correct participant changes to an incorrect answer. The figure reports simulated group means. Participants are debriefed about the prerecorded responses after the session.

column4: What happens during an intake?
column5:
1. The therapist gathers specific information to address the client’s immediate needs such as the presenting problem, the client’s support system, and insurance status. The therapist informs the client about confidentiality, fees, and what to expect in a therapy session.
  2. The therapist guides what happens in the therapy session and designs a detailed approach to resolving each member’s presenting problem.
  3. The therapist meets with a couple to help them see how their individual backgrounds, beliefs, and actions are affecting their relationship.
  4. The therapist examines and discusses with the family the boundaries and structure of the family: For example, who makes the rules, who sleeps in the bed with whom, and how decisions are made.

column8: CMS · Emergency Medical Treatment and Labor Act · https://www.cms.gov/medicare/regulations-guidance/legislation/emergency-medical-treatment-labor-act · https://www.cms.gov/Priorities/your-patient-rights/emergency-room-rights

column4: A patient with hand symptoms says, “I can’t finish my shift.” What follow-up would most directly establish functional impact?

column7: Ask about the activity the patient can no longer do.
column8: NICE CG138 · Patient experience in adult services · https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg138/chapter/Recommendations

column4: A stable patient asks what happens if they choose monitoring for a condition that can safely be observed. What should the clinician explain?

column7: Observation can be an active option with a follow-up plan.
column8: AMA Code of Medical Ethics · Informed consent · https://code-medical-ethics.ama-assn.org/ethics-opinions/informed-consent

column7: The patient needs a reference point for the proposed benefit and harm.
column8: AMA Code of Medical Ethics · Informed consent · https://code-medical-ethics.ama-assn.org/ethics-opinions/informed-consent

column4: A patient with a time-sensitive condition asks whether waiting is an option. What should the clinician disclose about waiting?
column6: The risks of delay, including loss of benefit if a treatment window closes.
column7: Respecting choice includes explaining time-sensitive consequences.
column8: AMA Code of Medical Ethics · Informed consent · https://code-medical-ethics.ama-assn.org/ethics-opinions/informed-consent

column4: A ten-year-old understands an elective procedure when it is explained simply, but nobody has spoken to them. What should the clinician seek in addition to parental permission?
column7: Speak directly to the child and invite questions.
column8: AMA Code of Medical Ethics · Pediatric decision making · https://code-medical-ethics.ama-assn.org/ethics-opinions/pediatric-decision-making

column7: Participation can match the child's abilities.
column8: AMA Code of Medical Ethics · Pediatric decision making · https://code-medical-ethics.ama-assn.org/ethics-opinions/pediatric-decision-making

column6: The patient's wish to be present for their children.
column7: Reflecting the personally meaningful reason can invite elaboration.
column8: SAMHSA TIP 35 · Enhancing motivation for change · https://library.samhsa.gov/sites/default/files/tip-35-pep19-02-01-003.pdf

column4: What is the clinician listening for when eliciting change talk?
column6: The patient's own reasons, desire, ability, need or commitment to change.
column7: These statements can guide a collaborative next step.
column8: SAMHSA TIP 35 · Enhancing motivation for change · https://library.samhsa.gov/sites/default/files/tip-35-pep19-02-01-003.pdf

column4: A patient says, “Drinking helps me unwind, and I'm not ready to change.” What response can keep the conversation open?
column6: Acknowledge the perceived benefit and ask permission to explore the patient's perspective.
column7: Arguing for immediate action can obscure the ambivalence.
column8: SAMHSA TIP 35 · Enhancing motivation for change · https://library.samhsa.gov/sites/default/files/tip-35-pep19-02-01-003.pdf

column4: What does appreciation mean in a decision-specific capacity assessment?
column6: Recognizing how the condition and likely consequences apply to oneself.
column7: Repeating general facts demonstrates a different ability.
column8: Paul S. Appelbaum · Assessment of patients' competence to consent to treatment · https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMcp074045

column4: A patient says, “I know this could kill me soon, but the treatment burden is more than I want.” Does that statement by itself demonstrate impaired appreciation?
column6: No. It shows recognition that the risk can apply personally.
column7: Assess the other abilities and voluntariness.
column8: Paul S. Appelbaum · Assessment of patients' competence to consent to treatment · https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMcp074045

column7: A sound indication does not remove the competing interest.
column8: AMA Code of Medical Ethics · Physician self-referral · https://code-medical-ethics.ama-assn.org/ethics-opinions/physician-self-referral

column7: Evaluate the actual relationship and alternatives.
column8: AMA Code of Medical Ethics · Physician self-referral · https://code-medical-ethics.ama-assn.org/ethics-opinions/physician-self-referral

column4: A patient signs consent for a left-sided elective procedure. The team also wants to perform an unrelated elective procedure on the right. What further decision is needed?
column6: Specific informed authorization for the additional procedure.
column7: The original permission has a defined scope.
column8: AMA Code of Medical Ethics · Informed consent · https://code-medical-ethics.ama-assn.org/ethics-opinions/informed-consent

column4: A proceduralist describes the chance of symptom relief but omits a serious recognized complication relevant to the decision. What part of the consent discussion is missing?
column6: Disclosure of the material risk and its consequences.
column7: The chance of benefit alone cannot support an informed comparison.
column8: AMA Code of Medical Ethics · Informed consent · https://code-medical-ethics.ama-assn.org/ethics-opinions/informed-consent

column4: What is the purpose of explaining benefits and burdens before seeking treatment authorization?
column6: To let the patient weigh the likely consequences in light of their own goals.
column7: Discuss the nature and purpose of the intervention and reasonable alternatives.
column8: AMA Code of Medical Ethics · Informed consent · https://code-medical-ethics.ama-assn.org/ethics-opinions/informed-consent

column2: MCAT and USMLE::USMLE Step 1::Communication
column4: A professional singer asks about a low-frequency risk of persistent voice change. Why does this merit specific discussion?
column6: It could materially affect an outcome the patient especially values.
column7: Clinical importance depends partly on the patient's circumstances.
column8: AMA Code of Medical Ethics · Informed consent · https://code-medical-ethics.ama-assn.org/ethics-opinions/informed-consent

column2: MCAT and USMLE::USMLE Step 1::Communication
column4: A stable patient asks, “Do I definitely have this illness?” The findings favor it but a confirmatory test is pending. How can the clinician answer accurately?
column6: Explain that it is the most likely explanation so far and agree who will communicate the result and when.
column7: Give the best-supported assessment and a concrete way to resolve the uncertainty.
column8: NICE CG138 · Patient experience in adult services · https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg138/chapter/Recommendations

column4: What does calling a diagnosis “the working diagnosis” communicate?
column6: It is the leading explanation and can change as evidence develops.
column7: Distinguish the current interpretation from a confirmed finding.
column8: NICE CG138 · Patient experience in adult services · https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg138/chapter/Recommendations

column4: A patient awaiting confirmation of a working diagnosis reports new difficulty breathing. What should the clinician say about waiting for the scheduled result call?
column7: A safety-net plan must account for deterioration before a test returns.
column8: NICE CG138 · Patient experience in adult services · https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg138/chapter/Recommendations

column2: MCAT and USMLE::USMLE Step 1::Communication
column4: What should the clinician do with an emotional cue before moving on to technical details?
column6: Acknowledge it and give the patient room to respond.
column7: The patient's response helps determine when they are ready for information.
column8: NICE CG138 · Patient experience in adult services · https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg138/chapter/Recommendations

column4: A patient asks why the infusion was given too quickly. The team knows the rate delivered but has not determined the cause. What should the clinician say about the cause?
column6: Acknowledge that the cause is still being investigated and arrange an update.
column7: Share the known facts and effects now without guessing.
column8: AHRQ · CANDOR response and disclosure · https://www.ahrq.gov/patient-safety/settings/hospital/candor/modules/guide5/notes.html

column2: MCAT and USMLE::USMLE Step 1::Communication
column4: A review confirms that a dose was ten times the order. The contributing system failures remain uncertain. Which fact can be stated plainly now?
column6: The patient received ten times the ordered dose.
column7: Uncertainty about why the error occurred does not erase what has been verified.
column8: AHRQ · CANDOR response and disclosure · https://www.ahrq.gov/patient-safety/settings/hospital/candor/modules/guide5/notes.html

column2: MCAT and USMLE::USMLE Step 1::Communication
column4: Through a qualified interpreter, a patient gives a long account of their symptoms. To whom should the clinician direct the next question?

column7: Allow enough time for accurate interpretation.
column8: US Department of Justice · ADA requirements for effective communication · https://www.ada.gov/resources/effective-communication/

column4: A capable adult using a qualified interpreter asks to discuss medications without their visiting relatives. How should the room arrangement change?

column7: Interpretation supports direct communication while preserving privacy.
column8: HHS Office for Civil Rights · Language access and effective communication · https://www.hhs.gov/sites/default/files/ocr-dcl-section-1557-language-access.pdf

column4: A patient who agreed to a placebo reports less pain after taking it. Does that response show the original pain was fabricated?

column7: A placebo response cannot separate genuine from feigned pain.

column4: What makes a substance a placebo for the specific condition being treated?
column6: It has no expected specific pharmacologic effect on that condition.
column7: Context and expectations can still affect the patient's experience.
column8: AMA Code of Medical Ethics · Use of placebo in clinical practice · https://code-medical-ethics.ama-assn.org/ethics-opinions/use-placebo-clinical-practice

column4: A patient reports no relief after an agreed placebo. Does this prove the symptom has a specific organic cause?
column6: No. Lack of a placebo response does not determine etiology.
column7: Investigate according to the clinical history and findings.
column8: AMA Code of Medical Ethics · Use of placebo in clinical practice · https://code-medical-ethics.ama-assn.org/ethics-opinions/use-placebo-clinical-practice

column4: What is the purpose of an open invitation at the beginning of a nonurgent consultation?
column6: To learn what matters to the patient in their own words.
column7: Early details can change which questions the clinician asks next.
column8: NICE CG138 · Patient experience in adult services · https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg138/chapter/Recommendations

column4: A patient stops talking after being interrupted twice and says, “You're already deciding for me.” What could the clinician say to reopen the conversation?

column7: Acknowledge the interruption and give the patient the floor.
column8: NICE CG138 · Patient experience in adult services · https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg138/chapter/Recommendations

column2: MCAT and USMLE::USMLE Step 1::Communication
column4: What gives a capable adult's refusal of a recommended treatment ethical authority?
column6: A voluntary, informed choice about their own care.
column7: Explore understanding and reasons without coercion.

A sleep study shows intermittent pauses in breathing while the upper airway remains patent. During an episode, rising blood carbon dioxide produces little increase in inspiratory stimulation.

Which of the following failures most directly accounts for this pattern?
column5:
1. Excessive inspiratory stimulation despite a patent airway

  3. Excessive pharyngeal relaxation closing the upper airway

column2: MCAT and USMLE::USMLE Step 2 CK::Anesthesiology
column4:
During an adult cardiac arrest, a tracheal tube is passed under direct view. Waveform capnography attached immediately shows a regular waveform with every breath, but the end-tidal CO2 is only 12 mmHg. One team member says the value is too low for a tracheal tube and wants it removed. Breath sounds are difficult to hear over the compressions.

What is the best interpretation?
column5:
1. Tracheal, with low CO2 from low cardiac output
  2. Oesophageal, as end-tidal CO2 is under 35 mmHg
  3. Uncertain until a chest radiograph is reviewed
  4. Uncertain until breath sounds are clearly heard
  5. Uncertain until oxygen saturation has improved
column6: Tracheal, with low CO2 from low cardiac output
column7: A sustained waveform with every breath shows CO2 returning from the lungs, which confirms tracheal placement. During CPR pulmonary blood flow is low, so end-tidal values are commonly low; the value then guides CPR quality and can signal return of circulation.

column2: MCAT and USMLE::USMLE Step 2 CK::Anesthesiology
column4:
During adult CPR, a patient has a tracheal tube and an arterial line. A rescuer begins squeezing the bag rapidly with large breaths at about 30/min. Arterial diastolic pressure during compressions falls from 30 to 18 mmHg, and end-tidal CO2 falls from 22 to 12 mmHg. The team leader asks for 10 breaths per minute.

Which mechanism best explains the fall in perfusion pressure?
column5:
1. Raised intrathoracic pressure cutting venous return
  2. Hypocapnia causing coronary arterial vasoconstriction
  3. Alveolar overdistension impairing oxygen uptake
  4. Compression pauses needed to deliver each breath
  5. Gastric inflation splinting the diaphragm
column6: Raised intrathoracic pressure cutting venous return
column7: Frequent large breaths raise mean intrathoracic pressure, which impedes venous return and reduces the output each compression generates, so arterial diastolic pressure falls. End-tidal CO2 falls both from washout and from the lower flow, so the diastolic pressure is the cleaner signal here.

column4: Two populations have the same life expectancy at birth, but people in one spend more years with disabling illness of the same severity. Which is expected to have lower healthy life expectancy?
column6: The population spending more time with disability.
column7: HALE adjusts expected years of life for time lived in less than full health.
column8: WHO Global Health Observatory · https://www.who.int/data/gho/data/indicators/indicator-details/GHO/gho-ghe-hale-healthy-life-expectancy · healthy life expectancy

column2: MCAT and USMLE::USMLE Step 2 CK::Biostatistics
column4: Hand hygiene improves while staff know an auditor is watching, then falls after the auditor leaves. What response can explain the temporary change?
column6: Behavior change due to awareness of observation, often called the Hawthorne effect.

column4: A program sees fewer infections among unvaccinated infants after eligible older children are vaccinated. Which population effect could contribute?
column7: A before-after pattern alone does not prove this explanation. Other time trends require evaluation.
column8: CDC, Principles of Epidemiology · https://archive.cdc.gov/www_cdc_gov/csels/dsepd/ss1978/lesson1/section10.html · chain of infection and herd immunity

column4: What is the modal length of stay in this cohort?
column7: Both bars reach 12 patients. A mode can have more than one value.
column8: Penn State STAT 200 · https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat200/Lesson02 · distributions, location and variation

column4: A hospital wants a typical length of stay from the cohort shown. Why report a median alongside the mean?

column2: MCAT and USMLE::USMLE Step 2 CK::Biostatistics
column4: A proportional-hazards model reports a treatment hazard ratio of 0.70. How should that ratio be expressed in words?
column6: An estimated 30% lower instantaneous hazard in the treatment group, conditional on still being at risk.
column7: A claim of 30 percentage points fewer events would need cumulative event risks.
column8: NCI Dictionary of Cancer Terms · https://www.cancer.gov/publications/dictionaries/cancer-terms/def/hazard-ratio · hazard ratio. Cochrane Handbook ch 6 · https://www.cochrane.org/authors/handbooks-and-manuals/handbook/current/chapter-06

column2: MCAT and USMLE::USMLE Step 2 CK::Biostatistics
column4: An association emerged from a search of thousands of variables. What evaluation gives a stronger independent test of that specific hypothesis?
column6: Prespecify the association and analysis in a new dataset or trial.
column7: Reusing the discovery data does not provide independent confirmation.
column8: ICH E9 · https://database.ich.org/sites/default/files/E9_Guideline.pdf · sections 3 and 5, trial size, estimation, multiplicity and subgroups

column2: MCAT and USMLE::USMLE Step 2 CK::Biostatistics
column4: A trial reports mean improvement with treatment versus control of 3.0 points, 95% CI 2.4 to 3.6. The selected patient-important threshold is 2 points. Does the interval support an average benefit above that threshold?
column6: Yes. Even the lower confidence limit exceeds 2 points.
column7: This concerns the trial average. Individual benefit is still uncertain.
column8: Cochrane Handbook chapter 15 · https://www.cochrane.org/authors/handbooks-and-manuals/handbook/current/chapter-15 · absolute effects, applicability and implications for practice

column2: MCAT and USMLE::USMLE Step 2 CK::Biostatistics
column4: In another trial the average symptom benefit is 1.3 points, 95% CI 0.9 to 1.7. Patients consider 2 points worthwhile. The p-value is below 0.01. Does the interval support a two-point average benefit?
column6: No. Its upper limit of 1.7 is below the worthwhile threshold.
column7: The interval excludes zero but also excludes the specified clinically important benefit.
column8: Cochrane Handbook chapter 15 · https://www.cochrane.org/authors/handbooks-and-manuals/handbook/current/chapter-15 · absolute effects, applicability and implications for practice

column2: MCAT and USMLE::USMLE Step 2 CK::Biostatistics
column4: A patient reports that a two-point reduction on a symptom scale would make treatment worthwhile. Which trial quantity should be compared with two points?
column6: The estimated between-group symptom difference and its confidence interval.
column7: Use the same units and time horizon. A p-value alone does not quantify benefit.
column8: Cochrane Handbook chapter 15 · https://www.cochrane.org/authors/handbooks-and-manuals/handbook/current/chapter-15 · absolute effects, applicability and implications for practice

column2: MCAT and USMLE::USMLE Step 2 CK::Biostatistics
column4: A closed cohort has 500 participants, including 100 with prior disease. Over one year 20 of the remaining people develop disease, with complete follow-up. What is the one-year risk among those initially disease-free?
column7: 20 new cases divided by 400 people at risk equals 0.05.
column8: CDC, Principles of Epidemiology · https://archive.cdc.gov/www_cdc_gov/csels/dsepd/ss1978/lesson3/ · measures of frequency, association and public health impact

column2: MCAT and USMLE::USMLE Step 2 CK::Biostatistics
column4: A trial tests efficacy at p < 0.05 every month and stops at the first favorable result. What error rate is inflated without a sequential plan?
column6: The overall Type I error rate.
column7: Repeated opportunities to reject the null raise the chance of a false-positive result.
column8: FDA, Clinical Trial Data Monitoring Committees · https://www.fda.gov/media/75398/download · interim review, committee independence and recommendations

column2: MCAT and USMLE::USMLE Step 2 CK::Biostatistics
column4: An investigator has funding and departmental approval for a nonexempt human-subjects trial requiring IRB review. May enrollment begin before the IRB approves the work?
column6: No. Obtain the required IRB approval before initiating the research.
column7: Funding and internal administrative approval do not substitute for independent human-subject review.
column8: FDA, Clinical Trial Data Monitoring Committees · https://www.fda.gov/media/75398/download · interim review, committee independence and recommendations

column2: MCAT and USMLE::USMLE Step 2 CK::Biostatistics
column4: A participant randomized to the intervention stops taking it after a side effect, but agrees to follow-up. What should investigators do about later outcomes for the assignment-effect analysis?
column6: Continue collecting and analyzing outcomes under the original assignment.
column7: Stopping treatment need not mean withdrawing permission to collect outcomes. Respect the participant's choices.
column8: Cochrane Handbook chapter 8 · https://www.cochrane.org/authors/handbooks-and-manuals/handbook/current/chapter-08 · randomization, deviations, measurement and missing outcomes

column2: MCAT and USMLE::USMLE Step 2 CK::Biostatistics
column4: A participant randomized to intervention receives usual care instead. Where does their observed outcome belong in a conventional intention-to-treat comparison?
column7: Classifying patients by treatment received can reintroduce prognostic differences.
column8: Cochrane Handbook chapter 8 · https://www.cochrane.org/authors/handbooks-and-manuals/handbook/current/chapter-08 · randomization, deviations, measurement and missing outcomes

column2: MCAT and USMLE::USMLE Step 2 CK::Biostatistics
column4: At what month does estimated event-free survival first reach or fall below one half in this cohort?
column7: The estimate remains above 0.5 at month 6 and crosses it at the next event time.

column4: Without screening, diagnosis would occur at age 70 and death at 73. Screening finds disease at age 67, and death still occurs at 73. How much apparent survival gain is due to lead time?

column2: MCAT and USMLE::USMLE Step 2 CK::Biostatistics
column4: A patient has pretest odds of 1:9 and a positive result with LR+ of 3. What are the posttest odds?
column7: Multiply odds 1/9 by 3 to get 1/3. The resulting probability is 25%.
column8: AHRQ, Test Performance Metrics · https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/sites/books/NBK98249/ · predictive values, likelihood ratios and ROC curves

column2: MCAT and USMLE::USMLE Step 2 CK::Biostatistics
column4: Participants and treating clinicians know treatment assignment, but outcome adjudicators receive anonymized records stripped of treatment indicators. Which group is masked?
column7: This can reduce biased outcome classification even when participant or clinician masking is infeasible.
column8: Cochrane Handbook chapter 8 · https://www.cochrane.org/authors/handbooks-and-manuals/handbook/current/chapter-08 · randomization, deviations, measurement and missing outcomes

column4: Cases and controls are individually matched by age. A researcher concludes educational level is balanced because age was matched. Is that warranted?

column7: Check other confounders and use an analysis appropriate to the matching.
column8: CDC Field Epidemiology Manual · https://www.cdc.gov/field-epi-manual/php/chapters/design-conduct-analyze-field-studies.html · sampling, study design and controls

column4: A region records four maternal deaths meeting the standard definition and 20,000 live births in a year. What is its maternal mortality ratio per 100,000 live births?
column7: 4/20,000 × 100,000 = 20. Use qualifying maternal deaths and live births for the same period.
column8: WHO · https://www.who.int/data/gho/indicator-metadata-registry/imr-details/26 · maternal mortality ratio

column2: MCAT and USMLE::USMLE Step 2 CK::Biostatistics
column4: In a large trial, the one-year risk difference is −10 points in one prespecified age group and +3 points in another. What comparison formally assesses whether effects differ by age?

column7: Separate significance tests within age groups do not test whether treatment effects differ.
column8: ICH E9 · https://database.ich.org/sites/default/files/E9_Guideline.pdf · sections 3 and 5, trial size, estimation, multiplicity and subgroups

column4: A linear model predicts systolic blood pressure in mm Hg. Its age coefficient is +0.4 per year after adjustment for weight. How should it be interpreted?

column4: A treatment reduces two-year fracture risk from 12% to 8%. What is the two-year NNT?
column7: Absolute risk reduction is 0.04, and 1/0.04 = 25.
column8: CDC Field Epidemiology Manual · https://www.cdc.gov/field-epi-manual/php/chapters/analyze-interpret-data.html · risk, rates and interpreting comparisons

column4: A registry codes blood groups A, B, AB and O as 1, 2, 3 and 4. Which summary preserves the measurement scale?

column7: The numeric codes are nominal labels. Their arithmetic mean has no clinical interpretation.
column8: Penn State STAT 200 · https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat200/Lesson02 · distributions, location and variation

column4: For an approximately normal measurement, a threshold is two standard deviations above the mean. Roughly what fraction exceeds it?
column6: About 2.3%, or roughly 2.5% using the 95% rule.
column7: The remaining observations are below the upper threshold. This approximation depends on the shape of the distribution.
column8: NIST Engineering Statistics Handbook · https://www.itl.nist.gov/div898/handbook/eda/section3/eda3661.htm · normal distribution

column4: Among 300 negative tests, independent follow-up identifies disease in 6. What is the negative predictive value?
column7: 294 true negatives divided by 300 negative tests = 0.98.

column4: Among 60 cases, 30 had the exposure. Among 80 controls, 20 had the exposure. What is the exposure odds ratio?

column4: A large randomized trial reports p = 0.001 for a tiny mean difference. Does the p-value measure the probability that patients will find the benefit worthwhile?

column4: One-year risk in a population is 5%. It would be 3% if a causal exposure were removed. What fraction of population events is attributable to the exposure?
column7: (0.05 − 0.03)/0.05 = 0.40. The absolute attributable risk is 2 percentage points.

column4: A large confirmatory trial tests clinical benefit and monitors harms in the intended patient population before a marketing application. Which phase is typical?

column4: After initial safety work, investigators seek a preliminary efficacy signal and refine dose in patients with the target condition. Which phase is typical?
column7: Larger confirmatory studies usually follow if the benefit–risk profile supports further work.
column8: FDA, Step 3 Clinical Research · https://www.fda.gov/patients/drug-development-process/step-3-clinical-research · phases of drug development

column2: MCAT and USMLE::USMLE Step 2 CK::Biostatistics
column4: An FDA-approved drug is prescribed off-label to one patient. Does the off-label designation itself turn that encounter into a phase 4 clinical trial?
column6: No. A clinical trial requires a research design evaluating an intervention.
column7: Off-label describes use outside the approved labeling. Postmarketing research is a separate activity.
column8: FDA, Understanding Unapproved Use of Approved Drugs · https://www.fda.gov/understanding-unapproved-use-approved-drugs-label · clinical use outside labeling

column2: MCAT and USMLE::USMLE Step 2 CK::Biostatistics
column4: Both arms improve after receiving indistinguishable pills. Can the change from baseline in the placebo arm be attributed entirely to a placebo effect?
column6: No. Natural history, regression to the mean and measurement variation can also contribute.
column7: A placebo arm estimates outcomes under its entire comparison condition.
column8: Cochrane Handbook chapter 8 · https://www.cochrane.org/authors/handbooks-and-manuals/handbook/current/chapter-08 · randomization, deviations, measurement and missing outcomes

column2: MCAT and USMLE::USMLE Step 2 CK::Biostatistics
column4: A trial would withhold proven life-saving therapy from one arm, creating serious avoidable harm. What comparator design could preserve established care?
column6: Give standard therapy to both arms and randomize the additional intervention versus a suitable control when scientifically justified.
column7: Evaluate the entire benefit–risk balance and ethical acceptability.
column8: WMA Declaration of Helsinki · https://www.wma.net/policies-post/wma-declaration-of-helsinki/ · risk, consent and use of placebo

column2: MCAT and USMLE::USMLE Step 2 CK::Biostatistics
column4: Two comparable trials estimate a mean benefit of 2 and 6 points on the same scale. In a fixed-effect synthesis their normalized inverse-variance weights are 0.75 and 0.25. What is the pooled mean benefit?
column7: 0.75 × 2 + 0.25 × 6 = 3. The pooled estimate stays closer to the more heavily weighted trial.
column8: Cochrane Handbook chapter 10 · https://www.cochrane.org/authors/handbooks-and-manuals/handbook/current/chapter-10 · forest plots, synthesis and heterogeneity

column2: MCAT and USMLE::USMLE Step 2 CK::Biostatistics
column4: A trial is redesigned to detect a smaller difference at the same alpha, power and variance. In what direction must its sample size change?
column7: Smaller effects are harder to distinguish from random variation.
column8: ICH E9 · https://database.ich.org/sites/default/files/E9_Guideline.pdf · sections 3 and 5, trial size, estimation, multiplicity and subgroups

column2: MCAT and USMLE::USMLE Step 2 CK::Biostatistics
column4: For a fixed rejection threshold, shifting the alternative sampling distribution farther into the rejection region changes power in which direction?
column7: A larger true effect is easier to detect at the same standard error and alpha.
column8: ICH E9 · https://database.ich.org/sites/default/files/E9_Guideline.pdf · sections 3 and 5, trial size, estimation, multiplicity and subgroups

column2: MCAT and USMLE::USMLE Step 2 CK::Biostatistics
column4: A trial tests a service in ordinary primary care with broad eligibility and routine delivery. Is its primary aim closer to efficacy under ideal conditions or effectiveness in practice?
column7: Check whether sites and patients resemble the setting where the service will be offered.
column8: Cochrane Handbook chapter 15 · https://www.cochrane.org/authors/handbooks-and-manuals/handbook/current/chapter-15 · absolute effects, applicability and implications for practice

column2: MCAT and USMLE::USMLE Step 2 CK::Biostatistics
column4: A study reports equal average symptom relief with a daily pill or weekly injection. What patient-specific information is needed before choosing between them?
column6: The patient's preferences and practical constraints for each regimen, alongside harms and other outcome differences.
column7: When average benefits are similar, treatment burden and route may matter substantially to the patient.
column8: Cochrane Handbook chapter 15 · https://www.cochrane.org/authors/handbooks-and-manuals/handbook/current/chapter-15 · absolute effects, applicability and implications for practice

column2: MCAT and USMLE::USMLE Step 2 CK::Biostatistics
column4: Treatment prolongs survival with a chronic disease but changes neither cure nor the rate of new disease. In a stable population, which frequency measure is expected to rise?
column7: Longer average disease duration increases the number living with the condition.
column8: CDC, Principles of Epidemiology · https://archive.cdc.gov/www_cdc_gov/csels/dsepd/ss1978/lesson3/ · measures of frequency, association and public health impact

column2: MCAT and USMLE::USMLE Step 2 CK::Biostatistics
column4: A community offers recommended screening to asymptomatic residents and arranges follow-up for abnormal results. Which level of prevention does early detection represent?
column7: Assessing someone who already has symptoms is diagnostic evaluation.
column8: CDC Field Epidemiology Manual · https://www.cdc.gov/field-epi-manual/php/chapters/analyze-interpret-data.html · risk, rates and interpreting comparisons

column2: MCAT and USMLE::USMLE Step 2 CK::Biostatistics
column4: At a HIPAA-covered hospital, a researcher wants identifiable records without individual authorization and claims the project qualifies for a research waiver. Who can approve a HIPAA waiver if the criteria are met?

column7: A researcher's assertion does not establish the waiver. Apply the HIPAA requirements and document the approval.
column8: HHS, HIPAA and Research · https://www.hhs.gov/hipaa/for-professionals/special-topics/research/index.html · authorization, IRB or Privacy Board waivers

column2: MCAT and USMLE::USMLE Step 2 CK::Biostatistics
column4: In a population 20% have A, 30% have B and 8% have both. What percentage have A or B or both?

column2: MCAT and USMLE::USMLE Step 2 CK::Biostatistics
column4: A trial's interim endpoint is added after the investigators inspect outcomes. What document should reveal whether this analysis was prespecified?

column7: Distinguish planned analyses from post hoc additions in the report.
column8: HHS, Protection of Human Subjects · https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-45/subtitle-A/subchapter-A/part-46/subpart-A · §§46.108, 46.111, 46.116, review, risk and consent

column4: A town's age pyramid has a broad base and very narrow oldest bands. Which feature of the data supports prioritizing pediatric service capacity?
column6: A large number or share in the youngest age groups.
column7: Use absolute counts and local needs to size services. Shape alone does not determine all priorities.

column4:
On the second day after severe head injury, a patient develops urine output of 450–600 mL/hour. He has received no mannitol, diuretic or lithium, kidney function is stable, and urine testing shows no glucose. Paired samples show:

| Measurement | Result | Reference or context |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Serum sodium | 159 mmol/L | 135–145 |
| Serum osmolality | 326 mOsm/kg | 275–295 |
| Urine osmolality | 95 mOsm/kg | Varies with hydration; should rise with hyperosmolar plasma |

Which diagnosis best explains the pattern?
column5:
1. Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion
  2. Cerebral salt wasting after the head injury
  3. Central diabetes insipidus after brain injury
  4. Primary polydipsia with excess water intake
  5. Appropriate renal excretion of an excessive sodium load
column6: Central diabetes insipidus after brain injury
column7: Hypothalamic or pituitary injury can impair vasopressin release. High urine volume that remains dilute despite hyperosmolar plasma is the characteristic failure of water conservation.
column8: Diabetes insipidus · https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/diabetes_insipidus/ · https://github.com/todd866/cohort/blob/276ce7e9bff5296f5a7d88808bcfdee7c21fe5f5/open-content/modules/questions/icu/q-7d2c230b019e.v1.json

An awake adult on a NSW ward has a new nasogastric tube inserted for feeding; insertion was uneventful, with no coughing or distress. The aspirate, tested on a graded pH strip, reads 4.5. She takes a proton-pump inhibitor, and the nurse asks whether a chest x-ray is needed before use because acid suppression makes pH testing unreliable.

What should the medical officer advise?
column5:
1. Order a chest x-ray, as the PPI makes the pH unreliable
  2. Confirm with air insufflation and listening over the stomach
  3. Document the pH and use the tube; no x-ray is needed
  4. Use a carbon dioxide detector before allowing any feed
  5. Repeat the pH in four hours before giving anything
column6: Document the pH and use the tube; no x-ray is needed
column7: Under NSW guidance an aspirate pH of 5 or below on a graded strip confirms gastric placement on insertion. Document the pH and external length and use the tube; an x-ray is needed when the pH is above 5, no aspirate is obtained or there is clinical concern.

column4:
A 22-year-old nonsmoker sees his GP about episodes of cough, chest tightness and wheeze over two years, usually with colds, exercise or cold air, and he is well between them. Today he is asymptomatic, his chest is clear and spirometry is normal, with no significant bronchodilator response. He asks for an inhaler to start now, as he has a work fitness test in two months.

What should the GP do next?
column5:
1. Tell him that asthma is excluded by today’s normal spirometry
  2. Start as-needed ICS–formoterol and confirm asthma by response
  3. Retest when symptomatic or arrange a bronchial challenge test
  4. Diagnose exercise-induced bronchoconstriction only, with SABA
  5. Refer for laryngoscopy to look for vocal cord dysfunction
column6: Retest when symptomatic or arrange a bronchial challenge test
column7: The history suggests asthma, but variable expiratory airflow limitation has not been shown. Repeat spirometry when he has symptoms, or arrange a bronchial provocation test, to document it before committing him to long-term treatment.
column8: Australian Asthma Handbook: Diagnosing asthma in adults and adolescents · https://files.asthmahandbook.org.au/pdfs/pdf-43.pdf · https://github.com/todd866/cohort/blob/276ce7e9bff5296f5a7d88808bcfdee7c21fe5f5/open-content/modules/questions/icu/q-ef859a235c32.v1.json

column2: MCAT and USMLE::USMLE Step 2 CK::Critical care
column4:
A ward medical officer reviews a patient admitted with vomiting and dehydration. Urine output has remained above 0.5 mL/kg/hour throughout. The same laboratory reports the following creatinine results.

| Time | Creatinine | Reference interval |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Admission | 62 µmol/L | 45–100 µmol/L |
| 36 hours later | 90 µmol/L | 45–100 µmol/L |

How should the trend be interpreted?
column5:
1. Not AKI, because the rise is less than 1.5 times baseline
  2. AKI, because the 48-hour rise exceeds the absolute threshold
  3. Not AKI, because both results lie within the reference interval
  4. Not AKI, because urine output has stayed above the threshold
  5. Stage 2 AKI, because creatinine has risen by almost half
column6: AKI, because the 48-hour rise exceeds the absolute threshold
column7: Creatinine rose by 28 µmol/L within 48 hours, which meets the KDIGO criterion of a rise of at least 26.5 µmol/L in 48 hours. This is stage 1 AKI even though both values are within the reference interval.
column8: Acute kidney injury: prevention, detection and management · https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng148/chapter/Recommendations · https://github.com/todd866/cohort/blob/276ce7e9bff5296f5a7d88808bcfdee7c21fe5f5/open-content/modules/questions/icu/q-f60aa1dd0a85.v1.json

A 71-year-old man falls forwards down two steps and strikes his forehead. He is alert, with no intoxication or head-injury findings. Cervical CT shows multilevel degenerative change but no fracture or malalignment. He now has no midline tenderness but describes burning in both hands, and examination finds mild bilateral grip weakness with normal power and sensation in the legs. The ED consultant asks whether the normal CT allows the collar to be removed.

What should happen next?
column5:
1. Remove the collar, as CT has shown no bony injury
  2. Keep spinal motion restriction and arrange cervical MRI
  3. Obtain flexion–extension radiographs to look for instability
  4. Remove the collar and request outpatient nerve studies
  5. Request CT angiography to assess the vertebral arteries
column6: Keep spinal motion restriction and arrange cervical MRI
column7: Bilateral hand burning and weakness, worse in the arms than the legs, after a hyperextension injury in a spondylotic neck suggest a central cord injury without fracture. MRI shows the cord, discs and ligaments; keep spinal motion restriction until it is done.

column4:
Tom, aged 12, is brought to his GP because his parents think his puberty has begun. For about a year he has had body odour and a few fine hairs at the base of the penis. He has grown steadily along the 25th centile with no recent acceleration. On examination, both testes measure 2 mL with an orchidometer.

Which is the correct interpretation?
column5:
1. Puberty has begun, as pubic hair is its first sign in boys
  2. Puberty is delayed for his age and needs investigating now
  3. Central puberty has not begun, as the testes are under 4 mL
  4. Puberty is precocious, as hair appeared before he turned 12
  5. Puberty has begun but stalled, as his growth has not sped up
column6: Central puberty has not begun, as the testes are under 4 mL
column7: Testicular enlargement to 4 mL or more marks the onset of central puberty in boys, normally between 9 and 14 years. At 2 mL, his hair and odour reflect adrenarche, and central puberty has not yet begun.

  2. Direct antiglobulin test and reticulocyte count
  3. Thyroid function tests (TSH and free T4)

  2. A small fissure and fresh blood on the paper
  3. Overflow soiling and a palpable faecal mass
  4. A low-fibre diet and very little water
  5. Flat buttocks, deep pit above the cleft

The vomiting stopped, but since then he has had frequent loose, frothy, sour-smelling stools and a red, sore bottom, and he is windy and unsettled after his cow's milk drinks. There is no blood in the stool and no rash. He drank cow's milk without problems before the illness and is still growing along the 50th centile.

What is the most likely cause of his diarrhoea?
column5:

  2. Primary lactase non-persistence
  3. Toddler's (chronic non-specific) diarrhoea

column4:
A 6-year-old boy of Greek background develops jaundice, dark urine and pallor 2 days after starting trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole for a urinary tract infection. He has mild tachycardia but no bleeding or rash, and his urine output is normal.

| Test | Result | Reference range |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Haemoglobin | 72 g/L | 115–155 |
| Reticulocytes | 9% | 0.5–2.5 |
| Platelets | 260 × 10⁹/L | 150–450 |
| Creatinine | 40 µmol/L | 25–60 |
| Direct antiglobulin test | Negative | Negative |
| Blood film | Blister cells and irregularly contracted cells; no schistocytes | No abnormal forms |

Which underlying disorder is most likely?
column5:
1. Drug-induced immune haemolytic anaemia
  2. Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency
  3. Hereditary spherocytosis with haemolytic crisis
  4. Haemolytic uraemic syndrome after infection
  5. Paroxysmal cold haemoglobinuria after infection
column7: Correct. Acute haemolysis 2 days after an oxidant drug in a boy of Mediterranean background, with a negative antiglobulin test and blister and irregularly contracted cells, fits G6PD deficiency. The enzyme level can be falsely normal during the reticulocytosis, so repeat it later if needed.

column4:
An 8-month-old boy who is exclusively breastfed has become floppy over 6 weeks, has stopped reaching for toys and no longer babbles. He had a cold 3 weeks ago. His mother had weight-loss surgery 4 years ago and stopped the injections prescribed afterwards when she became pregnant; she feels well. He is pale, with no jaundice or organomegaly.

| Test | Result | Reference range |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Haemoglobin | 78 g/L | 105–135 |
| MCV | 96 fL | 70–86 |
| Reticulocytes | 12 × 10⁹/L | 25–100 |
| Bilirubin | 14 µmol/L | 3–20 |

Which diagnosis best unifies the neurological and haematological findings?
column5:
1. Transient erythroblastopenia of childhood
  2. Anaemia of chronic inflammation
  3. Hereditary spherocytosis
  4. G6PD enzyme deficiency
  5. Vitamin B12 deficiency
  6. Acute blood loss
  7. Autoimmune haemolytic anaemia
  8. Beta-thalassaemia major
column7: Correct. Macrocytic anaemia with low reticulocytes and loss of motor, language and social skills in an exclusively breastfed infant points to vitamin B12 deficiency. Weight-loss surgery impairs B12 absorption, his mother stopped her B12 injections, and her milk is low in B12 even though she feels well; his stores at birth also depended on her. Both need treatment, and early treatment can reverse much of the regression.

column4:
A previously healthy 14-month-old girl has had fever to 40 °C for 3 days with a mildly runny nose. On day 2 she had a 2-minute generalised seizure during the fever. She had her MMR vaccine at 12 months. This morning she is afebrile and playful, and a pink, blanching maculopapular rash has appeared on her trunk and is spreading to her neck. She has no mouth ulcers, red eyes or cough.

Which diagnosis best fits this sequence?
column5:
1. Hand-foot-and-mouth disease
  2. Roseola infantum
  3. Kawasaki disease
  4. Rubella infection
  5. Measles infection
  6. Parvovirus B19 infection
  7. Varicella infection
  8. Scarlet fever
column7: Correct. Three to five days of high fever in a child who stays fairly well, then a pink trunk rash as the fever settles and the child brightens, is roseola (human herpesvirus 6). HHV-6 is a common cause of febrile seizures at this age. A rash that comes after the fever, not with it, separates roseola from measles and rubella.

Aisha, 3, has moderate eczema that flares every few weeks. Her parents wonder whether foods are making it worse, so a specific IgE blood test was ordered: it is positive for cow's milk, hen's egg, wheat, soy and peanut. She drinks milk and eats eggs, bread and soy yoghurt most days, with no hives, vomiting or wheeze after them. She has never eaten peanut or any other nut. Her parents ask what to change.

What is the most appropriate advice?
column5:
1. Avoid all five foods until an allergist has seen her
  2. Keep the four foods; start peanut at home this week
  3. Stop milk and egg, the likeliest drivers of her eczema
  4. Repeat the tests by skin prick, then decide on the diet
  5. Keep the four foods; peanut after specialist review
column6: Keep the four foods; peanut after specialist review
column7: Correct. Foods she eats regularly without a reaction stay in her diet, whatever the test shows. Peanut, never eaten and with a positive test, needs specialist assessment, which may include a supervised food challenge, before it is given.

At 2 years he had a neck lymph node abscess that needed drainage twice and grew Staphylococcus aureus, and at 4 years a pneumonia caused by Burkholderia cepacia complex. Between infections he is well and thriving, with height and weight on the 25th centile and normal development. His full blood count, including the neutrophil count, is normal.

Which diagnosis best accounts for his infections?
column5:
1. Severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID)
  2. X-linked agammaglobulinaemia (XLA)
  3. Leucocyte adhesion deficiency (LAD)
  4. Chronic granulomatous disease (CGD)
  5. Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome (WAS)
column7: Correct. Neutrophils engulf but cannot kill because NADPH oxidase is defective: staphylococcal abscesses, Burkholderia and invasive Aspergillus in a well-grown child. A DHR or NBT test of neutrophil oxidase activity is the next step.
