column4:
A 7-year-old boy was admitted yesterday with fever and red, swollen left eyelids after a week-long cold. On admission his eye movements were full and painless, and IV antibiotics were started. Twenty-four hours later his temperature has fallen from 39.2 °C to 38.1 °C and the lid swelling looks no worse, but he now says it hurts to look to the left and he sees double at the extremes of gaze. The left eye looks slightly more prominent than the right. Visual acuity is 6/9 on the left and 6/6 on the right.

What is the most appropriate next step?
column5:
1. Contrast CT of the orbits and sinuses now
  2. Continue IV antibiotics, as the fever is settling
  3. Change to oral antibiotics, as the lids are no worse
  4. Ultrasound of the orbit to look for an abscess
  5. CT only if not improving after 48 hours of IV antibiotics
column6: Contrast CT of the orbits and sinuses now
column7: Correct. New pain on eye movement, diplopia, proptosis and reduced acuity mean the infection has spread behind the orbital septum. Contrast-enhanced CT of the orbits and sinuses looks for a subperiosteal or orbital abscess that may need drainage, and ophthalmology and ENT should review him today.

A 5-month-old boy has had fever for 7 days and has been irritable throughout. Blood and urine cultures taken 3 days ago are negative, and he is still febrile despite IV ceftriaxone. His eyes are red without discharge and his lips are red, but he has no rash, no swelling of his hands or feet and no enlarged neck nodes. He has no cough or runny nose.

| Test | Result | Reference range |
| --- | --- | --- |
| CRP | 142 mg/L | < 5 |
| Haemoglobin | 92 g/L | 100–140 |
| White cells | 19.5 × 10⁹/L | 6–17.5 |
| Platelets | 610 × 10⁹/L | 150–450 |
| Albumin | 27 g/L | 35–50 |
| ALT | 72 U/L | < 40 |
| Urine microscopy | 30 white cells/µL, culture no growth | < 10 white cells/µL |

Which diagnosis best fits his illness?
column5:
1. Partially treated urinary tract infection
  2. Roseola infantum
  3. Rubella
  4. Scarlet fever
  5. Hand-foot-and-mouth disease
  6. Kawasaki disease
  7. Measles
  8. Parvovirus B19 infection
column7: Correct. Infants under 6 months often have incomplete Kawasaki disease, with fewer than four principal features, and they have the highest risk of coronary artery aneurysms. Fever for 5 days or more with two principal features (non-purulent conjunctival injection and red lips), a raised CRP and several supporting results (anaemia, low albumin, raised ALT, a high white cell count, thrombocytosis after day 7 and sterile pyuria) fits incomplete Kawasaki disease. He needs echocardiography and treatment with IV immunoglobulin.

She is too frightened to lie down. Her airway is secured by an anaesthetist in theatre, and her blood culture becomes positive the next day.

Which organism is most likely?
column5:

  3. Group B streptococcus
  4. Staphylococcus aureus
  5. Streptococcus pneumoniae
  6. Neisseria meningitidis

column7: Correct. Abrupt fever, drooling, a muffled voice, soft stridor, a tripod posture and no cough are epiglottitis, and in an unvaccinated child the cause is Haemophilus influenzae type b, a Gram-negative coccobacillus that caused over 95% of cases before vaccination.

A 5-year-old girl has had fever and a sore throat for 2 days. Today a fine, red, blanching rash appeared on her neck and chest and spread to her trunk; it feels rough and is most marked in her elbow creases and groin. Her tongue is red with prominent papillae, her lips are red, and there is a tender 1.5 cm node below the angle of her jaw. Her tonsils are swollen and covered with exudate. Her eyes are not red, and her hands and feet are normal.

Which diagnosis is most likely?
column5:
1. Partially treated urinary tract infection
  2. Roseola infantum
  3. Rubella
  4. Scarlet fever
  5. Hand-foot-and-mouth disease
  6. Kawasaki disease
  7. Measles
  8. Parvovirus B19 infection
column7: Correct. Exudative tonsillitis with a fine, rough rash accentuated in the skin creases after 1 to 2 days of fever is scarlet fever from group A streptococcus. The red tongue, red lips and neck node overlap with Kawasaki disease, but the exudate, the rough flexural rash, the clear eyes and only 2 days of fever point to scarlet fever. A throat swab confirms it, and it is treated with penicillin.

  7. Developmental dysplasia of the hip

A 7-year-old boy has had colicky abdominal pain for 2 days and this morning passed a stool containing dark blood. He had a cold a week ago. Today raised, non-blanching spots have appeared on both legs and ankles, and his ankles are swollen and tender. His temperature is 37.8 °C, and he is alert and well perfused, with no mucosal bleeding. Blood pressure is normal. Urinalysis shows blood and protein.

| Test | Result | Reference range |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Haemoglobin | 122 g/L | 115–155 |
| Platelets | 310 × 10⁹/L | 150–450 |
| Creatinine | 38 µmol/L | 25–60 |
| Blood film | No fragmented red cells | No fragmentation |
| PT and APTT | Normal | — |

Which diagnosis best unifies these findings?
column5:
1. Haemolytic uraemic syndrome after a bloody stool
  2. Meningococcal septicaemia with early purpura
  3. IgA small-vessel vasculitis after his cold
  4. Immune thrombocytopenia with a gut bleed
  5. Acute post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis
column6: IgA small-vessel vasculitis after his cold
column7: Correct. Palpable purpura on the legs with normal platelets and clotting, arthritis, colicky abdominal pain with gut bleeding, and blood and protein in the urine after a respiratory infection is IgA vasculitis (Henoch–Schönlein purpura). The abdominal pain can come before the rash. Intussusception is the main gut complication to watch for, and urine and blood pressure are monitored for 6 to 12 months for nephritis.

column4:
A 46-year-old woman has had migraine with aura since her teens. Nine hours ago, while lifting a heavy box, she developed a severe occipital headache that reached maximum intensity within seconds. She says it is unlike her migraines; she vomited and briefly collapsed. She is now alert with no focal deficit and mild neck stiffness. A non-contrast CT brain performed now, 9 hours after onset, is reported as normal. She would like to go home with her usual triptan.

What is the most appropriate next step?
column5:
1. Discharge with her triptan, as the CT is normal
  2. Outpatient MRI brain within the next week
  3. Lumbar puncture at least 12 hours from onset
  4. Repeat non-contrast CT the next morning

column4:
A 4-day-old baby has bilateral eyelid swelling and thick, copious purulent discharge that began yesterday and has worsened rapidly; the conjunctivae are markedly swollen. She is afebrile and feeding well. Her mother had no antenatal screening. Conjunctival swabs for Gram stain, culture and PCR have been sent, and results are pending.

Which cause is most likely?
column5:
1. Staphylococcus aureus
  2. Allergic conjunctivitis
  3. Adenovirus infection
  4. Chlamydia trachomatis
  5. Neisseria gonorrhoeae
  6. Nasolacrimal duct obstruction
  7. Herpes simplex virus
  8. Chemical conjunctivitis
column7: Correct. Rapidly worsening, copious purulent discharge with marked chemosis starting in the first days of life is gonococcal ophthalmia until proven otherwise. It can perforate the cornea, so it needs admission and systemic treatment while results are pending.

column5:
1. Keep it: on the tooth surface it slows acid loss and aids repair

column5:

  2. Serum bilirubin with a blood count, blood group and antiglobulin test

column5:

  3. Formal cognitive testing for a specific learning disorder
  4. A repeat classroom rating scale from a second teacher

A GP assesses an 8-year-old referred for new classroom inattention and irritability. Similar difficulties occur at home, but earlier school reports show good concentration. His parent describes loud nightly snoring, pauses followed by gasping, restless sleep and morning headaches. He often falls asleep in the car. There is no current medication or sustained mood syndrome.

Which assessment should take priority before considering an ADHD medicine?
column5:
1. A trial of methylphenidate to see whether attention improves
  2. Parent and teacher rating scales repeated in three months
  3. Paediatric sleep and ENT review, with a sleep study if needed
  4. Keep a sleep diary for a fortnight before deciding about referral
  5. Hearing and vision screening, then reassess his attention
column6: Paediatric sleep and ENT review, with a sleep study if needed
column7: Snoring with witnessed pauses, gasping, morning headaches and daytime sleepiness suggest sleep-disordered breathing, which can itself cause inattention and irritability. Sleep and ENT assessment should come before an ADHD medicine.

column4:
A 52-year-old man had panic disorder in his twenties that resolved with CBT. Over the past month he has had spells of pounding heartbeat and breathlessness, and he asks his GP whether the panic attacks have come back. He has also lost 3 kg without trying and has a fine tremor of his outstretched hands. Today he feels anxious but comfortable; blood pressure is 128/80 mmHg. His radial pulse is 106/min and irregular, with no pattern to the beats. He has no chest pain, fever or goitre.

What should the GP do first?
column5:
1. Request thyroid function tests and act on them before any cardiac test
  2. Start propranolol, which treats both the tremor and the fast pulse
  3. Send him to the emergency department by ambulance
  4. Record a 12-lead ECG during this consultation
  5. Book a 24-hour Holter monitor for next week
column6: Record a 12-lead ECG during this consultation
column7: The pulse is irregular now, so a 12-lead ECG in the consultation can capture and confirm the rhythm immediately. Thyroid tests, stroke-risk assessment and other work-up follow.

His partner found him unresponsive and paramedics gave intramuscular naloxone twice. Thirty minutes later in the emergency department he is restless and vomiting, with sweating, yawning, a runny nose, gooseflesh and dilated pupils.

| Observation | Result |
|---|---|
| Heart rate | 108/min |
| Respiratory rate | 18/min |
| Oxygen saturation | 97% |

His skin is moist, reflexes are normal with no clonus, and he is fully oriented. He wants to leave.

Which interpretation and plan are most appropriate?
column5:
1. Methamphetamine intoxication; sedate him before he can leave
  2. Precipitated opioid withdrawal; keep him for prolonged observation
  3. Serotonin toxicity; give cyproheptadine and observe for an hour
  4. Opioid withdrawal; he may leave once the vomiting has settled
  5. Anticholinergic toxicity; monitor him for urinary retention
column6: Precipitated opioid withdrawal; keep him for prolonged observation
column7: Naloxone has precipitated opioid withdrawal, but its effect lasts well under the duration of methadone. As it wears off he may become sedated and stop breathing again, so he needs prolonged observation, not discharge.

column4:
A 52-year-old who drinks heavily every evening had an elective knee replacement yesterday morning; his last drink was at 8 pm the evening before surgery. At 10 am today he develops a tremor, sweating, anxiety and nausea.

| Observation | Result |
|---|---|
| Pulse | 112/min |
| Blood pressure | 156/94 mmHg |
| Temperature | 37.6 °C |

He rates his knee pain 2/10 at rest. He is fully oriented, can say the months backwards and reports no hallucinations. Capillary glucose is 6.4 mmol/L and the wound is clean.

Which explanation best fits the change?
column5:
1. Alcohol withdrawal
  2. Early postoperative sepsis
  3. Alcohol withdrawal delirium
  4. Inadequate postoperative analgesia
  5. Wernicke encephalopathy
column7: Tremor, sweating, anxiety, nausea and autonomic arousal about 38 hours after the last drink in a habitual heavy drinker fit alcohol withdrawal. A low-grade temperature is common after surgery and in withdrawal, and intact attention excludes delirium.

A GP conducts a planned review of a 43-year-old woman with bipolar disorder who has been stable on lithium for two years. Her lithium trough concentration is within her agreed target, but no other monitoring blood tests have been done for a year. She has no new symptoms, and her weight is unchanged.

Which group of tests is most important to arrange alongside ongoing lithium levels?
column5:
1. eGFR and full blood count
  2. TSH and fasting lipids
  3. eGFR, TSH and calcium
  4. eGFR, liver enzymes and ECG
  5. TSH, calcium and HbA1c
column7: Lithium can cause chronic kidney disease, hypothyroidism and hyperparathyroidism with hypercalcaemia. Kidney function, TSH and calcium are monitored with the lithium level, at least every six months.

A man with schizophrenia developed stiffness, tremor and slowed movement on haloperidol. After a supervised switch to aripiprazole at a dose that occupies most striatal D2 receptors, his psychosis remains controlled and the parkinsonism resolves.

Which property of aripiprazole at the D2 receptor best explains this combination?
column5:
1. Rapid dissociation that leaves most receptors unoccupied
  2. Blockade restricted to mesolimbic rather than striatal receptors
  3. Partial agonism that preserves low-level receptor stimulation
  4. Full agonism matching the intrinsic activity of dopamine
  5. Irreversible blockade with compensatory dopamine synthesis
column6: Partial agonism that preserves low-level receptor stimulation
column7: As a partial agonist, aripiprazole blocks excess dopamine signalling yet gives low-level stimulation of the receptors it occupies. That residual striatal activity limits parkinsonism despite high occupancy.

An emergency doctor assesses a 17-year-old girl, weight 50 kg, six hours after a witnessed single deliberate overdose of 10 g of immediate-release paracetamol taken all at once. She is medically stable, has had an initial safety assessment and is under observation. She has no abdominal pain and the initial ALT is normal. The laboratory will return a paracetamol concentration at seven hours after ingestion. A nurse suggests starting acetylcysteine straight away 'because it's already past four hours'.

What should guide the acetylcysteine decision?
column5:
1. A urine drug screen for other co-ingested substances
  2. A repeat ALT tomorrow morning before deciding
  3. Nothing further: start acetylcysteine now regardless
  4. The paracetamol level plotted on the nomogram
  5. An INR and liver function tests for liver injury
column6: The paracetamol level plotted on the nomogram
column7: After a single immediate-release ingestion at a known time, a level taken from four hours onwards is plotted on the nomogram. When it will be available within eight hours of ingestion, it decides whether acetylcysteine is needed.

A 24-year-old who smoked cannabis every night for three years stopped five days ago before starting a new job. She is irritable and anxious, has little appetite, and lies awake for hours despite feeling exhausted, with vivid dreams when she does sleep. She feels ‘flat’ and has cried twice this week, but enjoyed a friend’s birthday dinner on Saturday. She had a depressive episode two years ago. She has not felt elevated or needed less sleep, and uses no alcohol or other drugs.

Which explanation best fits?
column5:
1. Recurrent major depressive episode
  2. Hypomanic episode
  3. Cannabis withdrawal syndrome
  4. Generalised anxiety disorder
  5. Chronic insomnia disorder
column7: Irritability, anxiety, poor appetite, insomnia and vivid dreams beginning within days of stopping daily cannabis are cannabis withdrawal, which usually peaks in the first week and settles over one to two weeks.

Which blood tests are needed to establish his metabolic baseline?

1. Prolactin and lipids
  2. HbA1c and thyroid function
  3. Liver enzymes and fasting insulin
  4. Glucose or HbA1c, and lipids
  5. Glucose and full blood count
column7: Olanzapine carries a high risk of weight gain, dyslipidaemia and diabetes. Baseline glucose or HbA1c and a lipid profile, alongside weight, waist and blood pressure, allow change to be detected.

A 48-year-old taking sertraline and regular oxycodone for back pain could not fill her oxycodone prescription and has had none for 30 hours. Her sertraline dose was increased last week. She is restless and sweaty, with pulse 112/min and dilated pupils. She is yawning, with watery eyes, a runny nose, gooseflesh and cramping diarrhoea. Temperature is 37.2°C, reflexes are normal and there is no clonus.

What best explains this presentation?
column5:
1. Opioid withdrawal after the oxycodone ran out
  2. Anticholinergic toxicity from a new medicine
  3. Gastroenteritis with dehydration and anxiety
  4. Serotonin toxicity after the sertraline increase
  5. Sympathomimetic toxicity from a decongestant
column6: Opioid withdrawal after the oxycodone ran out
column7: Yawning, lacrimation, rhinorrhoea, piloerection, mydriasis and diarrhoea beginning a day after regular oxycodone stopped is opioid withdrawal. Normal reflexes and absent clonus argue against serotonin toxicity.

A 39-year-old woman has been well on venlafaxine for nine months. She returned yesterday from a five-day trip on which her tablets were in a lost suitcase. From the second day away she had dizziness made worse by turning her head, nausea, irritability, insomnia with vivid dreams, aching muscles and two tearful evenings. On day 3 she took tramadol for a back strain. She still enjoys seeing friends and has no pervasive low mood. Temperature is 37.2 °C; she has no tremor, clonus or hyperreflexia.

What best explains her symptoms?
column5:
1. Relapse of major depression
  2. Serotonin toxicity from tramadol
  3. Viral labyrinthitis
  4. Antidepressant withdrawal
  5. Recurrence of an anxiety disorder
column7: Dizziness, nausea, flu-like aches, sleep disturbance with vivid dreams, irritability and tearfulness beginning a day or two after stopping venlafaxine, a short half-life drug, is antidepressant withdrawal. Restarting her usual dose usually settles it quickly.

column4:
A 19-year-old man's parents bring him in because they fear he is depressed. For four days he has been irritable and anxious, has slept poorly with vivid dreams, has barely eaten, wakes in sweats and says nothing feels enjoyable. They believe depression is 'coming out' now that he has stopped 'self-medicating': he smoked cannabis every day for three years and stopped on the day he accepted a job that drug tests its staff. He starts the job next week and is worried about coping. Last year he had a similar 'flat week' while on a remote camping trip, which lifted when he got home. His mood was not persistently low before he started cannabis, and he has no suicidal thoughts or psychotic symptoms.

What is the most likely explanation?
column5:
1. Adjustment disorder with anxiety and depressed mood
  2. Generalised anxiety disorder
  3. Persistent depressive disorder unmasked by abstinence
  4. Cannabis withdrawal
  5. Major depressive episode
column7: Irritability, anxiety, poor sleep with vivid dreams, reduced appetite, low mood and sweating within a week of stopping daily cannabis is withdrawal, which usually settles over one to two weeks. The 'flat week' on a camping trip, away from his supply, was probably the same thing.

column4:
An old-age psychiatrist reviews a 74-year-old three months after effective treatment of a first depressive episode. Mood, sleep, appetite and motivation have returned to baseline, and he again enjoys company. His daughter still has to supervise bills and medicines because of repeated errors; the difficulties have progressed despite the mood improvement. Physical examination, medication review and initial blood tests have not identified another reversible cause.

What is the most appropriate next step?
column5:
1. Arrange comprehensive cognitive and functional assessment
  2. Increase antidepressant treatment for residual cognitive symptoms
  3. Attribute the ongoing cognitive impairment to the depressive episode
  4. Start donepezil for presumed Alzheimer disease
  5. Continue mood treatment and repeat cognition in six months
column6: Arrange comprehensive cognitive and functional assessment
column7: Persistent, progressive functional impairment after mood improvement warrants further assessment for a coexisting neurocognitive disorder. A depressive episode does not settle the cause of every cognitive symptom.

A 78-year-old admitted with a chest infection has become quiet and withdrawn. His daughter says he has been a little forgetful for a year but lived independently and was chatty until two days ago. He now answers slowly and says he “can’t be bothered”. Nursing entries record:

| Time | Observation |
| --- | --- |
| 09:00 | Drowsy; drifts off mid-sentence |
| 14:00 | More alert and recognises the ward, but loses track of questions |
| 22:00 | Says there are children at the end of the bed; cannot hold attention |

Which syndrome best accounts for this change?
column5:
1. Major depressive episode
  2. Progression of Alzheimer’s dementia
  3. Mild cognitive impairment
  4. Dementia with Lewy bodies
  5. Delirium, hypoactive type
column7: Acute onset over two days, fluctuating attention and arousal, drowsiness and perceptual disturbance during an infection are delirium; the quiet presentation is the hypoactive type, often mistaken for depression.

A woman who has taken clozapine for three years phones the clinic with painful mouth ulcers, a sore throat, chills and a temperature of 38.6 °C since yesterday. Her routine four-weekly full blood count, taken five days ago, was normal. She has stopped smoking since becoming unwell. She has no chest pain or breathlessness. The duty doctor arranges same-day medical assessment.

Which blood test is most time-critical because she takes clozapine?
column5:
1. Troponin and CRP to look for clozapine-induced myocarditis
  2. A clozapine level, as illness and stopping smoking raise it
  3. Liver function tests for clozapine-induced hepatitis
  4. Blood cultures before any other test is requested
  5. A full blood count with differential, though one was normal
column6: A full blood count with differential, though one was normal
column7: Fever, sore throat and mouth ulcers on clozapine need an urgent differential count regardless of a recent normal result, because severe neutropenia can develop between scheduled tests. The result determines whether clozapine is stopped and neutropenic sepsis treated.

  2. Insulin-mediated intracellular phosphate uptake
  3. Reduced phosphate absorption due to steatorrhoea
  4. Phosphate release from injured skeletal muscle

A GP reviews a woman taking oxycodone under one clinician’s supervision for persistent pain. A gradual dose increase had been needed to maintain the same effect, and missed doses cause sweating and diarrhoea. A careful review finds no loss of control, craving, hazardous use, continued use despite identified harm, or disruption of roles and relationships. She takes only the agreed doses.

What is the most accurate conclusion from this history?
column5:
1. Mild opioid use disorder, since tolerance and withdrawal make two criteria
  2. Opioid-induced hyperalgesia, shown by her need for dose increases
  3. Physical dependence from treatment, without opioid use disorder
  4. Iatrogenic addiction requiring prompt oxycodone cessation
  5. Opioid use disorder in early remission while doses are controlled
column6: Physical dependence from treatment, without opioid use disorder
column7: Tolerance and withdrawal during supervised treatment reflect physiological adaptation. Without impaired control, craving, harm or role disruption, she has physical dependence but not opioid use disorder.

| --- | --- | --- |
| Serum albumin | 16 g/L | 35–50 |
| Creatinine | 28 µmol/L | 20–45 |
| Urine protein:creatinine ratio | 950 mg/mmol | < 20 |
| C3 | 1.1 g/L | 0.9–1.8 |

column5:

column2: MCAT and USMLE::USMLE Step 2 CK::Reproductive and obstetric
column4:
A 45-year-old sees her GP about regular but very heavy periods over the past year, flooding on the first two days. She feels tired and has occasional hot flushes. A full blood count three months ago, taken when she first mentioned tiredness, was normal. Pregnancy has been excluded, there is no intermenstrual or postcoital bleeding, no history of easy bruising or bleeding and no thyroid symptoms, and pelvic examination is normal. She asks whether blood tests are needed again so soon.

Which blood tests should the GP arrange?
column5:
1. No tests now, since her blood count three months ago was normal
  2. FSH and oestradiol, to show the bleeding is from perimenopause
  3. A full blood count alone, adding ferritin if she proves anaemic
  4. Coagulation studies and a von Willebrand screen, as flow is heavy
  5. A full blood count and a serum ferritin to check her iron stores
column6: A full blood count and a serum ferritin to check her iron stores
column7: Heavy menstrual bleeding is routinely assessed for anaemia and iron deficiency with a full blood count and serum ferritin. Iron stores fall before haemoglobin does, and three more months of heavy loss have passed since the last count.

A 49-year-old presents with frequent small voids and intermittent urinary leakage. Over the past month she has also noticed hesitancy, a weak stream and a persistent feeling that she has not emptied her bladder. A completed three-day bladder diary confirms frequent low-volume voids. She is able to pass urine and has no pain, fever or visible haematuria. Urinalysis is normal; pelvic and focused neurological examinations reveal no abnormality.

Which investigation is most appropriate next?
column5:
1. Repeat the three-day bladder diary over a further week
  2. Flexible cystoscopy to inspect the bladder and urethra
  3. A standardised one-hour pad-weight test of leakage
  4. Multichannel pressure-flow urodynamic studies
  5. A bladder scan immediately after voiding
column6: A bladder scan immediately after voiding
column7: Hesitancy, weak stream and incomplete-emptying sensation suggest voiding dysfunction. Postvoid bladder ultrasound is an appropriate initial way to assess retained urine and is preferred to diagnostic catheterisation when available.

What is the next step?
column5:
1. Colposcopy now, as an oncogenic HPV type has been found
  2. Return to routine five-yearly screening, as cytology is normal
  3. Repeat cytology alone in six months, then colposcopy if abnormal
  4. Repeat HPV testing in three years, as her cytology is normal
  5. Repeat HPV testing in 12 months, without colposcopy now
column6: Repeat HPV testing in 12 months, without colposcopy now
column7: HPV (not 16/18) with negative cytology in an on-time, immunocompetent screener is followed with a repeat HPV test in 12 months, because many of these infections clear in that time.

A 30-year-old woman and her partner have been trying to conceive for 18 months. She has regular 28-day cycles, no pelvic pain and no history of PID, ectopic pregnancy or pelvic surgery. Her partner’s semen analysis and her routine pelvic ultrasound are normal. The fertility clinician now needs to assess whether her fallopian tubes are patent.

Which investigation is most appropriate from this list?
column5:
1. Laparoscopy and dye test, the reference standard for tubal patency
  2. Hysteroscopy, inspecting the tubal openings within the uterine cavity
  3. Transvaginal ultrasound with Doppler assessment of both adnexa
  4. Serum anti-Müllerian hormone, to judge her reproductive potential
  5. Hysterosalpingography, an outpatient X-ray test of tubal patency
column6: Hysterosalpingography, an outpatient X-ray test of tubal patency
column7: For a woman with no history or symptoms suggesting tubal disease, hysterosalpingography is an appropriate first-line test of tubal patency that avoids surgery.

His full blood count from a recent insurance medical showed haemoglobin 152 g/L and MCV 88 fL. The couple want to understand the risk to the baby before deciding about invasive fetal testing.

Which investigation should the GP arrange next?
column5:
1. No partner testing, because his normal MCV excludes a relevant trait

She had an episode of depression treated with an SSRI five years ago and has been well since. Between episodes she enjoys her baby, is feeding well and sleeps when her partner settles the baby. She has no hopelessness, thoughts of harm, confusion, unusual beliefs or reduced need for sleep.

  2. Early postpartum psychosis; arrange urgent psychiatric review
  3. Baby blues; offer support and review her mood within two weeks
  4. Adjustment to a first baby; no further mood follow-up is needed
  5. Postpartum thyroiditis; check thyroid function before deciding

An early-pregnancy registrar assesses a stable 28-year-old with light spotting and uncertain menstrual dates. Her first transvaginal scan shows an intrauterine gestational sac, yolk sac and embryo with a crown–rump length of 5.5 mm. No cardiac activity is detected. She has no pain or heavy bleeding and wishes to continue the pregnancy if viable.

Which plan best establishes viability without prematurely diagnosing miscarriage?
column5:
1. Repeat transvaginal ultrasound in 48 hours and diagnose loss if unchanged
  2. Repeat transvaginal ultrasound after at least seven days
  3. Diagnose miscarriage now, as the CRL exceeds 5 mm without cardiac activity
  4. Measure serum hCG twice, 48 hours apart, to establish viability
  5. Arrange a second-sonographer scan today to confirm the loss
column6: Repeat transvaginal ultrasound after at least seven days
column7: With a crown–rump length below 7 mm and no cardiac activity on a first scan, a repeat scan at least seven days later is needed before miscarriage can be diagnosed.

A 30-year-old at 34 weeks, whose booking blood pressure was 112/70 mmHg, has readings of 152/98 and 150/96 mmHg four hours apart. She has new swelling of her hands and face and has gained 2 kg this week. She has no headache, visual symptoms or epigastric pain. Urine dipstick shows 1+ protein, but the protein:creatinine ratio is 16 mg/mmol (significant ≥30). Uric acid is raised.

| Measurement | Result | Previous result |
|---|---|---|
| Creatinine | 104 µmol/L | 58 at booking |
| Platelets | 212 × 10^9/L | — |
| ALT | 24 U/L | — |

Which diagnosis best accounts for these findings?
column5:
1. Gestational hypertension, as the protein:creatinine ratio is below 30
  2. Chronic kidney disease unmasked by the demands of pregnancy
  3. Pre-eclampsia, with renal involvement shown by the creatinine
  4. HELLP syndrome evolving from gestational hypertension
  5. Chronic hypertension first detected in the third trimester
column6: Pre-eclampsia, with renal involvement shown by the creatinine
column7: A creatinine above 90 µmol/L with new hypertension after 20 weeks counts as renal involvement, so this is pre-eclampsia despite a normal protein:creatinine ratio. Oedema, weight gain, uric acid and a 1+ dipstick are not criteria.

Transvaginal ultrasound shows neither an intrauterine nor an adnexal pregnancy and no free fluid. Serum hCG was 650 IU/L at presentation and is 720 IU/L 48 hours later.

How should the clinician classify and manage this pregnancy at present?

  2. Tubal ectopic pregnancy, so methotrexate can be started today
  3. Probable viable intrauterine pregnancy, so rescan in two weeks
  4. Failed pregnancy, so she can be discharged without hCG follow-up
  5. Pregnancy of unknown location, with review and repeat hCG and scan

column7: With no pregnancy seen on ultrasound, this remains a pregnancy of unknown location. The plateauing hCG makes a failing or ectopic pregnancy likely, so she needs senior review within 24 hours, repeat hCG and ultrasound, and clear advice to return with pain or bleeding.

Her blood pressure at booking and on arrival was normal and urinalysis showed no protein. She develops oozing from cannula sites. Results:

| Test | Result | Laboratory reference range |
|---|---:|---|
| Platelets | 58 × 10⁹/L | 150–400 × 10⁹/L |
| Prothrombin time | 23 seconds | 11–14 seconds |
| Fibrinogen | 0.8 g/L | 2.0–4.0 g/L, non-pregnant |

  3. Gestational thrombocytopenia unmasked by the haemorrhage
  4. HELLP syndrome presenting without hypertension or proteinuria
  5. Immune thrombocytopenia with bleeding from the abruption
column6: Disseminated intravascular coagulation from the abruption
column7: Very low fibrinogen, prolonged prothrombin time and low platelets with oozing after a major abruption indicate consumptive coagulopathy.

There is a single 3.5 cm node there, tender and warm, with red overlying skin; it is firm, with no fluctuance. Small, soft, non-tender nodes are felt on both sides of his neck. He has no weight loss, night sweats or hepatosplenomegaly.

column5:
1. Thyroid enlargement
  2. Reactive viral lymphadenopathy
  3. Acute bacterial lymphadenitis
  4. Branchial cleft cyst
  5. Dermoid cyst
  6. Cystic lymphatic malformation

column4:
A 5-week-old boy was seen by his GP at 3 weeks with small vomits after feeds, and reflux was diagnosed. Since then the vomits have become larger and more forceful and now follow most feeds. They are milky, never green, and he seems hungry straight afterwards. He has lost 150 g since his last weigh-in and has fewer wet nappies. His abdomen is soft and not distended, and no mass is felt during a test feed. A venous gas shows:

| Observation | Result |
|---|---|
| pH | 7.48 |
| Chloride | 94 mmol/L |
| Bicarbonate | 31 mmol/L |

What is the most appropriate next investigation?
column5:
1. None yet: thickened feeds for a week, imaging if vomiting persists
  2. Upper GI contrast study, as no pyloric mass can be felt
  3. Plain abdominal radiograph for a single large gastric bubble
  4. Repeat test feed by a surgeon, imaging only if a mass is felt
  5. Abdominal ultrasound of the pylorus, without waiting for a mass
column6: Abdominal ultrasound of the pylorus, without waiting for a mass
column7: Correct. Progressive, forceful non-bilious vomiting at 3 to 6 weeks, weight loss and a hypochloraemic metabolic alkalosis point to pyloric stenosis even without a palpable mass and despite the earlier diagnosis of reflux. Ultrasound of the pyloric muscle confirms it. The dehydration and alkalosis are corrected with IV fluids before surgery.

column4: After starting folic acid alone, a patient's hemoglobin improves but gait and vibration sense worsen. What should the clinician do about possible B12 deficiency?
column6: Evaluate urgently and start B12 replacement promptly when clinical suspicion is high.
column7: Hematologic improvement does not establish recovery of the nervous system. Draw helpful tests first if this will not delay treatment.

column4: During planned advancement of parenteral feeding, phosphate drops markedly and the patient develops weakness. What should happen to the planned calorie increase?
column6: Defer the increase, urgently assess and correct the disturbance, and reassess the feeding prescription.
column7: Provide necessary electrolytes and vitamin support with close monitoring. The existing rate may also need reduction depending on severity.

column2: MCAT and USMLE::USMLE Step 3::Advanced Clinical Medicine
column4: In a severely malnourished adult starting parenteral nutrition, what should guide advancement beyond the initial prescription?
column6: Clinical tolerance, fluid status and serial electrolyte and glucose measurements.
column7: Individualized monitoring is especially important early in refeeding.
column8: NICE CG32, Nutrition Support for Adults, Recommendations · https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg32/chapter/recommendations

column4: After cautious initiation, a high-risk patient's phosphate, potassium, magnesium, glucose and fluid balance remain stable and they tolerate the regimen. How should energy delivery progress?
column6: Advance gradually toward the individualized target with continued monitoring.
column7: A stable response allows progression; it does not remove the need to monitor during subsequent increases.
column8: NICE CG32, Nutrition Support for Adults, Recommendations · https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg32/chapter/recommendations

column4: An adult recovering from diet-related pellagra plans to return to the same low-protein diet that preceded treatment. Besides replacing niacin now, what dietary problem merits correction?
column6: Inadequate sustained intake of niacin and tryptophan-rich protein foods.
column7: Correcting the underlying intake problem reduces recurrence after repletion.
column8: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements, Niacin · https://ods.od.nih.gov/factsheets/Niacin-HealthProfessional/

column4: Why does adequate dietary protein contribute to prevention of pellagra in addition to niacin-containing foods?
column6: Tryptophan can be converted to niacin equivalents.
column7: Low intake of both niacin and tryptophan raises the risk of deficiency.
column8: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements, Niacin · https://ods.od.nih.gov/factsheets/Niacin-HealthProfessional/

column2: MCAT and USMLE::USMLE Step 3::Advanced Clinical Medicine
column4: A patient with a serotonin-producing neuroendocrine tumor develops pellagra despite access to protein foods. Why might dietary availability alone fail to explain the deficiency?
column6: Tryptophan is diverted toward serotonin production, reducing substrate for niacin synthesis.
column7: Treat the deficiency and address the underlying tumor syndrome.
column8: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements, Niacin · https://ods.od.nih.gov/factsheets/Niacin-HealthProfessional/

column2: MCAT and USMLE::USMLE Step 3::Advanced Clinical Medicine
column4: An adult at dietary risk avoids animal foods, eats few vegetables and has normal fat absorption. Which familiar plant foods could provide provitamin A in a long-term prevention plan?
column6: Orange vegetables or dark-green leafy vegetables, such as carrots or spinach.
column7: These supply carotenoids that can be converted to vitamin A. Clinical deficiency requires appropriate treatment as well.

column4: Why can cholestasis increase the risk of vitamin A deficiency even when the diet contains enough of the vitamin?
column6: Reduced intestinal bile availability impairs absorption of fat and fat-soluble vitamins.
column7: Dietary intake and intestinal uptake are separate parts of the assessment.
column8: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements, Vitamin A and Carotenoids · https://ods.od.nih.gov/factsheets/VitaminA-HealthProfessional/

column4: An adult with cholestatic disease and steatorrhea remains vitamin A deficient despite adequate intake. Which factor must a treatment plan address beyond the food list?
column6: Persistent fat malabsorption and the adequacy of the replacement regimen.
column7: Review response and coordinate specialist-guided replacement. Simply repeating dietary advice does not correct impaired uptake.
column8: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements, Vitamin A and Carotenoids · https://ods.od.nih.gov/factsheets/VitaminA-HealthProfessional/

column4: A patient treated for scurvy has no cold storage but can obtain a shelf-stable fruit product that lists vitamin C. What should guide whether it can contribute enough over time?
column6: The vitamin C per usual portion and how regularly the patient can consume it.
column7: Storage constraints change which sources are practical. Plan a sustainable source alongside prescribed repletion.

column4: After initial replacement for scurvy, what history best guides recurrence prevention?
column6: Which vitamin-C-containing foods the patient can reliably obtain, tolerate and eat.
column7: Short-term replacement treats the deficiency. The longer-term plan must address the cause.

column4: A child treated for scurvy continues to exclude all vitamin-C-containing foods because of severe sensory restriction. Is giving a list of citrus foods an adequate maintenance plan?

column7: Maintaining intake may require coordinated nutritional and behavioral care.

column4: In suspected acute Wernicke encephalopathy, why is a routine oral multivitamin alone inadequate initial therapy?
column6: Urgent therapeutic thiamine must be delivered reliably, usually parenterally.
column7: An oral maintenance dose cannot be relied on for acute neurologic treatment.

column6: Ensure sustained thiamine intake with appropriate oral supplementation and correction of the underlying intake problem.
column7: Maintenance planning differs from the urgent parenteral phase. Tailor it to the cause and follow-up.

column7: Symptoms during continued exposure do not establish refractory disease.

column2: MCAT and USMLE::USMLE Step 3::Foundations of Independent Practice

column4: Adherence depends on baseline health. The investigators compare only adherent intervention patients with all controls. Why can this break the randomized comparison?

column8: Cochrane Handbook chapter 8 · https://www.cochrane.org/authors/handbooks-and-manuals/handbook/current/chapter-08 · randomization, deviations, measurement and missing outcomes

column2: MCAT and USMLE::USMLE Step 3::Foundations of Independent Practice
column4: A local public health advisory lists a potential exposure, affected dates and a callback number. What information makes its message actionable to a patient?

column7: State where to obtain help and how updates will be communicated.
column8: CDC, Updated Guidelines for Evaluating Public Health Surveillance Systems · https://stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/248461 · purpose, completeness and timeliness of reporting

column2: MCAT and USMLE::USMLE Step 3::Foundations of Independent Practice
column4: The share of residents over 80 rises while age-specific dementia prevalence stays constant and total population stays fixed. Why might total demand for memory care still rise?

column7: Service counts depend on population composition as well as stratum-specific disease risk.

column4: Recruiters know the full computer-generated assignment list. What design change protects a future trial against selective enrollment?

column2: MCAT and USMLE::USMLE Step 3::Foundations of Independent Practice
column4: A committee proposes lowering alpha from 0.05 to 0.01 without changing sample size, effect or test. What is the usual tradeoff?

column8: ICH E9 · https://database.ich.org/sites/default/files/E9_Guideline.pdf · sections 3 and 5, trial size, estimation, multiplicity and subgroups

column2: MCAT and USMLE::USMLE Step 3::Foundations of Independent Practice
column4: A cafeteria report divides ill salad eaters by everyone in the building, including non-diners. Which denominator should estimate the salad-specific attack proportion?
column6: All at-risk people who actually ate the salad during the relevant meal.
column7: Use the corresponding exposed and unexposed denominators for the comparison.
column8: CDC, Principles of Epidemiology · https://archive.cdc.gov/www_cdc_gov/csels/dsepd/ss1978/lesson3/ · measures of frequency, association and public health impact

column2: MCAT and USMLE::USMLE Step 3::Foundations of Independent Practice
column4: A report says that 60% of cases among exposed people are attributable to a causal exposure. Can the same fraction be quoted for the whole community?
column6: No. Community impact also depends on how common the exposure is.
column7: The population attributable fraction has all population cases as its denominator.
column8: CDC Field Epidemiology Manual · https://www.cdc.gov/field-epi-manual/php/chapters/analyze-interpret-data.html · risk, rates and interpreting comparisons

column2: MCAT and USMLE::USMLE Step 3::Foundations of Independent Practice
column4: Pretest odds of disease are 1:4. A negative result has LR− 0.25. What is the posttest probability?
column7: Posttest odds are (1/4) × (1/4) = 1/16. Probability is odds divided by one plus odds.
column8: AHRQ, Test Performance Metrics · https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/sites/books/NBK98249/ · predictive values, likelihood ratios and ROC curves

column2: MCAT and USMLE::USMLE Step 3::Foundations of Independent Practice
column4: Which quantity do you multiply by a likelihood ratio to update a patient's disease probability?
column7: Convert the resulting posttest odds to probability when counseling the patient.
column8: AHRQ, Test Performance Metrics · https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/sites/books/NBK98249/ · predictive values, likelihood ratios and ROC curves

column2: MCAT and USMLE::USMLE Step 3::Foundations of Independent Practice
column4: A patient has a pretest probability of 80%. A negative result has LR− 0.5. Is the posttest probability now below a 10% rule-out threshold?
column7: Pretest odds 4 become posttest odds 2, corresponding to probability 2/3. A weak negative result leaves substantial risk.
column8: AHRQ, Test Performance Metrics · https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/sites/books/NBK98249/ · predictive values, likelihood ratios and ROC curves

column2: MCAT and USMLE::USMLE Step 3::Foundations of Independent Practice
column4: A stroke program reduces long-term disability without changing survival. Which population summary can register that benefit even if life expectancy stays fixed?
column6: Healthy life expectancy or another disability-sensitive measure.
column7: Survival alone misses years lived with impairment. A reduction in disability can also reduce DALYs lost.
column8: WHO Global Health Observatory · https://www.who.int/data/gho/data/indicators/indicator-details/GHO/gho-ghe-hale-healthy-life-expectancy · healthy life expectancy

column2: MCAT and USMLE::USMLE Step 3::Foundations of Independent Practice
column4: Several patients improve after a new therapy in an uncontrolled case series. Which next design would more directly test whether treatment caused improvement when randomization is feasible and ethical?
column6: A randomized trial with an appropriate concurrent comparator.
column7: A case series cannot separate treatment effects from natural recovery or selection.
column8: CDC Field Epidemiology Manual · https://www.cdc.gov/field-epi-manual/php/chapters/design-conduct-analyze-field-studies.html · sampling, study design and controls

column2: MCAT and USMLE::USMLE Step 3::Foundations of Independent Practice
column4: A study of low physical activity and pain is cross-sectional. What design change would help distinguish activity preceding pain from pain reducing activity?
column6: Measure activity before incident pain and follow an initially pain-free cohort.
column7: Establishing temporal order helps evaluate reverse causation. It does not by itself eliminate confounding.
column8: Penn State STAT 507 · https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat507/Lesson08 · confounding, bias, random error and effect modification

column2: MCAT and USMLE::USMLE Step 3::Foundations of Independent Practice
column4: A registry can identify nearly all new cases of an uncommon outcome, but following an entire disease-free population is impractical. Which efficient observational design samples by outcome status?
column6: A case-control study using controls from the source population.
column7: Define comparable opportunities for exposure ascertainment and avoid selecting controls because of exposure.
column8: CDC Field Epidemiology Manual · https://www.cdc.gov/field-epi-manual/php/chapters/design-conduct-analyze-field-studies.html · sampling, study design and controls

column2: MCAT and USMLE::USMLE Step 3::Foundations of Independent Practice
column4: What does a median answer about a patient's experience when costs are markedly skewed?
column6: It describes the middle individual cost.
column7: The mean, by contrast, is relevant when estimating total expenditure over a group.
column8: Penn State STAT 200 · https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat200/Lesson02 · distributions, location and variation

column2: MCAT and USMLE::USMLE Step 3::Foundations of Independent Practice
column4: A trial compares symptom-resolution status across two independent groups using a chi-square test. The p-value is 0.02. What additional result is needed to judge the magnitude of benefit?
column6: The group's event risks and an effect estimate with its confidence interval.
column7: The chi-square p-value alone gives neither direction nor clinical magnitude.
column8: NIST Engineering Statistics Handbook · https://www.itl.nist.gov/div898/handbook/ · tests for two means, contingency tables and confidence intervals

column2: MCAT and USMLE::USMLE Step 3::Foundations of Independent Practice
column4: A report calls all deaths before the first birthday neonatal deaths. Which age group must be removed for a neonatal mortality indicator?
column6: Deaths from 28 completed days of age up to the first birthday.
column7: Those are postneonatal infant deaths. Retain deaths before 28 completed days in the neonatal numerator.
column8: WHO · https://www.who.int/data/nutrition/nlis/info/under-five-mortality-rate · child survival indicators. Neonatal period · https://data.who.int/indicators/i/E3CAF2B/2322814

column2: MCAT and USMLE::USMLE Step 3::Foundations of Independent Practice
column4: A report says there is a 95% chance the fixed true effect lies in its observed frequentist 95% interval. What is the usual repeated-sampling interpretation?
column6: Under the model, about 95% of intervals built by this procedure would contain the true parameter.
column7: Coverage describes the procedure over repetitions.
column8: ICH E9 · https://database.ich.org/sites/default/files/E9_Guideline.pdf · sections 3 and 5, trial size, estimation, multiplicity and subgroups

column2: MCAT and USMLE::USMLE Step 3::Foundations of Independent Practice
column4: A trial has four times the sample size of another trial with the same design, event distribution and allocation. Approximately how does its standard error compare?
column7: For many independent-sample estimates, standard error scales as 1/√n. Increasing n cannot repair systematic bias.
column8: ICH E9 · https://database.ich.org/sites/default/files/E9_Guideline.pdf · sections 3 and 5, trial size, estimation, multiplicity and subgroups

column2: MCAT and USMLE::USMLE Step 3::Foundations of Independent Practice
column4: Which two quantities should be compared before calling an average treatment benefit clinically important?
column6: The estimated benefit with its uncertainty and the smallest difference important to patients.
column7: Interpret both in the same units over the same time horizon.
column8: Cochrane Handbook chapter 15 · https://www.cochrane.org/authors/handbooks-and-manuals/handbook/current/chapter-15 · absolute effects, applicability and implications for practice

column2: MCAT and USMLE::USMLE Step 3::Foundations of Independent Practice
column4: A trial estimates a 2.4-point mean improvement with 95% CI 0.4 to 4.4. The smallest worthwhile improvement is 2 points. How certain is a worthwhile average effect?
column6: The interval includes both subthreshold and worthwhile effects.
column7: It excludes zero, but the clinically relevant boundary is 2 points.
column8: Cochrane Handbook chapter 15 · https://www.cochrane.org/authors/handbooks-and-manuals/handbook/current/chapter-15 · absolute effects, applicability and implications for practice

column2: MCAT and USMLE::USMLE Step 3::Foundations of Independent Practice
column4: A very large trial estimates a 0.4-point pain improvement, 95% CI 0.3 to 0.5. Patients consider 2 points the smallest worthwhile benefit. How does the interval compare with that threshold?
column6: It excludes zero but also excludes an average benefit as large as the worthwhile threshold.
column7: A statistically detectable average difference may be too small to matter clinically.
column8: Cochrane Handbook chapter 15 · https://www.cochrane.org/authors/handbooks-and-manuals/handbook/current/chapter-15 · absolute effects, applicability and implications for practice

column2: MCAT and USMLE::USMLE Step 3::Foundations of Independent Practice
column4: A policy is randomized by nursing home but outcomes are measured in residents. What must the uncertainty estimate account for?
column7: Analyzing residents as independent usually understates uncertainty when outcomes within homes are positively correlated.
column8: Cochrane Handbook chapter 10 · https://www.cochrane.org/authors/handbooks-and-manuals/handbook/current/chapter-10 · forest plots, synthesis and heterogeneity

column2: MCAT and USMLE::USMLE Step 3::Foundations of Independent Practice
column4: Reports of a rare diagnosis triple after the local laboratory changes its test and reporting policy. What should be verified before declaring a new disease cluster?

column7: Use consistent case definitions, geography, time and population denominators.
column8: CDC, Updated Guidelines for Evaluating Public Health Surveillance Systems · https://stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/248461 · purpose, completeness and timeliness of reporting

column4: A closed historical roster lists exposed and unexposed workers, and subsequent outcomes can be ascertained for both. Which design permits direct estimation of risks by exposure?
column7: An exposure-defined roster supplies denominators that conventional case-control sampling does not.
column8: CDC Field Epidemiology Manual · https://www.cdc.gov/field-epi-manual/php/chapters/design-conduct-analyze-field-studies.html · sampling, study design and controls

column2: MCAT and USMLE::USMLE Step 3::Foundations of Independent Practice
column4: A patient with a previous negative population screen now reports unexplained bleeding from the organ that was screened. Should the next evaluation follow a routine screening interval or a diagnostic pathway?
column6: Use the diagnostic pathway for the current symptom.
column7: Screening intervals apply to asymptomatic populations. A new symptom changes the clinical question.
column8: FDA, Statistical Guidance on Reporting Results from Studies Evaluating Diagnostic Tests · https://www.fda.gov/regulatory-information/search-fda-guidance-documents/statistical-guidance-reporting-results-studies-evaluating-diagnostic-tests-guidance-industry-and-fda · reference standard and test interpretation

column2: MCAT and USMLE::USMLE Step 3::Foundations of Independent Practice
column4: Important new safety information emerges during a trial and might change whether participants wish to continue. What is the research team's obligation?

column7: Determine and follow the approved process for notification or re-consent.
column8: HHS, Protection of Human Subjects · https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-45/subtitle-A/subchapter-A/part-46/subpart-A · §§46.108, 46.111, 46.116, review, risk and consent

column2: MCAT and USMLE::USMLE Step 3::Foundations of Independent Practice
column4: A proposed lab method correlates almost perfectly with the reference method, but every value is systematically higher. Does this establish agreement sufficient for interchangeability?
column6: No. Assess differences between methods and their clinical acceptability.
column7: Correlation measures association. An offset can leave correlation high despite poor agreement.
column8: Bland and Altman, Agreement between two methods of clinical measurement · https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/2868172/ · differences versus means and limits of agreement

column2: MCAT and USMLE::USMLE Step 3::Foundations of Independent Practice
column4: A program reduces disability-weighted years by 80 with no change in years of life lost. What happens to DALYs lost, all else equal?

column8: WHO Global Health Estimates · https://cdn.who.int/media/docs/default-source/gho-documents/global-health-estimates/ghe2021_daly_methods.pdf · calculating burden in DALYs

column4: In the DPP, relative reductions in diabetes incidence were reported for lifestyle and metformin versus placebo. A clinic can offer a leaflet but no comparable lifestyle program. What limits using the trial's lifestyle result as its expected benefit?

column8: Diabetes Prevention Program Research Group, original randomized trial · https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa012512 · incidence by treatment group and three-year NNT. Figure redrawn from published aggregate data.

column4: Comparative data already strongly establish that one arm exposes the target group to serious harm with no compensating benefit. Can a signed consent document alone justify randomization to that arm?

column2: MCAT and USMLE::USMLE Step 3::Foundations of Independent Practice
column4: The forest plot shows one trial consistent with harm and another with clear benefit. What review decision should precede a single pooled recommendation?

column8: Cochrane Handbook chapter 10 · https://www.cochrane.org/authors/handbooks-and-manuals/handbook/current/chapter-10 · forest plots, synthesis and heterogeneity

column2: MCAT and USMLE::USMLE Step 3::Foundations of Independent Practice
column4: A review's funnel plot is asymmetric. What investigation can examine possible missing evidence without assuming the cause from the plot?

column4: A new therapy causes 12 serious adverse events per 1,000 treated versus 8 per 1,000 controls over two years. What is the two-year NNH?
column7: The excess risk is 4/1,000 = 0.004. Its reciprocal is 250.

column2: MCAT and USMLE::USMLE Step 3::Foundations of Independent Practice
column4: A hand-hygiene audit shows unusually strong performance only when a visible observer is present. How could the team check for reactivity to observation?

column7: Triangulate the measures while respecting staff and patient privacy.

column2: MCAT and USMLE::USMLE Step 3::Foundations of Independent Practice
column4: A county has high average vaccine coverage but one neighborhood has low coverage. Why can the county average overstate protection for susceptible residents there?

column2: MCAT and USMLE::USMLE Step 3::Foundations of Independent Practice
column4: Relative risks are 0.5 in both an 8%-risk and a 40%-risk group. Are their absolute risk reductions also equal?

column2: MCAT and USMLE::USMLE Step 3::Foundations of Independent Practice
column4: Survival curves cross and the estimated treatment hazard ratio changes markedly with time. What is the main limitation of quoting one constant hazard ratio?

column7: Inspect time-specific survival or other suitable summaries over clinically relevant intervals.

column2: MCAT and USMLE::USMLE Step 3::Foundations of Independent Practice
column4: In a community, one-year disease risk is 10%. Under removal of an established causal exposure, the estimated risk would be 6%. What fraction of all cases is attributable to the exposure?

column2: MCAT and USMLE::USMLE Step 3::Foundations of Independent Practice
column4: In a community the observed one-year risk is 6.5% and estimated risk without a causal exposure is 6%. Is more or less than 10% of all cases attributable to the exposure? Give the approximate fraction.
column7: (0.065 − 0.060)/0.065 ≈ 0.077. A smaller population risk difference changes the preventable fraction.
column8: CDC Field Epidemiology Manual · https://www.cdc.gov/field-epi-manual/php/chapters/analyze-interpret-data.html · risk, rates and interpreting comparisons

column2: MCAT and USMLE::USMLE Step 3::Foundations of Independent Practice
column4: To express the fraction of all population events preventable by removing a causal exposure, which risk is used in the denominator?
